should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has he had an invitation from the U.S.S.R. for an exchange of parliamentarians? What is the reaction of the government, and what are the circumstances under which the offer was made?
Hon L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs): I am grateful to the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of this question. It deals with a matter which I had
hoped to include in my remarks winding up the debate on external affairs. But in view of the fact that I might not have that opportunity today, and in view of the interest in this matter, possibly I could answer by reading a short statement concerning it.
Hon members have shown, of course, an understandable interest in the declaration of the Supreme Soviet of February 9. After making strong and grossly misleading attacks on the policies of this and allied governments, that declaration does include three paragraphs at the end on the desirability of direct contacts between parliaments throughout the world. Presumably, Mr. Speaker, that is the invitation to our parliament.
When news was first received from Moscow of this declaration by our ambassador in Moscow, it will be recalled that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in answer to a question, replied as follows:
The suggestion that has been reported will no doubt come to us in some more official manner than merely this report in the newspapers, and it will certainly be given careful consideration.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
I think the situation is such that we should all do our best to take advantage of any suggestion that might bring about an easing of the tension in the world.
The official text of the Soviet note to our embassy in Moscow on this subject and the declaration have both now been received and have been transmitted to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Speaker in another place for the information of members of parliament. And consideration is being given, I understand, as to how this matter can best be brought to the attention of those directly concerned.
So far as this government is concerned, it has been our constant view that there is a continuing need for contacts between the Soviet union and the non-communist world. It is not we who have lowered the iron curtain; and we would welcome opportunity, I am sure, for genuine, as distinguished from propaganda, contacts, between peoples and between their parliamentary representatives.
We could have wished, I think, Mr. Speaker, that the declaration in question might have been couched in language less reminiscent of the too-familiar propaganda line uttered by Soviet representatives at official conferences, and disseminated through their less official channels outside, and that it had not been approved by the Supreme Soviet so quickly,

Inquiries of the Ministry with customary unanimity, and in the shadow of Mr. Molotov's speech on foreign affairs of the same date which dwelt on the need for Soviet policy to take into account what he called significant contradictions both between individual capitalist countries and within these countries. So, having regard to the background of this declaration, of which this invitation is a part, there is need for us, I think, to be cautious, but not necessarily to turn a deaf ear to the suggestion which has been advanced.
I am not convinced, myself, by the argument that the propaganda intentions of the Soviet government, their unending lack of cordiality with the West in so many spheres of our relations and the lack of deeds to support their protestations of friendship, means that Western countries should not respond at all to gestures of this kind. The implications of such an argument as that might be that we should take no initiative to improve relations, because the Soviets would interpret it as a sign of weakness and would speak of a further communist victory.
There is, therefore, as I see it, much to be said for giving serious consideration to invitations of this kind, whatever their background may be, and there is certainly a good deal to be said for visits by Canadian parliamentarians to the Soviet union either individually or as a group in response to invitations which would be of a kind to make the visit worth while.
It might also I think be valuable to receive Soviet parliamentarians in this country-* which is, of course, not the same thing as inviting members of a visiting delegation to participate in the deliberations of the House of Commons. Nor-and I think it is only fair to add this-has the word "parliamentarian" the same meaning in Moscow as it has in Ottawa, especially in relation to the opposition.
If and when such visits took place, I think we should never neglect, nor would we wish to neglect, any opportunity to create the conditions which might lead to a better understanding between peoples. In a world living under the shadow of the hydrogen bomb, it is of course essential that such an understanding be reached. And that is only possible if one side succeeds in convincing the other that they are not bent on mutual destruction.
And so, if no obstacles were put in the way of holding free and frank discussions during any such visit to Moscow-there would certainly be no such obstacles in Ottawa-I think it should not be difficult for members of parliament to convince representatives of 

the Supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R., or the people of that country, that we in Canada have no such design of mutual destruction.

The Supreme Soviet of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics considers that the establishment of direct links between parliaments, the exchange of parliamentary delegations, and speeches by parliamentary delegations of one country in the parliament of another, will correspond to the desire of the people for the development of friendly relations and for co-operation.

But it may be that it is not intended the invitation be taken quite

so literally, and that all it involves is an exchange of views between parliamentarians of each country.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the secretary of state of the United States landed at Uplands airport a little over two weeks ago, one of the first statements made by him was of great interest to me. He was reported in the press as follows:
In his brief statement at the Canadian airport, Mr. Dulles referred to Canada as "a Pacific power" and said he looked forward to talks with Canadian ministers during his two-day visit.
Some of us have been trying to emphasize that fact for several years, and yet it must have come as a surprise to many hon. members that the United States secretary of state would make a statement of that kind. Of course, it is very true; Canada is, and has been for some years, one of the leading Pacific powers. Today the greatest threat to civilization is in the Pacific.
I propose to speak this afternoon as one of those Canadians, living west of the Rockies, whose outlook is to the Pacific, and to those nations which lie around that great ocean. After all, Canada is in the north Pacific where

there has been actual armed aggression for nearly five years, starting with the North Korea attack on South Korea in June of 1950. Now, we have in Korea an uneasy truce which has been broken by North Korea and by the red Chinese on more than one occasion. I need only remind Your Honour that eleven United States airmen are still being held by the red Chinese in violation of the terms of that truce agreement. Our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) indicated in this house on March 22 the nature of aggression by red China. The minister was asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about a proposal by the United States that certain clauses of the Korean armistice agreement should be denounced. This is what the minister had to say, as reported on page 2250 of Hansard:
That situation is a difficult one because of violations by the North Korean government of article 13D of the armistice agreement which prohibits the importation into Korea of military equipment and because of the inability of the neutral nations supervisory commission set up by the United Nations, which has two communist members out of four, to take effective action to control such imports. Proof of the violation of this article was indicated on February 5 when communist jet planes attacked a United States aircraft. These jet planes were based on North Korea, though there had been no jet planes based on North Korea before the armistice.
In addition to the fact that there have been these breaches of the armistice agreement we know that once the armistice had been negotiated the red Chinese turned their attention to Indo-China and in due course took over the northern part of Viet Nam. We now have aggression and threats against Formosa. At the moment the red Chinese are exceedingly truculent and I have verification of that fact by the Secretary of State for External Affairs who spoke on Thursday last in this debate. I quote from page 2341 of Hansard of March 24 as follows:
And so we cannot ignore in this connection the communist intention, loudly and frequently proclaimed, to attack and occupy Formosa and the islands.
I would point out that in the Pacific area there is no protective fence such as we have in the Atlantic in the form of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The only agreements for maintaining peace in the Pacific consist of several bilateral treaties between the United States and other countries, one with Japan, another with South Korea, the third with nationalist China and a fourth with the Philippines. In addition there is the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, the member nations of which are the three Asiatic nations of the Philippines, Thailand and Pakistan; also our sister commonwealth
External Affairs
nations of Australia and New Zealand; and France, the United Kingdom and the United States. Finally, there is the tripartite treaty between the United States, Australia and New Zealand, which as hon. members know is called the ANZUS treaty.
These various nations to which I have just referred have established a line of defence which includes the Aleutian islands, which stretch out for several hundred miles west of the mainland of Alaska, Japan, Okinawa, Formosa, the Philippines, southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand. This line of defence has been in existence for some time and it is the line of defence nearest to communist China.
This brings me to the question of Formosa. In June, 1950, when North Korea started the aggression against the republic of Korea the United States seventh fleet was ordered to protect Formosa from communist invasion. This year we have had threats by the communists that they were going to take Formosa. On January 24, President Eisenhower delivered his famous message to the United States congress and I should like to read the pertinent paragraphs of that message dealing with the importance of Formosa. The President had this to say:
In unfriendly hands, Formosa and the Pescadores would seriously dislocate the existing, even if unstable, balance of moral, economic and military forces upon which the peace of the Pacific depends. It would create a breach in the island chain of the western Pacific that constitutes, for the United States and other free nations, the geographical backbone of their security structure in that ocean. In addition, this breach would interrupt north-south communications between other important elements of that barrier, and damage the economic life of countries friendly to us.
The United States and the friendly government of the republic of China, and indeed all the free nations, have a common interest that Formosa and the Pescadores should not fall into the control of aggressive communist forces.
That was a clear-cut declaration by the President of the United States, a declaration which I believe accurately reflects the opinion of the American people.
What about Canada? The following day, on January 25, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) for the views of the Canadian government on this question of Formosa. I do not intend to refer to the statement made by the minister in reply to that question, but when he had finished I asked a supplementary question, to be found on page 499 of Hansard and which reads:
May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a Eurther question? Does the Canadian government take the stand, or does it not, that Formosa is in the first line of defence for Canada's west coast?

External Affairs
Here is the minister's answer which I suggest is rather surprising:
' That also is another question dealing with far-reaching matters of strategy on which I would hesitate to express an opinion at this moment.
The other day when he delivered the opening speech in this debate the minister made another statement about Formosa, to be found on page 2342 of Hansard. He said:
-we have to recognize that in dangerous times like these positions which are demonstrably of tactical or strategic advantage in the struggle with communist aggression or imperialism cannot likely be abandoned in the face of communist threats by those who hold them.
Then he went on to make this significant statement:
Formosa is considered by many to be one such important position.
No attempt to say what he thought or what the Canadian government thought, merely the most indefinite statement that Formosa is considered by many to be one such important position.
When the minister speaks he sometimes reminds me of an incident which occurred in a Vancouver court a number of years ago when a Chinese witness was under interrogation by a counsel through an interpreter. The counsel put a question to the interpreter and then there followed about 15 minutes of dialogue between the interpreter and the witness. Finally the counsel became desperate and could wait no longer. He said, "Well, well, what does he say?" And the answer came back, "He says yes".
Now, there is one big difference between the witness in that incident and the minister, in that one frequently can never be certain whether the minister says yes or no.
This Formosa policy of the government is extremely indefinite and I submit that the Canadian people are entitled to have an answer to the question which I asked on January 25. In other words, does the Canadian government take the stand, or does it not, that Formosa is in the first line of defence for Canada's west coast?
I believe that Formosa is in fact in the first line of defence for Canada just as it is for the United States. Canada is much nearer to Asia than is the United States, apart, of course, from Alaska. Canada is on the route from Siberia which, as we know, is Russia in Asia, to the United States. During the war many Russian airmen flew United States lend-lease planes from Edmonton up through the northeastern corner of British Columbia, across the Yukon and Alaska over the Bering strait to Siberia. Canada is nearer by sea to Siberia and red China than is the United States, apart from Alaska. The Russians have a great submarine fleet. If there should ever

be submarine attacks across the Pacific ocean the Canadian coast would be a closer target than the coast of Washington, Oregon or California.
I point out to hon. members what happened during the second war. The day after Japan struck at Pearl Harbor we had an air alarm in Vancouver and the entire city was blacked out. It was believed that Japanese planes were attacking that city and, as a matter of fact, Canada had on her coast at that time as many planes as could be carried on one Japanese aircraft carrier and most of the Canadian planes were obsolescent. Later we had an attack by a Japanese submarine on the west coast of Vancouver island. Then we had Kiska in the Aleutians seized by the Japanese and an attempt was apparently made to attack Dutch Harbor which was the next United States air base to the east. This was supposed to have been prevented only because the United States air force flew out beyond the Japanese ships and then flew back in at them, with the result that the Japanese thought there was a United States force in the rear.
On the west coast of Canada during the last war-less than ten years ago-we had two Canadian divisions, one to protect Vancouver island and the other to protect Prince Rupert. We had an armoured train operating on the Canadian National Railways from Prince Rupert for 100 miles inland up the Skeena river to Terrace. On the west coast we know what it means to have no defence line for Canada off the Asiatic coast. Now, in 1955, Canada is a prime target. Today this country is worrying about continental defence and quite rightly so. Canada and the United States are prime targets at the present time.
I remind hon. members that the policy of Canada has always been to defend herself as far as possible from her own shores, and that policy is more important today than it has ever been before both in the Atlantic and the Pacific. An attack on the west coast or by air through Alaska would be very unlikely while Japan, Formosa and the Philippines are held by the free nations. On the other hand, if Formosa is allowed to fall or is given to red China, as some of the members of this house on my left seem to advocate, then the first line of defence for Canada has been broken.
Therefore I repeat that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should give the Canadian people an answer to my question about Formosa when he closes this debate. The people of Canada are entitled to leadership on that question.
President Eisenhower has given leadership. In his message to congress delivered on

January 24 of this year he gave red China fair warning that the Americans would fight to protect Formosa. In giving them that warning he left himself room for bargaining with regard to the offshore islands of Quemoy and Matsu. I quote again from his message. He said:
Moreover, we must be alert to any concentration or employment of Chinese communist forces obviously undertaken to facilitate attack upon Formosa, and be prepared to take appropriate military action.
I do not suggest that the United States enlarge its defensive obligations beyond Formosa and the Pescadores as provided by the treaty now awaiting ratification. But unhappily, the danger of armed attack directed against that area compels us to take into account closely related localities and actions which, under current conditions, might determine the failure or the success of such an attack.
Later he continued:
In the interest of peace, therefore, the United States must remove any doubt regarding our readiness to fight, if necessary, to preserve the vital stake of the free world in a free Formosa, and to engage in whatever operations may be required to carry out that purpose.
The president went further; he said they would welcome action by the United Nations. He was very careful to make that clear in his message. He said:
Clearly, this existing and developing situation poses a serious danger to the security of our country and of the entire Pacific area and indeed to the peace of the world. We believe that the situation is one for appropriate action of the United Nations under its charter, for the purpose of ending the present hostilities in that area. We would welcome assumption of such jurisdiction by that body.
And again he said:
Again I say that we would welcome action by the United Nations which might, in fact, bring an end to the active hostilities in the area. This critical situation has been created by the choice of the Chinese communists, not by us. Their offensive military intent has been flaunted to the whole world by words and by deeds. Just as they created the situation, so they can end it if they so choose.
Not only did he do that but he has restrained nationalist China by making them vacate the Tachen and Nankishen islands. In addition he went to congress for approval of his policy in the very finest parliamentary tradition and he received overwhelming support-practically unanimous support-from the congress of the United States.
When I hear attacks made on the United States in this house I wonder if those who are making them have read this resolution passed by congress. It reads:
Whereas the primary purpose of the United States, in its relations with all other nations, is to develop and sustain a just and enduring peace for all; and
Whereas certain territories in the west Pacific under the jurisdiction of the Republic of China are now under armed attack, and threats and
External Affairs
declarations have been and are being made by the Chinese communists that such armed attack is in aid of and in preparation for armed attack on Formosa and the Pescadores,
Whereas such armed attack if continued would gravely endanger the peace and security of the west Pacific area and particularly of Formosa and the Pescadores; and
Whereas the secure possession by friendly governments of the western Pacific island chain, of which Formosa is a part, is essential to the vital interests of the United States and all friendly nations in or bordering upon the Pacific ocean; . . .
And then follows a recital of the treaty between the United States and nationalist China, followed by this resolution:
Resolved . . . that the President of the United States be and he hereby is authorized to employ the armed forces of the United States as he deems necessary for the specific purpose of securing and protecting Formosa and the Pescadores against armed attack, this authority to include the securing and protection of such related positions and territories of that area now in friendly hands-
The President is not given any authority to attack lands now held by the Chinese. The remainder of the resolution reads as follows:
-and the taking of such other measures as he judges to be required or appropriate in assuring the defence of Formosa and the Pescadores.
Then follows the final paragraph:
This resolution shall expire when the President shall determine that the peace and security of the area is reasonably assured by international conditions created by action of the United Nations or otherwise, and shall so report to congress.
I think we should take note that there has been no attack since this declaration was made or since this resolution was passed by the United States congress and I doubt very much whether there will be one. In any event the decision rests with President Eisenhower personally. We know him. We have seen him and heard him right here in this chamber. We know President Eisenhower's record. We know his character. We know that his aim is peace. There is no member in this house who can get to his feet and say honestly that President Eisenhower is not a man of peace.
For myself, I am prepared to leave this extremely difficult decision to President Eisenhower. I do not want to be accused of having become pro-American or anything of that kind. I come of United Empire Loyalist stock, and you are not likely to see any Canadians of that descent taking an attitude that is too much pro-American. In fact, in 1947 I voted against my party and with the
C.C.F. on the bill which became the Visiting Forces CU.S.A.) Act, which was giving the United States forces in this country certain rights over their troops. I must admit that I did not vote against it for the same reason as did the C.C.F. but still I voted against it.

External Affairs
On this question the Canadian government seems to disagree with President Eisenhower's plan for elbow room for giving himself room in which to bargain. As reported at page 2342 of Hansard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said:
It is true that some members of that coalition, including Canada, cannot subscribe to all aspects of United States policy in this Asian area, especially in regard to the coastal islands.
That was a sort of half-clear statement of government policy. But I ask the minister, when he closes this debate, to answer this question: Is it the belief of the Canadian government that the offshore islands, Quern oy and Matsu, should be handed over to red China in the hope of inducing the communists to stop fighting, even though the red Chinese are still demanding Formosa itself and show not the slightest indication of any other intention but to try to seize Formosa?
I point out that the United States is not asking Canada for any help. To hear some speeches made here, one might think that the Americans were wanting us to do any fighting for them that might arise or might begin as a result of this policy; but they are not asking Canada for any help. I point out further that if they turn these islands over to the red Chinese, it might break the morale of the national Chinese army. Do not forget that in that army there are thousands of troops who deliberately chose freedom as against going back to red China, although they were subjected to every kind of pressure in order to try to persuade them to go back to the communist army. More serious still, it might destroy the confidence of the Asian allies of the free countries in their intentions. In addition, of course, it might hamper the defence of Formosa. This second question I have placed before the minister today should be answered when he closes the debate. I repeat that the Canadian people are entitled to an answer.
This brings me to a third and broader question, and it is this. Does the government believe or does it not that in the Pacific communist aggression can be stopped by giving up territory-and that, of course, means giving up people as well-which is what was done in northern Viet Nam? Or putting the question in another way, does the Canadian government believe or does it not that in the Pacific a stand must be taken at some point by some nation or group of nations? For instance, will the minister tell us whether the Canadian government believes that the British should give up Hong Kong? That question was raised in the British house a few days ago, and we all know the prompt and

indignant answer given by Sir Winston Churchill to the effect that Britain had no intention of giving up Hong Kong. What does the Canadian government think about that question?
Let us recall what we have seen in Korea and in Indo-China. Let us recall-and all too often people in the free countries seem to forget this-that the communists have followed consistently a policy of fighting or threatening to fight, then getting what they want by negotiation, and then starting all over again. We know or should know by now that peace can never be gained by appeasing an aggressor any more than a bully can be handled by giving in to him. On February 16 Secretary of State Dulles put the situation clearly when he said this:
It should not ... be carelessly assumed that peace and security will be promoted merely by the non-communist nations indefinitely granting onesided concessions to the communist nations . . .
If the non-communist Asians ever come to feel that their western allies are disposed to retreat whenever communism threatens the peace, then the entire area could quickly become indefensible.
In my opinion, appeasement can end only in communist conquest. Appeasement is contrary to the character of the Canadian people. This nation was not built by leaders who believed in appeasement, and this nation will not achieve its true destiny by following any policies of appeasement. A firm stand has been taken in Europe. At this very session this house put Canada firmly behind the rearmament of Germany. If any step could have been expected to antagonize the Russians and to lead to war, that was such a step. Yet this parliament took it. Now, some steps must be taken in Asia to stop aggression in that area of the world.
Finally, I have a fourth question for the minister. Will the Canadian government work for and advocate a protective grouping of the nations of the Pacific such as exists in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I have raised this question on different occasions in the house, and the Conservative party has taken this stand, that there should be a security pact of the free nations in the Pacific area. I should like to know now from the Secretary of State for External Affairs where the government stands on this question. Such a protective grouping would be the most effective way of stopping communist aggression. If it were taken, Canada would have a voice in the policies that are adopted, instead of being in the position in which she is now, of being bound by the decisions made by others. Furthermore, Canada would benefit greatly in a material way if there were a grouping, not only for protection but also for the promotion of trade

and friendly intercourse between the nations who were parties to any such pact.
In the past, the government attitude on this question has not been very helpful. Canada would have nothing to do with the ANZUS treaty. I was told Canada had not been invited to join the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Then, when I asked whether Canada wanted to be invited or had ever intimated she wanted to be invited, I was met by a stony stare or a pleasant smile. I could never get an answer to that question. I believe that if Canada had asked to become a party to that treaty, she could have been. Certainly the Canadians who live on the west coast believe it is of the utmost importance that our ties with Australia and New Zealand be kept as close as possible.
The government attitude with regard to the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization also has not been one of very much enthusiasm. There may be more reason for that because most of the nations, or at least some of the nations in that organization, quite rightly appear remote from the northern Pacific. However, I am afraid the government has not been very alert to things that have been happening in the Pacific. It is far more interested in things going on across the Atlantic in Europe, and there is also some reason for that, of course, because most of our people stem from European stock.
However, I believe the Canadian government has failed and is failing today to give the Canadian people leadership in facing Pacific problems. I repeat my request of the minister, that when he closes this debate he give the house an answer to the four questions I have placed before him. I believe answers to those questions will help Canadians clarify their thinking on Pacific problems, and that of course is of the utmost importance in a democratic nation.

In parliament and out of parliament, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) delivers a great many speeches. He is kind enough to send me copies of those speeches. Most of them are very good; some of them are not so good and others are very bad, in my opinion. I am sure the minister will excuse me if I cannot subscribe to the theory of infallibility which seems to be accepted by so many government supporters. Actually, I do not believe the minister does require so many bouquets as he receives.
I should like to say, however, that I think the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs need not take an inferior position to his opposite number in either the United States or the United Kingdom. One of the
External Affairs
misfortunes of Canada during my lifetime has been that we have suffered from an inferiority complex for so many years. We allowed Westminster to formulate our foreign policies, and more recently we seem prepared to allow Mr. Dulles to decide what is good and what is not good for Canada.
I have a copy of the minister's speech at the Geneva conference in May, 1954. I feel that this is one of the speeches the minister delivered that will be remembered for a long time. The information I received in Europe last summer was that the minister, and the Canadian delegation, deserved the major credit for achieving the cease-fire in Korea and preventing the war spreading to Indo-China. The minister having taken a firm stand on that occasion, I wish he would place the Canadian point of view more firmly on a great many other occasions. Speaking on the radio on March 6, in connection with education week, he delivered a speech on education, foreign policy and the hydrogen bomb. This was another very valuable contribution made to the appreciation of world problems. Regarding the hydrogen bomb he said:
If one of these thermonuclear weapons burst near the surface of Ottawa, it would, by its blast and heat, not only obliterate this city, but through the fall-out effect of radioactive material, it would probably gravely endanger the lives of all people exposed in Montreal and its vicinity as well; so contaminate that city that it would have to be evacuated. If the winds, including those up to 80,000 feet above the earth were going faster than usual, the area of lethal contamination might be much larger. . .	.
So we must face the practical certainty that if any general war is allowed to begin, it would become nuclear war, and both sides would have to face the catastrophic consequences. Surely, any creature capable of reason must prefer the present situation, however unsatisfactory, to such consequences. Surely, too. both sides would prefer to tolerate the uncertainties of present-day life to the certainties of nuclear war.
Then later on the minister said:
Our method is peaceful persuasion and perhaps we are approaching a juncture in history when violence might seem less attractive to its devotees than discussion and agreement. We must work on in that hope; never give up.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, both the speeches at Geneva and his radio address were very useful contributions to a better understanding. I come now to his address on Canadian-United States relations in Toronto, March 14. Unfortunately, in this address he put on the Dulles record with all its harsh tones. His criticism of Russia, I am sure, would be very pleasing to Mr. Dulles; but the suggestion that Canada is prepared to let the United States decide whether war in Formosa is of vital concern to Canada, whether the defence of Quemoy and the Matsu islands is essential to our defence, is a question concerning

External Affairs
which the minister, both in his Toronto address, and in his speech here a week ago yesterday, did not do justice to the thinking of the Canadian people.
He mentioned in his speech on March 24, as reported at page 2343 of Hansard:
It is inconceivable to Canadians, it is inconceivable certainly to me, that the United States would ever initiate an aggressive war. It is also inconceivable that Canada would ever take part in such a war.
The second reason, as I see it, is that the only aggressive force that threatens us today, or that could commit a major aggression, is communist imperialism. Does anybody believe that we could or should keep out of an all-out struggle precipitated by communist aggressive power which, if victorious, would end everything that makes for free and decent existence?
This is one of his blasts against communism in Russia and China. And he says:
It would be impossible, in my view, for either the United States or Canada to be neutral if the people of the other country were engaged in a major war in which their very existence as a people was at stake.
The minister would no doubt argue that if war over Quemoy and Matsu should develop, and if the United States were getting the worst of it, and if China did invade the United States and it appeared as though that country was going to be defeated decisively, we in Canada would not stand by. I think that is very far-fetched, to say the least. I think the Canadian people just cannot be sold on the idea that Quemoy, at the mouth of one of China's main harbours, and less than five miles from the mainland, is necessary to the defence of the United States.
At a round table conference in Toronto over the week end I might say there happened to be eight Americans and one Canadian discussing matters of international concern. This would seem to indicate that those who arranged the conference seemed to think that probably Canadians did not have valid opinions on these questions. But when the question of China, Formosa and the offshore islands was under discussion, an American, who was defending the Dulles policy in the area, was asked this question: How far is Quemoy from the mainland and how far from San Francisco? His reply was that it was something less than five miles from the mainland, and 12,000 miles from San Francisco. I think he was out somewhat in the distance from San Francisco. Anyway, we know it is a long distance.
Anybody on this side of the Pacific who argues that the defence of these islands is necessary either for the defence of the United States or for the defence of Canada, must have a pretty vivid imagination.

The Ottawa Citizen of February 2 carried a story from Hong Kong written by Homer Bigart of the New York Herald Tribune service suggesting that, without exception, top officials of the British crown colony, both civilian and military, think the United States would be foolish to fight for Quemoy and Matsu. From a purely military point of view, these offshore islands just are not worth fighting for, was the comment this correspondent heard over and over again.
Then, in one of his week-end reviews, a few weeks ago, Mr. J. B. McGeachy said something about the history of Formosa, and drew our attention to the fact that this area has belonged to China for a long time. I have done a little reading about the history of the area, and find that over 2,000 years ago Formosa was part of China. Then, a hundred years before this continent was discovered by Christopher Columbus, Formosa had an official governor general, or one in some similar office, looking after its affairs on behalf of China.
I think it is unreasonable for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to suggest that Canadians cannot make up their minds, and that this parliament cannot decide on its own account whether or not the defence of these islands would be necessary for the defence of Canada.
I suggest that he should be on the side of J. B. McGeachy. And then, of course, along with this very controversial question is that of recognizing communist China. Since Great Britain has recognized her, and since it has been suggested that the United Nations should try to get communist and nationalist China around a conference table, I think it would be a great help if the Canadian government would now come out in support of the recognition of communist China.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), speaking at Seoul on March 8 last year, is reported by Associated Press as saying:
I do feel that some day we are going to have to be realistic. We are going to have to admit the present government of China is the government the people want.
And Clement Attlee, former prime minister of Great Britain, speaking at Margate, at the Labour conference said:
It is absolutely ridiculous not to recognize what is the effective government of China. And that government is not the regime of Chiang Kai-shek.
And Premier Nehru of India has gone on record in this fashion:
There will always be trouble in Asia and elsewhere until communist China is recognized in the United Nations.
And foreign minister T. Clifton Webb of New Zealand urged the admission of communist China to the United Nations.

Someone was good enough to send me a clipping from the Vancouver Sun headed "Mather's Nightcap", written by Barry Mather. It bears the subheading "Looking Backward and Sideways at the 4th of July", and the dispatch from Chungking states:
The Chinese government today flatly rejected a French proposal, that the Great Powers recognize Rebel America. The Chinese Foreign Office stated: "China is unalterably opposed to the recognition of a subversive and revolutionary regime which has gained power through force and violence."
And in the same article a dispatch from Upper Canada bearing the notation "With the liberation army, by our own military correspondent" states:
A top-level spokesman for General Johnston's headquarters told the press today that the rebel leader, Washington, and his followers have been "completely out-manoeuvred." "By withdrawing steadily to the north," he said, "we have lured the bulk of the rebels after us. Their line is now so extended that surrender is expected within a few days."
And then in the same article this dispatch from Moscow:
The Russian ambassador to Britain, Boris Shudemov, called today on His Majesty, George III, and extended, on behalf of the Russian government, "full assurances of good will" in connection with Britain's speedy action to put down an attempted leftist-led revolt in the Americas.
\
So much for Formosa and China. I now come to the diplomatic front. As I indicated earlier, I think the minister's remarks this afternoon were most unfortunate in a world with so many tensions. He accused the Russians of using offensive language and, from his lofty pinnacle, discussed a proposal which has come to him. I wonder what he thinks the reaction would be if someone asked him to dinner and, before deciding whether he would accept the invitation or not, he expressed his views with as much feeling and as much heat as he did this afternoon regarding the shortcomings of his prospective host, and said that later on he would consider it.
I notice in the press that the minister was on television last night. I am told that he is a very personable person on television. Although he has had information regarding this matter for some time, I understand that he muffed very badly the question of this invitation to Russia.
The hon. member for Kamloops was asked a similar question when he was on television some time ago.
The hon. member was on television recently.

Yes, I was on television but not on press conference. I thought that the question asked by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) might have received
External Affairs
a more courteous reply. The minister might have said: "Yes, certainly we have received the information; we shall give most careful consideration to it."
At this stage I wish to repeat the suggestion I made a year ago when a similar debate took place. At that time I thought that a useful purpose would be served by Canada taking the initiative in proposing a visit with a view to having a better understanding, and if I recall correctly I suggested that the delegation should be led by His Honour the Speaker and should include the minister, the Leader of the Opposition, our own leader, the leader of the Social Credit party, one of the women from the Conservative group and the only woman member on the government side. I repeat that suggestion at this time. I might say that it is one of the few suggestions I have made since coming to parliament that brought me a great many letters and quite a number of editorial comments. There were very few critical comments as a result of that suggestion. A great many people seemed to think that a useful purpose would be served. At this time I would suggest that the Prime Minister also be included in the delegation.
I hold in my hand a souvenir of the visit of the Prime Minister of Canada to India. I do not think there is anyone in the world who would expect that if the Prime Minister went to Russia he would return as an avowed communist. I am sure that those who know the Leader of the Opposition would not have any worry about his changing his mind if he should pay a visit to Russia. I submit that if a multimillionaire like William Randolph Hearst could risk his reputation by going to Russia when the Formosa crisis was at its height and could risk his life in that country, this land of freedom which is surrounded by two giants, one to the north and the other to the south, might well consider sending a delegation.
The Nation had a story in its issue of March 12, mentioning that Mr. Hearst on his return was quite favourably impressed with some of the things he saw. He was convinced that the present leaders were:
-not possessed with the madness that drove Hitler to bring Germany down in ruins nor by the recklessness that led Mussolini to tie Italy's kite to the shooting war of nazidom's short-lived conquest.
Mr. Hearst, speaking to the Press Club in New York on his return, said that Mr. Khrushchev mentioned to him in the Kremlin before he left that if he got into trouble with Senator McCarthy on his return he might call on Mr. Khrushchev to testify that during his stay in Russia he was a loyal and capable spokesman for the capitalist point of view.

Just prior to going to press the Nation telephoned Mr. Hearst and asked him a few questions. He assured the Nation that his visit was prompted by a desire to get a firsthand glimpse of the country and the people of Moscow; secondly, that he did not receive any prior suggestion or intimation from the Russians directly or indirectly that he would be welcome. And of course they did not bother asking the question whether he had any subversive interest whatever. He explained that within a week after his request had been made to the Soviet embassy in Washington he had received the necessary visas for himself and his two associates. He felt that the Formosa situation was sufficiently important to warrant his visit. He pointed out that his interviews were reported accurately and fully by the Soviet press. He mentioned a discussion with General Zhukov. General Zhukov was asked whether he had been invited by General Eisenhower to visit the United States and he replied:
Yes, General Eisenhower invited me to the United States on two occasions.
He was asked whether he would go and he replied:
I have received no invitation so far, and I think that the state of relations between our countries just now does not favour such a visit. Neither the American nor the Soviet people would understand it if Marshal Zhukov were to go to America in the present state of relations between the U.S.S.R. and the United States. I sincerely desire better relations betwen our two countries. I should like to visit the United States, and would do so with pleasure if relations improved.
What document is the hon. member reading from?
I am reading from a Soviet news bulletin which I am sure the minister receives through the mail. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs will indicate that it is an improper bulletin-
