Does the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicate that it is not a proper bulletin to read from? I might say that Mr. Hearst has never questioned the accuracy of the reported interviews that he had with Zhukov and other top people; I might say, incidentally, at this time that at a press conference in Washington, President Eisenhower was asked a question regarding his friendship with General Zhukov. He replied that they were very good friends during their stay in Germany. He was asked whether he had not invited General Zhukov to Washington and he replied that he had. He was then

asked whether he would extend that invitation now and he said that he would have to consult his advisers. A week later, after he had consulted his advisers, he said he could not extend the invitation now, which is a great pity.
I think those two generals who had to face so many problems in Germany in the years after the war should have a chance to come together and discuss what they might do at this particular time.
A dispatch from Washington by James Reston, a New York Times correspondent, mentioned that the policies that are being followed in the United States now create a great many problems for the people who should be their friends.
I now come to another section that I think is very important. While the Canadian people and the people of the world are agreed that the United Nations should be doing a worth-while job, the specialized agencies are not getting the assistance they deserve and should have. The Atlantic charter outlines some of the goals that we set for ourselves in the post-war years. I would like to remind hon. members that this was the objective that was set for us back in August, 1941. We wanted to see that people all over the world were able to have their full share of the things that were available so that there should not be hunger, poverty and disease in so many parts of the world. Well, the United Nations has set up machinery so that we now have fairly accurate information regarding the problems that exist in the world. I am not satisfied with the machinery that the minister has, first of all, to make information available to members of parliament and to the public.
A year ago when I was getting ready for my speech I telephoned the information section of the minister's office to find out specifically something about the work that is being done by FAO, WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF and the technical assistance branch. I was referred to the Department of National Health and Welfare which has a very good information service. I phoned there but I was told that I would have to go to external affairs for information about WHO.
You should have called the minister.

I realize the minister has a great deal of information available and has also a most efficient staff, but I wanted information as to what was going on in the various departments. I got a run-around from the various government departments, agriculture, health and welfare and trade and commerce.

Since then I have been to headquarters of WHO in Geneva and FAO in Rome and have discussed this problem with them. They explained that they can provide information when requested, but unless a government requests it they do not dig it up. They told me that if I made my requests through the regular channels I would get the information in due course. On my return I asked the Department of Agriculture to get the information regarding two of my friends who are well known to everybody from Saskatchewan, Dr. J. B. Harrington of the field husbandry department of the university and Professor Hardy who was formerly head of the agricultural engineering division.
Dr. Harrington has had two very interesting assignments in Egypt and India. At his own expense he took some very good coloured pictures and since his refturn he has held many meetings in Saskatchewan on his own time telling service clubs and church organizations and any who were interested something about the problems and the solutions.
I thought that some department in Ottawa should have information that there was such a person as Dr. Harrington, where he had gone to, what he had done and that they would be interested in having his story told to the Canadian people. No one seems to worry about this particular problem.
We are spending some money on these agencies. We are going to spend $323,000 on FAO this year; $289,000 on WHO; $500,000 on UNICEF and $267,000 on UNESCO-we are down a bit there-and $850,000 on technical assistance. Mr. Harold Wilson in "The War on World Poverty" tells us something about the income problem that has to be faced. We are told that in Indonesia the national income is $25 per person per year; in China it is $27 and in South Korea $35. Then when you come to countries like the United States you find they have the highest income, $1,453; Canada is next with $870; then comes New Zealand with $856 and Switzerland with $849. Those figures were taken a few years ago and at the present time we are up to over $1,000 in Canada.
What year?

These are some United
Nations figures for 1949. It is now recognized that we cannot expect to continue to live in a world where two-thirds of the people have the sort of income that the people have in India, China, Korea and Burma, less than $50 a year, while one-third of the people living in countries such as this have incomes of upwards of $1,000 per person. Maybe years ago we could argue that it was no concern of ours how people lived in other parts of the 50433-1661
External Affairs
world, but radio, television and modern forms of communication have made our world so small that if we have two-thirds of its people living under conditions such as these we are bound to have trouble.
Dr. de Castro in "The Geography of Hunger" deals with this problem. Dr. de Castro who is chairman of FAO, was away from Rome while we were there but it was suggested that his book would give us all the information we wanted to get from Dr. de Castro. I hope that hon. members will find time to read this most excellent production. In his foreword to the book Sir John Boyd Orr points out:
Yet hunger has been from time to time the most dangerous force in politics. It was hunger which precipitated the French revolution. A mob of women from the slums of Paris marched to the parliament house demanding bread. The politicians fled. The women, joined by the men, then marched to the Bastille. The fall of the Bastille was the death knell of the feudal system in France, and the beginning of a new era in European polities. The revolutionary movement in the "hungry forties" of the nineteenth century was due to the same cause. The Chartist mob in England cried "Bread or blood". With the free import of cheap food the revolutionary spirit in England evaporated.
Dr. de Castro describes some of the conditions in his own country of Brazil, but it will be noted that he covers pretty well the whole world. I think he would prefer it if I used some of his references to his own country. He recalls a foreigner who was visiting Brazil and who was shocked with the living conditions in a country where nature had been so kind. The visitor said to one of the local people:
Don't beans grow in this country?
No, senhor.
Rice?
No, senhor.
Some fruit or other?
No, senhor.
The foreigner was puzzled to know why this was so when trees and everything else seemed to look so healthy. He could not understand why these things would not grow, so he asked the native if he had planted some of these things to see if they would not grow. The native's eyes lighted up and he said, "Ah! Plantando . . . da". That is, "Of course they will grow if you plant them." Two-thirds of the world's people never have enough to eat, nor do they have the know-how to cultivate their land. Dr. de Castro points out:
It is estimated that at least 25 per cent of South America could be cultivated for one purpose or another, but the land in use at the present time does not exceed 5 per cent of the total area.
If only 5 per cent out of a possible 25 per cent is being cultivated it is not surprising that the people in those areas are not getting their fair share of the world's food.

External Affairs
I see that my time is running out but I appeal again to the minister to ask his colleagues to permit him to set up an information service covering the work of the United Nations so there can be made available to members of parliament, the press and radio, up to date information regarding the problems being faced by these specialized agencies.
Two of the ministers attended the Danny Kaye picture which was made available by Paramount the other night entitled "Assignment Children". Mrs. Sinclair reminded us that we have contributed $500,000 toward the work of UNICEF, but one should realize that that works out to only three cents per person as compared with $58.81 for our liquor bill and $30.65 for our tobacco bill. When that is realized I think it will be conceded that we are falling down in our information branch getting across to the Canadian people the proportions of these world problems. The people at headquarters in Geneva, Paris and Rome are frustrated because governments are not making ample funds available to them with which to do a worth-while job. I am sure the minister will give us more information, and that his colleagues will in turn make it possible for him to have additional funds in order that Canada might give leadership in this important work in the troubled world in which we live.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on external affairs, I realize of course that we are debating something that is not just of local importance but something that has world-wide implications. As we are considering that, we are reminded of the fact that in his speech the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) referred to the place that Canada now holds in the councils of the world, the responsibility that is hers because of the position in which she finds herself and also that in the foreseeable future he did not see any lessening of that tremendous responsibility.
We are inclined to think of external affairs as something that can be understood by the great majority of Canadians, but apart from just hearing a few references such as Indo-China, Korea, and Formosa and some other places, I am sure that a great many of our Canadian people have little understanding of the world situation at the present time. Even we who are privileged to sit in this chamber must depend upon the sketchy pieces of information which are given to us from time to time and we find it extremely difficult to arrive at conclusions that we feel are right in the light of the great world conditions that exist at the present time.

In taking part in this debate I am not attempting to masquerade as an expert in these affairs at all, but for a considerable number of years I have been interested in human relations and so I find this area of parliamentary responsibility of special interest to me.
It was my privilege last fall to attend the United Nations general assembly as a parliamentary observer and although that experience may have become rather commonplace to those who attend year after year I must say I found it of exceptional interest. As I listened to the debates in the various committees and also in the plenary sessions I endeavoured to form a mental picture of world conditions at the present time. In endeavouring to assess the value that was placed upon the United Nations Organization by the various delegates I found a rather wide divergence of opinion as to its effectiveness in the world of today. Some people seemed to be of the opinion that with the new atomic era into which we have been so unceremoniously ushered the United Nations has to a greater or lesser degree outlived its usefulness. There are others who felt that the work of the United Nations was worth while in some respects but in many other respects it had failed to measure up to the expectations of the founders of that great organization. I found that others were hoping against hope that the United Nations Organization would be adequate for the challenge of this new age in which we find ourselves. They thought that if anything would accomplish the purposes and objectives for which we are striving, the United Nations would be the medium by which they would be realized. We are hoping, of course, and we are trusting, that through work of the United Nations and through the program it is carrying on something really worth while will be contributed to the welfare of the world.
Although I was interested in all the committees I must say I spent most of the time at my disposal sitting in at the first committee. It seemed as though I was especially drawn to that committee possibly because I knew that the question of disarmament was one of the greatest problems that faced the statesmen of our world today. The agenda for that first committee, as it appeared in the journal of the United Nations, was as follows:
1.	The regulation, limitation and balanced reduction of all armed forces and all armaments: report of the disarmament commission.
2.	Conclusion of an international convention (treaty) on the reduction of armaments and the prohibition of atomic, hydrogen and other weapons of mass destruction.

The debate in this committee was very-extensive with most of the members participating. Sitting on the sidelines, it seemed to me that the smaller nations appeared to think of the world political struggle as a battle of giants but in addition to that they felt there was a real danger that in the struggle they themselves would be trampled to death. As they had a perfect right to be, they were very vocal in their pronouncements and emphasized the importance and the necessity for these giants to resolve their differences, to call a halt to the gigantic armament race and begin to plan for an era of peace and progress.
During the time I was privileged to be there the outstanding event in that committee was the submission by the Canadian delegation of the draft resolution on disarmament. I have a copy of the famous Soviet news bulletin to which the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) referred It is not perhaps the same issue but it is the same publication. Although I have been tempted to digress somewhat and to reply to some of the statements that he made, I am not going to yield to that temptation. However, in this particular publication of Friday, March 11, 1955, it speaks of the ninth session of the general assembly held in September. I am afraid one would gather from reading the bulletin that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who was the acting head of the delegation at that time, did not have very much to do with the proceedings. Judging from this report it appears that the Soviet union made all the statements and proposals and then the committee simply fell in line and adopted them. However, this particular resolution called for further efforts to be made to reach an agreement on proposals to be embodied in a draft international disarmament convention providing for, as I have already intimated, the regulation, limitation and reduction of all armed forces and conventional armaments, prohibition of the use and manufacture of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction, and the establishment of controls adequate to ensure that no state would have cause to fear that its security was in danger. It also suggested, among other things, that the disarmament commission reconvene the subcommittee to continue its work in this regard. We are given to understand, of course, that this committee is in session at the present time.
This resolution was first submitted as a Canadian resolution and it later appeared with some amendments under the co-sponsorship of Canada, the United States, the U.S.S.R., France and Great Britain.
External Affairs
I have said this before, Mr. Speaker, but I repeat that great credit is due the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who was acting head of the delegation at that time, for the way in which he carried through that series of delicate negotiations with Mr. Vish-insky and the other powers in order to achieve agreement on the details of the draft resolution.
Without indulging in flattery I think I can say that the stature of Canada has been enhanced and her influence broadened through the course that was pursued on that occasion. At the assembly, and on different occasions since then, it was stated that the soviets did advance from their previously adamant position with respect to these particular issues. I remember the restrained optimism with which the news of the soviet co-sponsorship was received by the committee. There were, of course, very few who were prepared to accept the agreement as indicating a reversal of the previously held positions but most, if not all, felt that there was some softening of the soviets' attitude and that it was to be accepted that for some reason, understood or not understood, the way for further negotiation was opened.
Mr. Speaker, these events are now in the past. But the important question is this: What prospect does the future hold for the implementation of the desirable objectives outlined in the draft resolution? I think there is one thing that we should remember in spite of much that has been said to the contrary and that is that the long-range soviet policy remains unchanged. An article taken from the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 21, 1955, by Edward Crankshaw, reads as follows:
The communist drive toward world revolution is with us again, openly and harshly, and conditioning the actions of the new rulers of Russia.
Any doubt about the ideological background to the personal struggle in Moscow between former Premier Georgi Malenkov and party secretary Nikita Khrushchev are dispelled by an important policy statement in the January issue of the Soviet communist party journal Communist.
The article is called "The Strategy and Tactics of Leninism" and it restates the old bolshevik aim of world revolution more categorically and candidly than at any time for the past 30 years.
Those are just two brief paragraphs from that article. There has been a great deal of talk about coexistence. Speaking personally, I think all the talk about coexistence is just a blind to cover up the continuing plans for subversion, infiltration and aggression. The delegates at the United Nations expressed alarm-in spite of the vehement denial of the soviet delegation-that the U.S.S.R. was exporting revolution. I say the delegates expressed alarm at the continued advance

External Affairs
and the continued campaign being carried on in their own countries in an endeavour to overthrow the properly constituted governments of their countries and to bring them into line with the communist ideologies. I think that Korea and Indo-China are examples of what to expect as Russian imperialism continues its drive towards the ultimate objective of world domination. There is absolutely nothing to suggest that the "leopard has changed his spots" or to convince the world that the soviets are desirous of peaceful coexistence, but there is everything to prove that, as quickly as possible-yet as slowly as necessary-communism is seeking to bring nation after nation, and groups of nations, under its power.
As we think of the continued plans of communism, and as we consider their objectives, our attention is called to the suggestions that have been ventured by some nations with respect to our own program of atomic development and arms build-up wherein they have said that regardless of what soviet Russia does the western powers should take the lead and destroy all atomic weapons, and should prohibit their use. I think that suggestion is ridiculous. On the contrary, any proposed reduction, any suggested prohibition or any contemplated relaxation should take place only when there is foolproof assurance that it will not jeopardize our position with respect to self-defence and the ability to safeguard the welfare of the free nations of the world. As long as soviet long-range policies remain unchanged, there must be no let-up in our military preparedness program.
We welcome any sincere and straightforward negotiations to rid the world of threat of war, and any plan to ease the peoples of the world of the intolerable financial load of defence expenditures, but there must be no more retreat or compromise in the face of the diabolical menace of world communism. Any negotiations must see to it that the balance of strength does not pass from the free world to the side of Russian imperialism.
Perhaps it is superfluous to offer advice to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) but, Mr. Minister, we exhort you to be on guard as you have been in the past, lest expediency or desperate desire for peace, shared by us all, might tempt you to compromise or to follow the program of appeasement.
First of all, the first committee at the United Nations was to deal with the matter of the prohibition of nuclear weapons. We have all read of the fearsome power of atomic and hydrogen weapons. We have had pictures in the papers and broadcasts over the radio

with respect to the destructive power of these new weapons. I do not think any one of us is in the dark with regard to the terrible potentiality of the atomic and the hydrogen bombs. Another matter was the reduction in conventional armaments. I am not going to dwell on that matter. The third was the control body to be set up in order to see that any plan and the proposals or regulations of any plan were fully recognized and observed by the respective nations. As reported in Time magazine of March 14, 1955, Sir Winston Churchill said:
"What ought we to do? . . . It does not matter so much to old people; they are going soon anyway, but I find it poignant to look at youth in all its activity and ardour and, most of all, to watch little children playing their merry games, and wonder what would lie before them if God wearied of mankind.
Disarmament would be the best solution, said Churchill. "But facts are stubborn things, and one of the stubbornest is the soviet government refuses to accent any practical system of international inspection".
I am sure this afternoon we all agree that disarmament is desirable. We would like to see it accomplished. I think President Eisenhower recognized the desirability of that when he appointed a secretary to head up a disarmament department. There are many complications, as was pointed out just recently in an article in the newspapers. It spoke of the difficulties that confront us in any program of disarmament, such as, first, the accumulation of the stockpiles of atomic weapons; second, the small atomic weapons that we now have at our disposal; third, the problem of adequate control.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, in the face of the world conditions, with the constant threat that is before us and the absence of any great ray of light and hope, that we can do nothing less than maintain our military preparedness until such time as that control organ can be set up and we can be assured it will work adequately and effectively in seeing to it that the nations observe any plan for disarmament.
I think there is something else we have to do in the face of world conditions. We must recognize our responsibility with respect to the need of many nations for technical and material assistance. This has been referred to, and after all I have said about the necessity for military preparedness I must say that this, as well, is a matter of great importance. We do appreciate the programs that are now being carried on with respect to technical and material assistance to other nations, and we are reminded of the work of the United Nations technical assistance program with the contributions that are made to that particular fund. We have been reminded the

last several weeks of the contribution made through the Colombo plan to the nations of southeast Asia, and how Canada has increased her contribution by $1 million. We do appreciate what has been done and what is being done.
But I submit that there is a great deal more we could do, and should do, in order to discharge our moral obligation to the peoples of the world. The need is still with us. Starvation is still rampant in some sections of our world; malnutrition abounds, yet; we have the ability to meet these needs in such a wonderful way. We have surpluses that are causing us embarrassment. We have a tremendous productive capacity in our nation, and it would seem to me that we could do more and we should do more with respect to material and technical assistance to other nations of the world. It is a moral obligation that we have. Not only is it a moral obligation, but I believe self-defence requires that we do something to alleviate the distress of other nations. We cannot forever stand idly by when we have so much and they have so little. We must do our utmost to evidence our concern for, and our interest in, the welfare of other people.
The third thing I believe we must do is to carry on at every opportunity negotiations for the settlement of international problems. Now, I realize to a very small degree the problems that confront us when we talk about negotiations. Nevertheless, as has been mentioned today and on other occasions, I do not believe we can allow any opportunity to pass by that promises, in any degree whatever, to lessen international tension and maintain the peace in our world.
Another matter to which I wish to refer this afternoon, and perhaps this is a little out of the ordinary, is that as we think of the menace of communism we must realize the necessity for a strong moral and spiritual foundation. Think back into history, and not too far back, and we can recall occasions when we faced emergencies. There were crises. We all remember how our sovereign called us to prayer. We did not think that was strange. But somehow it seems rather strange to introduce suggestions like these into a debate such as we are having today. It may be that we are just unconsciously by-passing some of the important truths in this respect; but I believe, as I have said, that if we are going to face the problem that confronts us and present an adequate defence against communism while preserving our own freedoms and liberties, we must build our house upon strong moral and spiritual foundations.
External Affairs
The battle now is not just for territory; it is for national advantage. Some have said it is for the minds of men, Mr. Speaker, but I believe it is more than that. It is for the very souls of men. It is the conflict of the ages, if you please; right against wrong, truth against error, freedom against slavery, light against darkness, God against Satan. I introduce this theme into a debate on external affairs because we must recognize the essentiality of moral and spiritual resources in our endeavours to maintain our own security and in the defence of the free nations of the world.
I have a clipping taken from the Montreal Gazette of March 18, 1955, and I should like to give several brief paragraphs from it:
Ostensibly, the communist attack Is on capitalism; in fact, it threatens the moral foundations of society.
Communism is not merely materialistic and atheistic, it is anti-moral. Its basic doctrines are the negation of morality. Its theorists ridicule all the moral codes that mankind has so laboriously built up.
Communists teach that moral codes grow out of economic systems. That belief alone would destroy society. It would lead to the fatal falsehood that morality does not have to be taught. Morality has to be taught-and it has to be taught anew to every generation.
And another paragraph:
But that is not the worst of it. The communists' doctrine of the class war leads them to adopt a code of ethics that is the precise opposite of what all the great religious and moral systems of the world have agreed in calling good.
And that, Mr. Speaker, is why I say if we are going to combat communism we must not depend only upon weapons, no matter how destructive they may be. We must not depend only upon technical and material assistance to the underdeveloped nations of the world. We must build sure foundations in our nation that will make us strong to challenge evil in our day and generation.
Mr. Paul S. Peak, advertising and public relations manager of the Imperial Bank of Canada, addressing a meeting of the advertising and sales executives club of Montreal had this to say, when speaking of the choice given citizens of the free world, with the high standard of living they enjoy:
Such freedom, Mr. Peak said, needed absolute honesty, purity, unselfishness and love.
"There is one ideology which can beat the ideology of the totalitarian state," he said. "It is freedom to choose. We must choose to be governed by God or we will condemn ourselves to be ruled by tyrants.
I would like to see a little more emphasis on the spiritual wealth of the nation".
Empires in the past have perished not at the hands of invading armies but because of moral and spiritual deterioration and disintegration within. The great powers are

External Affairs
not the atomic bombs, with all their tremendous power potential. The greatest powers in the world are righteousness, faith in God and prayer.
I should like to quote from Time magazine of February 28, 1955. This article quotes the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I think these words are very true. He said:
We have gone from the iron to the uranium age, from the horse and buggy to the jet . . . Seventy-three years ago they hadn't heard of atom or jet. They had time to enjoy a sunset . . . They were more secure morally. This moral insecurity of ours means that men are turning to strange gods. Communism is the worst of these false gods. It is the black mass of our time, with its insistent, insidious appeal to the twisted, the frustrated, the perverted and the distressed. Nor will it be destroyed by material means alone, by bread or bayonets or circuses. It must be opposed by a strong moral belief, by a moral purpose which shows itself in service and sacrifice both in the individual and the nation.
Again I say I am in full agreement with these words attributed to the minister. I appreciate the wariness with which the Secretary of State for External Affairs views any and all proposals emanating from the Soviet union.
In closing let me say this: We do not want to miss any opportunity which may present itself to move toward the easing of international tension and the maintenance of peace. On the other hand we do not want to find ourselves in the position of being helpless in the face of communist intrigue and expansion.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have had presented a considerable variety of shades of opinion as to what should be the position and course of action of this country with regard to the various areas of international tension, and particularly of course with regard to the most potentially explosive of them all at the present time-Formosa, and the islands adjacent to the Chinese mainland.
Here the discussion necessarily resolves itself largely into a consideration of our attitude, wether it is to be approval or disapproval, support or otherwise, in relation to the policy of the United States in this area. It is not my primary purpose in joining in this debate to enlarge upon this particular question. My primary purpose is to make a few remarks about the United Nations. However, in view of all that has been said about the situation-and I have followed the debate with some attention-I wish to say that of the views I have heard expressed regarding the Formosa crisis, and certainly it is no less than a crisis, those of the Secretary of

State for External Affairs to my mind commend themselves as outlining the only rational and realistic position Canada could take under existing circumstances.
It seems to me that hon. members who have offered opinions differing from or contrary to those of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are veering too far in either one direction or the other. Certainly I fully agree that it is not compatible with our status of independent nationhood and with our increasing stature in the world-and I think I may be pardoned for beating the patriotic drum to that extent-that we should merely play the role of, shall we say, the tail to the American comet or the 49th state of the union. I think that is probably accepted by every member in the house. I believe if we were to do that it would not be in the best interests of either ourselves or the United States. We have our own part to play. We have our own contribution to make to the cause of world peace as well as to many other matters of world import.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, it certainly seems to me that it is in the highest degree unrealistic for us to lose sight of the fact as, I fear, some hon. members who have preceded me in the debate have been inclined to do, that our fortunes and our destiny and our national safety, indeed our very existence, are inextricably bound up with the United States of America, the strongest champion in the whole free world.
If in our best judgment any phase or detail of foreign policy of the United States with regard to Formosa or, for that matter, any other centre of world danger, is likely to imperil rather than strengthen the security of the community of free nations, it may very well be not only our right as a sovereign state but also our duty as a responsible member of that community to offer the soundest possible criticism we can of that aspect of American policy, possibly even to the extent of proposing a different course of action which we think may better cope with the exigencies of the situation. If we do that we shall render finer service than by any blind and unreasoning adherence to whatever our ally may propose.
We have seen that American statesmanship -and in this respect it is no different from that of any other country, including our own; I hope I am not treading on any honourable toes when I say that-is not infallible. We know that the statesmanship of any country is liable to error. It is certainly not our part, as I said, to adhere to any policy of any nation if we consider it to be faulty or dangerous in its probable consequences. But risk alone, the risk involved

in a policy, certainly cannot be the sole criterion since, as I think some hon. members said earlier in this debate, any policy that could be adopted to stem the tide of communism, except possibly one of abject appeasement, must necessarily involve a very weighty element of risk.
The present United States policy with regard to Formosa and the offshore islands is not necessarily, let us grant, the best one. It may be unsound; it may lead to an open clash in those waters, and it is well that we examine it with care rather than hurry to associate ourselves with it without giving it that degree of careful thought. But while red China shows no inclination whatever to even open negotiations for a peaceful settlement, is there any hon. member in this house who can propose a better alternative? I have not heard any proposed, and I doubt very much whether any can be proposed. We must never forget, Mr. Speaker, that our whole position in this world of democracy and communism is based upon a fundamental unity of aim and purpose as between ourselves and the United States. We are in complete and total agreement that the free world must be defended at all costs against the inroads of communism. Differences may arise and, as I said a moment ago, even the duty to differ may arise, concerning details or the best manner in which to achieve that aim and purpose. But if in some such instance a course of action pursued by our ally, though neither approved nor supported by ourselves, should bring in its wake the world holocaust, then what possible choice could we have? Could we stand aside in any major war involving the United States because it had been precipitated by what we regarded as mistaken United States policy in Formosan waters or elsewhere?
To me there is only one answer to such a question, and that is the one which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has already given. Indeed, it seems to me the question is fundamentally academic; for certainly the decision would not be one of our choice; it would immediately and forcibly be thrust upon us by the communist powers.
It is upon such reflections as these, Mr. Speaker, that I base my approval of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said in this debate concerning our position with regard to the present Formosa crisis. Above everything, of course, it is essential that we avoid any serious rifts in the united front against communism.
I should now like to turn to an aspect of the world situation which has not been greatly emphasized in this debate, namely the ultimate need to attain a lasting peace in the world rather than the immediate need 50433-167
External Affairs
to avert an imminent threat of war. That this debate should be primarily directed toward the latter consideration is, of course, existing circumstances being what they are, almost inevitable. The present division of the world into hostile camps practically prohibits, for the time being at least, any comprehensive policy for a universal and permanent settlement of differences. Even if the current moves toward disarmament meet with some measure of success, even if the North Atlantic treaty alliance provides a satisfactory level of armed strength in Europe, even if some form of truce-there does not seem to be any better possible settlement in sight at the present time-is arrived at in the Formosan strait, even if all this and more are accomplished, we shall still be far from an era of permanent peace.
All these things I have mentioned might be likened to the building of a shelter-it may very well be a strong shelter-against a storm; but certainly, Mr. Speaker, they will not themselves bring to the world the sunshine of perpetual peace. If a permanent solution is ever to be found it must be, I am convinced, by the creation or the development of some form of international organization working effectively and efficiently, representing all or substantially all the nations of the earth and eventually involving, no doubt, some degree at least of abandonment of the cherished principle of absolute national sovereignty.
Today, undoubtedly, that seems little more than a vain dream. Certainly its quick realization is no more than a vain dream today. But if we postulate that its ultimate attainment is impossible, then it is my belief that after all the days or the years or the decades of postponing the final disaster, total war must inevitably come upon us, or at least upon some future generation. The stakes are the highest humanity has ever played for. I remember, Mr. Speaker, that in my college days-and that was a relatively untroubled time, when hydrogen was chiefly known as a component of water-there was a very popular poem by Mr. T. S. Eliot entitled "The Hollow Men". The last two lines ran this way:
This is the way the world ends
Not with a bang but a whimper.
Today you might reverse that, because there is the very present danger that the world will end with a bang, and there will be very little of mankind left to whimper.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Thomas for the second reading of Bill No. 185, to amend the Canada Elections Act (ballot papers).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE POLITICAL AFFILIATION OF CANDIDATES ON BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks that were made by the sponsor of this bill when he spoke on March 11 last. I think it would be appropriate for me to say a few words about the principle of this bill. When the hon. member moved second reading of the bill the other day he expressed the view that the purpose of this measure was to remove the confusion which in his opinion would result from the fact that at
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
times there is more than one candidate with the same name running in the same constituency.
My first observation is that there are already in the act provisions which would dispel any such confusion. There is a considerable time between the issuance of the writs of election and polling day, and this would enable the electors to be told the exact identity of each candidate, what he stood for and the policies he would advocate if elected. The campaign is generally long enough and at times strenuous enough to afford to each candidate a full opportunity to make himself known to the electors to whom he is appealing for votes.
There is another provision in the act which requires a candidate to list not only his name but his occupation and place of residence on the ballot paper. I feel that is enough to dispel whatever confusion might be created by the existence of similar names on the ballot paper.
If there is confusion, as the hon. gentleman contends, my submission is that the proposals contained in this bill would not do much in the way of clarification or help in dispelling that confusion. In fact my view is that they would add to the confusion. May I state why I believe this would add to the confusion rather than clarify the issue.
The bill suggests that on each ballot paper would appear what is referred to as the political affiliations or interests of each candidate. I must admit that I cannot understand what is meant by those words. The hon. member for Greenwood thought perhaps it might refer to the occupation of the candidate. My view is that it cannot refer to that because the act already contains the provision that the occupation of the candidate must appear on the ballot paper.
What puzzles me even more is the procedure suggested in the bill under which the recognized leader of each political party or group would file with the returning officer a written direction indicating which candidates should appear on the ballot papers as representing the party he led. That of course would mean that there would have to be a recognized leader for each political group.

I shall a little later. We have at the present time different groups and parties represented in this house. At the present time there may be no dispute as to who are the leaders of these political groups, but the time might come when the leadership of a political group was in dispute. This has not happened so far in our country, but

we have seen where controversy has existed in other countries as to who is the leader of a political group.
Even though there may not be any difficulty about that and even though the recognized leader of a group could always be found to file this suggested written direction, greater confusion might be created if instead of having only a similarity of names you might have a similarity in the political affiliations of candidates. In other words you might have more than one candidate claiming to be a member of the same party, with the result that the so-called recognized leader would not know what to do.
If he made a choice and selected one candidate as being the candidate of his choice, that would be equivalent to declaring that the others were outcasts. In other words he would be deciding that so and so was the candidate for that political group and that no other could claim to represent it. I believe that ought to be determined by the electors themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on this question. I find it difficult to. understand the opposition expressed by the Secretary of State to the proposal that the political affiliation be shown along with the name of the candidate on the ballot paper. I am rather afraid that the Secretary of State has been raising obstacles that do not exist, and has been putting forward hypothetical instances which I greatly doubt would ever be experienced. We have had this system in

Canada Elections Act
the province of British Columbia for many years and it has worked out exceedingly well. There have not been all the complications-

speechtext:
Yes, it was brought in by the Liberals. There have not been all the complications that have been raised this afternoon by the Secretary of State. Not only have the problems he has envisaged not come about, but it should be recognized that when the Liberals brought in this system in the province of British Columbia, it was for extremely good reasons.
What were those reasons? First of all, it was the belief in British Columbia-and I think it should be the belief here-that every person whose name appears on the voters' list has the right to cast his ballot and to make sure that he casts his ballot for the person for whom he wants to vote.
Let us not fool ourselves at all. There are thousands upon thousands in this dominion who want to vote, but they are divided into three categories. There are those who know the names of the candidates for whom they want to vote and who know the party to which he belongs and for which they want to vote. Then there are those who remember only the name of the candidate. That is all right, because his name is on the ballot paper. But everyone in this house knows quite well that there are countless thousands who, when they go to the polls, know the party for which they want to vote but who

and it occurs time after time-have forgotten the name of the candidate of that party.
Any of us who have worked in our campaign offices and our committee rooms on election day and the week before-and I think all of us have done so-know what happens. I think it is safe to say that out of every ten calls we get, either by phone or in person, nine will be for the purpose of inquiring what is the name of the candidate of such and such a party in such and such a constituency. That being the case-and we all know it is true-and because we all want the voter to have the right to vote for the actual person or the party for whom he wants to cast his vote, then why should we not, in the name of democracy, have on the ballot paper the political affiliation along with each name?
This system has worked exceedingly well in British Columbia, and I am sure it would work just as well in a federal election. The job is not too severe as far as the party leader is concerned. I had the honour of

being party leader in the province of British Columbia for 14 years and under the authority of the act, as the recognized leader, I had the right to tell the returning officer who were the official candidates of the C.C.F. The Liberal premier had the same right, and he did on behalf of the Liberals exactly the same as I did on behalf of the C.C.F. There was no difficulty.
There is one other point I think should be noted, and that is the reason it is advisable to have this type of legislation. It is advisable in order that a person may be certain he is voting for the right candidate if there happens to be two who call themselves the official candidates of a certain party. Time after time in all parties, provincial and national, you have internal dissensions, disruptions and disputes, perhaps in one constituency or in two or three constituencies. The party know who is the official candidate, but somebody gets up on his own and says, "I am the official candidate"; yet he is not the man who was nominated and who the president says is the official candidate. It makes no difference whether it is the C.C.F. party, the Social Credit party, the Liberal party or the Conservative party. That is the sort of thing that happens.
The voter is entitled to know who is the official candidate of any party. It is not right that anyone else who wants to run for election should be able to falsely capitalize on the name of a political party when he is not the official candidate of that party. Of course he must have the right to run, but it is not right, fair or decent that he should be allowed to capitalize on the name of a political party. At the moment this can be done. There is nothing that can be done by a recognized party or by a recognized official candidate to prevent it.
We can very easily solve these problems and make certain that the voter is able to vote for the person and the party he wants, merely by accepting the proposal before us to have the party affiliation placed alongside the name of each candidate. I have said this has worked and is working in other parts of Canada. It could work just as efficiently in a federal election. I hope the Secretary of State will take a second look at his position on this matter and will remove his objections.

As a matter of principle, I would have no objection to having the party affiliation affixed beside my name on a ballot paper. However, I am not quite as enthusiastic about this bill as some of my colleagues. We are all, of course, entitled to our opinions and I am going to express mine.
In the first place, I have some grave doubts as to the effectiveness of this bill to do what it seeks to do, and in the second place as to the propriety of one part of it. As to the effectiveness, I believe that if the objective is to make clear the political affiliation of the candidate in question, it would be reached more effectively and more properly by having an amendment to the form of the nomination paper itself, rather than to section 28 of the act. If you take the stand that wherever
Canada Elections Act
there is no written direction by the recognized leader of the party in question to the returning officer, then the name of the candidate and name of his party shall be as it appears on the nomination paper, then it is the nomination paper that should be the governing factor in this whole question. From that point of view I believe the objective would be achieved in a more proper manner if the nomination paper were amended. Speaking personally, I do not believe it is up to the party leader to designate who is the official candidate in any election.
I agree with the Secretary of State that this would lead to a great deal of confusion. You will note the bill states that the name of the political party or interest represented by a candidate shall be shown in the manner required by a written direction, if any, of the recognized leader of such party, and it shall be filed with the returning officer before five o'clock in the afternoon of nomination day. This amendment deals with the Canada Elections Act which governs all the territory from coast to coast. This provision cuts the time rather fine when he has to file this direction before five o'clock on nomination day. In many constituencies it is not clear who is the candidate until the official nomination day ends, and that is about two o'clock in the afternoon, if I recall correctly. The party leader is thus given three hours to decide who is the official candidate in each constituency from coast to coast. The leader has to know the name of the candidate and whether or not he represents the party.
I think that is the greatest weakness in the bill. It leaves the onus on the leader of the party to do what, in my opinion, is the duty of the candidate himself. After all, the candidate is duly nominated under the provisions of the act by a number of persons who sign his nomination papers. He accepts that nomination by placing his signature on the nomination papers before witnesses. In other words it is the candidate, together with those who affix their signatures to the nomination papers, who are responsible for that act. I do not think it is right to make anyone else responsible for that nomination. The people who are performing that act of offering the candidate to the electors should accept full responsibility for it. As I said at the outset, I have no objection whatever to having the party affiliation included on the ballot paper, but I feel it would be far more effective to provide for that on the nomination paper itself.
At the moment, all the nomination paper calls for is the names of the persons endorsing the candidate and the candidate's signature and his occupation. It would be a simple

Canada Elections Act
matter to provide an additional space on the nomination paper calling for the political affiliation of the candidate and leaving it optional to him to fill in that space or leave it vacant. As a matter of fact as I read the act, and I read it quite carefully, there is nothing which would prevent a candidate from stating his party affiliations in his nomination paper now. The act does not state that he must do so, but there is nothing to say he cannot do so.
Section 28 of the act, which this bill seeks to amend, states that the ballot paper shall contain the names, addresses and occupations of the candidates set out in the heading of the nomination papers. We see that the word "occupation" is not defined in the interpretation section of the act. With due regard for those who may have had more experience in legal matters than I have, from my own observation I feel there would be nothing illegal in a person stating his party affiliations in the space provided for "occupation". There would be nothing wrong if a candidate said that his occupation was "Liberal", and there is nothing in the act to say he could not do this. It would be perfectly legal.
I am not saying that this is the best way to arrive at the objective. It would be more orderly if, on the nomination paper, together with the space provided for the occupation, for purposes of greater identification there were a space for the party affiliation of a candidate who might wish so to designate himself.
In saying this I come back to the original proposition, that I believe it is the responsibility of those who sign the nomination papers sponsoring a candidate, and of the candidate signing the papers accepting nomination, to decide who the candidate is and what he represents. And I do not think it is right to ask any person outside that constituency to have anything whatsoever to say about either the affiliations or the qualifications of the candidate concerned.
If it happened that there were two candidates with similar names, similar initials and similar occupations, and there was a danger of confusion on the day of voting which, I believe, is one of the reasons advanced for this bill, then I would refer hon. members to section 28 (3) which states:
Any candidate may, within one hour after the close of nominations, supply in writing to the returning officer any particulars of his address or occupation which he considers to have been insufficiently or inaccurately given in his nomination paper.
Then it goes on to say what shall be done. I have no doubt the purpose of this subsection was that if, on nomination day, a

candidate were to learn that another candidate with identical name, initials and occupation was to be nominated, he would have the opportunity within one hour to make whatever changes might be necessary in the designation of his name and occupation so as to distinguish between himself and the other candidate, and thus avoid confusion.
That is the safeguard set out in the act, and I think it is well to keep it in mind. I believe the purpose of the bill-and I am using my own imagination, realizing that the sponsor will speak for himself-is to clarify the identification of the candidate concerned. It is the belief of those who have put the bill before the house that the addition of party affiliations would aid in this identification. If that is the objective, then I suggest the proper way to attain it would be to have the nomination paper amended to provide an opportunity for the candidate wishing to exercise that privilege to do so.
For that reason I am in line with the principle of the bill, although it is difficult to distinguish between principle and method. However, if the principle is that the candidate who wishes to do so may designate his party affiliation, then I am in favour of that principle. But if this bill goes to the appropriate committee it is my intention to seek an amendment to it, because I do feel the onus should not be placed upon a party leader but rather upon the candidate and those who sponsor his nomination.

I will vote against implementation of this measure because I am convinced that it is far from being such as to clarify the issue at all. As a matter of fact I rather feel that in many cases it would have the very opposite effect.
I do not have to look very far for an illustration, no further, in fact, than the last election in my own constituency where there were three Liberal candidates. It has been suggested that the word "official" be added to the political affiliation. But suppose the party leader refused to designate his official choice? In that case all candidates would have the same political affiliation. For that reason I do not think the proposal is sound, and I will vote against it.
On three occasions I was called upon to act as returning officer in my own constituency, and never once did any voter suggest to me that the lack of any indication on the ballot as to political affiliation had given rise to any confusion whatever. I rather feel that adding it would only make for greater confusion. That is why I propose to vote against this proposal.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to assure the hon. member for Prince Albert that if his main objection is the fact that Mr. MacTavish could not get his name on the ballot, if this bill gets into committee we shall make the proper amendments to see that the gentleman may do so, either by cutting it down slightly or by making his particular ballot three times as wide.
One thing has been proven, and that is that there is no earthly reason why the political affiliations should not be put on the ballot paper. Not one logical reason has been

External Affairs
put forward why this should not be done. The main arguments of the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Quebec South, and the hon. member for Prince Albert were these. We are gathered here as a group of friends tied to no political affiliation. We are elected as individuals; we sit in the house as individuals, and this should be an association of friends and not an association of political groups.
I quite agree that probably should be so. But let us not forget that after we are sent here-and I am not going into all the details of how we are elected on party tickets, which ye are-we are segregated into political groups in this house. The seating plan gives the political affiliations of all hon. members. The list of members that is sent around to the offices by the queen's printer lists them all according to political affiliation. On the back pages of Hansard every Wednesday there appears an alphabetical list of the members of the House of Commons along with their constituencies, their addresses and their political affiliations. It does seem strange that if ye are to sit in this house as not only inembers of parliament but as members of groups in the house, and if we are designated as such in official documents, we should not be elected on the strength of our political as well as our personal qualifications.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Thomas the debate was adjourned.
