speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, five o'clock found me speaking on the very real danger of utter destruction which confronts the world today. Since then we have

had three hours' grace; we may have three years, or more for that matter; nonetheless the danger must be considered as of the very greatest imminence.
I had said also that in my view the only permanent solution was some effective form of world organization of nations. Therefore, Without minimizing in the least the importance of those policies which are our only immediate available resource for safety, let us never lose hope that the future may bring, and bring in time, that effective form of international organization of which I speak and therewith the end of wars and rumours of wars and the possibility of war.
Today, as we all know, there is a form of international organization, the United Nations, which was created in that very hope and for that very purpose of ending war. What I have said largely and what I am about to say, is inspired by my interest in that organization. I was fortunate enough to have the opportunity to attend the general assembly of the United Nations in New York last fall as a parliamentary observer with the Canadian delegation. While there I acquired as much knowledge as I could of that organization and its functioning. I see in it a hope for mankind not otherwise discernible.
It may be that I have been reading the wrong newspapers, but I have been disturbed by what seems to me increasing cynicism and pessimism with regard to the United Nations. I suggest that this attitude has become all too common in newspaper editorials and articles, those potent purveyors of digested opinion by which it is inevitably fostered in the minds of thousands. To a considerable degree, though perhaps not so much in this country, it has appeared in the utterances of many public figures.
We have heard and read that the United Nations is dying and that it has become a mere debating society; that there are few united notions in the United Nations. We have even heard such derogatory references as UN windbags, costly impotence and so on. We do not have to run far to read or hear such journalistic and other comment of this kind. I think perhaps it has spread more in the United States, but I am afraid it has also spread to a considerable extent on this side of the boundary also.
Perhaps an attitude of pessimism has been encouraged by the fact that so far the United Nations has fallen woefully short of its primary objective of being an effective instrument of world peace. Certainly today our hope for national safety must largely repose elsewhere. It is true, of course, that many measures are being taken, NATO for instance,

which come directly within the letter of the United Nations charter. But I must say that I have always had some difficulty in reconciling such alliances, at least on the military side, with the true spirit and ultimate purpose of that charter.
Of course it is usually easier to tear down than it is to build up, but apart from that I realize fully that such criticisms of the United Nations as I have mentioned are by no means baseless. They are founded on inescapable fact; as a matter of fact they even have their value in pointing out numerous weaknesses which are inherent in the organization as at present constituted and functioning.
In some aspects the United Nations does appear to be moribund. It is more noted for dispute than for agreement. Deadlock, usually achieved in important matters by the veto or threat of the veto, is a common result. There are windbags at the United Nations who often engage in endless and aimless debate. As a matter of fact I have endured their droning myself. I was able to go back to my chair quite frequently, shut my eyes, and think myself back in this very chamber. Of course none of us is perfect.
As a matter of fact I have wondered if back in the distant days of Simon de Mont-fort, at the news of the calling of the first English parliament, from which this House of Commons traces its proud lineage, the wiseacres of that day did not shake their heads and prophesy as many frustrations for that organization as now plague the United Nations, and if they did not mutter in their beards that it would not work. But at least they had no newspapers to write letters to in those times.
In any case, what is said in derogation of the United Nations has a solid if unpleasant basis of fact. Nor does the immediate prospect of greatly improving the effectiveness of the organization seem bright. Consider one matter, the admission of new members. With half the states of Europe and many of Asia, including the effective government of mainland China, on the outside and their entry barred by one faction or the other within, the United Nations is still far from being a representative world organization.
I have mentioned the effective government of mainland China. In case my meaning should be mistaken I wish to say at this juncture that I am certainly not advocating either the recognition or admission to the United Nations of the red Chinese government in its present mood. Certainly it could hardly qualify as peace-loving within the terms of the United Nations charter. I merely suggest that if a stable peace is to
External Affairs
be attained some day we must hope that government will eventually qualify itself in this regard. For all I say, indeed, is with an eye to the future, and not even the immediate future.
As against all the problems and failures of the United Nations let us set up a not inconsiderable tally of solid accomplishment. Let us remember that if there are aimless talkers at the United Nations there are also men of vision. The organization provides a forum for the expression of world opinion. I do not think even Russia is entirely indifferent to world opinion. The United Nations has been a strong champion of human rights. Although it has not attained its fundamental purpose, the abolition of war, it has composed numerous local conflicts, any one of which might have led to a major outbreak. Palestine, Kashmir, Indonesia, Korea, Greece, Berlin; all these might be inscribed on the United Nations banner as victories in the cause of peace, even though as yet some of these victories cannot be considered complete.
Through the activities of the United Nations and its associated specialized agencies much has been done to raise the standards of health, sustenance and education among the depressed millions of the earth. Much too has been done to strengthen the economy of backward nations. Those of you who saw the picture "Assignment Children" recently shown here can better appreciate that phase of United Nations work which is portrayed. The program of atoms for peace, instituted under the auspices of the United Nations last year, may prove to be one of its major accomplishments in ameliorating the lot of humanity.
Paradoxically enough, Mr. Speaker, I think that if the organization had come into being with no object beyond its work in the fields of health, education, and social and economic welfare, there would today be a much keener appreciation of its worth and far less talk of its failure. However, although its work in these fields is a very real contribution to the cause of peace-for peace cannot be soundly based on poverty and wretchedness-the failure of the United Nations in its primary objective, the permanent removal of the shadow of war, not unnaturally overbalances all else. But even here a proper perspective must be maintained. What are the ten years of the United Nations' existence as against the age-old search for peace? Indeed, those who founded the organization considered that the first ten years would be experimental only, a time for trial and error. I may add that the

External Affairs
American founders were by no means so oblivious to the likelihood of trouble with Russia as is often supposed.
At the end of ten years, therefore, there is in contemplation a thorough study of the United Nations charter with a view to effecting such changes and improvements as the experience of the decade may suggest. Whatever revisions may be made, we cannot suppose they will eliminate or avoid the present difficulty with which the organization contends; the cleavage and struggle between the world forces of democracy and communism. But I suggest that the likelihood of significant revisions emphasizes the fact that the organization is not static nor dormant, and that there is room for improvement and expansion; that what is now little more than the first draft of that buttress of peace which man aspires to build may yet develop into the complete structure. It is at least a hope, and to abandon it would be to my mind a counsel of despair, carrying the connotation that the horror of total war, soon or late, is inevitable.
I sincerely commend to this government, therefore, that it continue its policy of strong support of the United Nations organization, and endeavour in every way to increase its strength and prestige. In particular I should like to see an intensified program to disseminate knowledge of the United Nations and its functions more widely among the people of Canada. In the continued existence of the organization there lies at least some prospect of better things to come. But if the great experiment is allowed to fail, if the United Nations goes the way of the league of nations, it may well be a sign that man himself is far along the road to his own destruction.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on
external affairs is hardly the type of debate that many of us might have expected to be participating in when the war ended ten years ago. After one of the most decisive victories in all history there were few then who did not contemplate the possibility of long years of stability, long years of the kind of peace that had been earned by the sacrifice of so many young men and women, and older people as well, throughout the world.
We are confronted today with the dreadful reality that scarcely a day goes by without some new incident reminding us that we are living through a most precarious period of history, in which new forces are constantly forming to threaten the very survival of the system which we thought had been established with great security at the end of the last war.
At this time there are three places very much in our minds. These three places have
[Mr. Lusby.J	< j |
been brought to our attention in the press and over the radio very frequently in these past few days. The first of these is Formosa, to which most of the discussion in this debate has been directed. The second is Viet Nam, where we see not only a division of forces as between communists and non-communists, but a tragic division within the ranks of the non-communists as well. Then, to remind us that this is a world in which trouble might appear at any point or place or time, we have learned today that at midnight last night the communists who supervise the highways leading into Berlin suddenly imposed taxes that were 10 and 12 times what they had been previously on trucks carrying vital supplies into that isolated city. We see the beginning of something that conceivably might create all the pressures and difficulties that were encountered at the time the airlift was needed some years ago.
Formosa has attracted our attention because we are told of the massing of forces there which might lead to a general outbreak. It seems to me that one of the things we should bear in mind in connection with what is taking place there is the fact that was emphasized by Sir Winston Churchill in the House of Commons at Westminster only a short time ago, and which was repeated again within the past few days by Sir Anthony Eden. The threat to Formosa is a threat which particularly involves the forces of the United States.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said in this debate, circumstances might well arise out of any general conflagration which began there that would involve us as well as other freedom-loving nations. Nevertheless there is a particular obligation of the United States in connection with Formosa, and we can perhaps take some comfort in the knowledge that the decisions that will be made there will be decisions entirely within the hands of the President of the United States. I am sure there is not an hon. member of this house, and there are few Canadians, who would not express confidence in the judgment, military knowledge and desire for peace of that great leader in this democratic world of ours.
That does not mean, however, that we should be expected to follow the lead of the United States on every occasion. They have made it clear that they do not expect that of us. I must say that certain recent events have at least given considerable reason for the belief that we have some reason to look with admiration and respect to the wise, cautious and farsighted course followed by the British government in dealing with international affairs. We do not of necessity

follow any other government, but it has been pointed out to us that we live in times that no longer can be measured in terms of ordinary wars.
In this debate we are discussing-as we shall be doing in every debate on external affairs and defence, which are such closely related subjects-the survival of humanity itself; it is nothing less than that. It is hard yet for any of us to grasp the dreadful reality that it is now within the range of possibility that human beings could destroy life on this planet of ours by building and exploding a sufficient number of hydrogen bombs to contaminate the whole air about us for hundreds and perhaps thousands of years to come. It is like something out of a terrible nightmare, yet it is a reality.
This terrifying truth about the hydrogen bomb has produced in the minds of all too many people a form of hopeless fatalism which discourages positive action with regard to defence or those measures which seem to be essential for the preservation of our society. The picture is terrifying enough, Mr. Speaker. God forbid that we should ever lose hope for peace. God forbid that we should ever accept as inevitable the destruction that would follow the full use of all the explosive powers that have been created and built up within these past few years. God forbid that we should ever cease striving with all our strength to retain sanity and to preserve that peace that many of us here thought was so secure after the immense sacrifices of the last war.
The greatest living statesman-perhaps the greatest living human being; certainly the man with the longest knowledge of war and the possibilities of war based upon an infinite understanding of history-has given us hope even in these dreadful days. Only a short time ago, in the picturesque language he employed, Sir Winston Churchill held before us the possibility that peace and security might be the sturdy child of terror. At some point the power to destroy will be so great on both sides of the iron curtain that it does not matter much whether one side or the other has a little bit more of that power. If there is available enough power to destroy all the great centres of industry, of concentrated population and of transportation in the leading countries on either side, it does not make much difference if you have four or five times the number of bombs that would do that job. At some point we are going to reach a balance of terror. When that happens, much will depend upon the clarity of thinking of all people who are free to discuss, to talk and to think. Much will depend on the spirit of the free peoples. Much will depend upon
External Affairs
their determination to preserve in any way they can a sensible, orderly life under that overhanging cloud.
A great many who are in this house tonight will remember vividly that in the early days of the last world war no person was allowed to move around London or the larger cities of Britain without a gas mask. I think the same thing was probably true in the other countries. There were in existence at that time terrible and extremely destructive gases. They were never used. The reasons for that fact may still be difficult to determine. I prefer to believe that neither side wished to begin destruction of that nature.
Those who were in London in the early days of the last war will remember that ghastly figures were given of the expected casualties when gas attacks came. They were not saying, "if gas attacks come"; they were talking about the casualties when gas attacks came. They did not come. That kind of warfare did not happen.
Conceivably this new kind of warfare might not happen. After all, the Russians are people strangely like ourselves in many ways, except in the political thinking of those who have control. They have the same number of bones in their bodies. They have two eyes, a mouth, a nose, and most of the ordinary responses; and they like to live. It is not likely that, without a good deal of consideration, they would precipitate a situation in which they would know that within hours destruction which would make Hiroshima and Nagasaki seem like child's play would suddenly be visited upon Moscow, Stalingrad, Leningrad and all the great cities and industrial centres of Russia.
Naturally we do not contemplate such a possibility with any satisfaction. One thing we all know is that such a war is not going to be started from our side of the iron curtain. It is not within the realm of possibility that the United States, Britain or any of the democratic countries is going to start a war of that kind. There is therefore hope; and while there is hope each one of us should be constantly considering ways and means by which the possibility of peace may be extended.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned the suggestion that has been made that there be an interchange of parliamentary representatives between the countries beyond the iron curtain and those on this side. Well, why not? After all, people sometimes forget that it was quite easy to travel in Russia some years ago. In fact, when we talk about the days of the czars as though stern conditions existed then

External Affairs
which were relieved by the communists, it may be surprising to many people to learn that then there was no difficulty whatever in going to any ticket office here in Canada and buying transportation by boat and then by rail to anywhere in Russia. In fact you could cross Russia without a passport. Now no Russian can move from one town to another without a passport. It is not only people from outside who must have passports.
By all means let us hope that the opportunity to visit and see Russia will be extended. I should like to go back again, but under reasonable assurances. I have seen two of their jails, and I would prefer when I go back again that it be under appropriate arrangements that suggest the possibility of carrying on ordinary activities without interruptions of that kind. We must recognize that so far this is only a gesture. But if it should prove to be a reality, then I would hope that an appropriate number of the members of this house, which would be determined in the usual way, would visit Russia. I would hope they would have a chance to visit the Ukraine, which is a separate nation by declaration of Russia itself. I would hope they would have a chance to visit Poland, Rumania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and the Baltic states, and see exactly what the conditions are there. If there is anybody who has any softhearted attitude toward communism, if he keeps his eyes open when he is there he will come back with no uncertainty as to what communism really is.
I would hope that Russians would come here. We give them a good deal of freedom as it is. We certainly give their agents plenty of freedom. By all means let them come. Let the contacts be extended. But let us not lower our guard at any time. Let us not be led into any false sense of security. Let us hope that by exchanges of this kind the possibility of real contacts, real understandings, a real exchange of ideas, might be increased. Today this, at best, would only be a beginning.
During this time we may live with a balance of terror there still will be the necessity for what we loosely describe as conventional forces. Let us not get carried away with any idea that because there is this immense power in existence it is not going to be necessary to have the kind of forces that can deal with difficulties that arise from time to time, such as that which occurred in Korea. After all, the attack on Korea came many long years after the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Yet that war was carried on without a single atomic weapon being used.

I most earnestly hope that difficulties will not arise in the Formosa straits that will lead to a general conflagration in that area. I may be rash but nevertheless I have the hope that they would not lead to a world conflagration. They did not in Korea. I have very real doubts that the men in the Kremlin are going to invite that kind of destruction in Russia if China becomes involved in a local conflict of that nature, which only they will precipitate if its starts at all.
It is not my intention tonight to make extended remarks about Formosa or about Matsu and Quemoy, which have been under discussion. Nevertheless there are one or two things I should like to mention. I was intrigued by the emphasis placed on the distance from Quemoy and Matsu to the coast of the United States. This point was raised in the debate today, as though that proved outright that they were really not of much concern to the United States.
May I make it very clear that I am not going to engage in any speculation as to the strategic importance of those two islands; that is peculiarly the problem of the government of the United States at this moment. But the distance is not the test. Berlin is also a long way from here or from the east coast of the United States, as are a number of other places in which we are greatly interested.
One of the things which it seems to me would bring a greater sense of understanding among us all in discussing the situation at Formosa would be to stop talking about Chiang Kai-shek and comparing his qualities with those of Mao Tse-tung. I must admit that I find it difficult to understand from what source some of my friends to the immediate left have formed such a high impression of Mao Tse-tung. Without in any way comparing these two men, why not let us be quite clear about the fact that it is not Chiang Kai-shek the government of the United States is supporting. The government of the United States has decided that the island of Formosa and the Pescadores, at any rate, are part of a general defence line in the Pacific. They have not forgotten Pearl Harbor. They have not forgotten that at a time when the hitting power of aircraft was very limited compared with what it is today, for a time it seemed as though their whole west coast might be open to attack because of what happened at Pearl Harbor. They have decided that Formosa is an essential link in that chain of defence islands in the Pacific.
I think we would all keep our arguments on a much saner basis if we recognized that

fact. I do not subscribe for one moment to all the terrible descriptions of Chiang Kai-shek that are put forward by my friends to the immediate left. In fact I doubt if they have evidence of some of the things they say. I have not seen it, and I doubt if they have. Most certainly there is no reason for any of us to believe in the interpretation they put on the actions of Mao Tse-tung, who has murdered millions of his own people. But let us remember that if Chiang Kai-shek were not there today and someone else were there, the United States seventh fleet would still be in the Formosa straits and United States aircraft would be on the air bases in Formosa, as they are at this time.
I welcome that. I welcome it for more than one reason. It is the reality of the situation. It is the reality of a situation in which the government of the United States says, without reservation, "We are going to take the appropriate steps to see that communist aggression moves no farther west into our own area". Also I welcome it for another reason. It seems to me that perhaps they will understand a little better the presence of British troops in Hong Kong and Singapore if they realize exactly why it is that they are in Formosa, and thus dispel any of the illusions that might otherwise surround that situation.
I mention this because I believe that frankness, appreciation of definition and clarity of purpose are the proved essentials of peace. I believe that horse trading and loose situations are the very things that invite trouble. I think that is what we learned at the beginning of the last war. And I would hope to see within some not too distant time a more precise definition of what the real defence line is in that area, and in other areas of the Pacific. I think we have very convincing reasons why that should be a very hopeful thing for us.
We must try to preserve peace in every way we can. But surely if history teaches one thing it is that we will not preserve peace by some form of horse trading with the communists now or at any other time. We can no more buy off Peking or the Kremlin than we were able to buy off Hitler in the days before September, 1939.
I think we have received great encouragement from a place which has come back into the press prominently in the last 48 hours, and which is not far removed from Formosa in terms of principle even though it is half way across the world. If there is one thing we can learn from what has happened in Berlin it is the importance of a clear definition of the boundary line and of the issue, and of what will happen if that
External Affairs
division is not recognized. When we are sometimes told about the geographical location of certain places, and when it is argued that this place or that falls more logically into one area than another, let us remember that there is no more unreasonable situation in the world today, and I doubt if there ever was a more unreasonable situation, than that with which Berlin is confronted at this very moment.
There is a city with millions of people, a small island of freedom more than a hundred miles inside the Soviet zone. There does not seem to be any sense in it. They get all their supplies over two or three limited highways. There are three narrow air strips five miles wide which must be followed when flying in there. There are rail lines going there, passing through Soviet territory and supervised by the Russians. Yet Berlin has grown and prospered, and West Berlin today is a place of great vitality and confidence.
Why? Because of a very courageous decision, because of what seemed to be a very daring decision. The three western powers, Great Britain, France and the United States, said in simple, clear and unequivocal terms: West Berlin is part of West Germany; access to West Berlin is part of the survival of that city. No matter how irregular the boundaries may be-and they are very irregular between East and West Berlin-there are the boundaries; the moment those boundaries are threatened, that means war.
That was an ominous declaration. It was a declaration which aroused great concern at the time. There were British, French and American troops in that distant island of freedom, completely surrounded by Russian armour, Russian infantry and Russian aircraft. Yet there has been no attempt to change those boundaries. There was the blockade, when the airlift was suddenly brought into existence by the western powers to supply Berlin. Now we see this special tax measure as another attempt to interfere with transportation. But Berlin, with all the irregular boundaries passing through that city, remains as the junction point of two worlds, and West Berlin remains as an island of freedom. Never has there been a time, never, when the Russians could not have marched into that city within a comparatively few minutes. But they knew what that meant, and Berlin has remained free.
For that reason I suggest that appreciation of definition both as to boundaries, as to issues and as to consequences does assume tremendous importance in our efforts to preserve peace. I have mentioned Berlin as an illustration of why I hope we will have exact and precise definitions in the east.

External Affairs
Nevertheless we must remember that this is the responsibility of the United States. I for one do not believe that trouble there would bring about a general conflagration. I think we can therefore refrain from undue criticism of our friends in the United States in their efforts to deal with this particular problem. That does not mean we abandon any right to express our opinion, and I am expressing my own opinion once again. Preciseness of definition will be of maximum help.
I have used Berlin as an illustration, but let me refer to it in another way. Already there has been a debate in this house in regard to German rearmament. In that debate in this house as elsewhere there was heartburning, there were uncertainties, because it is not easy to forget that twice within the lifetime of most of us Germany has been the aggressor and that many in this house tonight bear on their bodies the marks of those struggles started by German militarism. Nor is it easy to forget the ghastly pages of history which contain the names of Dachau, Buchenwald and Belsen and those other horror camps which forever stand as a blight on the record of the German people, with all the great qualities they possess.
We made our decision. It was a right decision; it was the only decision which offered hope. It was the decision which the British people were called upon to make after the Napoleonic wars, when another dictator had visited destruction on the whole of Europe. History is useful as a guide. It is worth remembering that Napoleon was not regarded with any very friendly sentiments by the people of those nations into which his troops had entered in cold aggression. Whether it be in Madrid, in Vienna, in Prague, in Warsaw or in Moscow, there are memories of the aggression of that time.
When that war was over and Wellington was the head of the Grand Alliance, the very same arguments were put up to him. Never again must France be allowed to have arms with which to threaten the peace of Europe. It is worth remembering today that it was Wellington who said, "If France is to be a member of the society of Europe, then our purpose must be to gain the friendship of the people of France, and that can be done only if they are treated on terms of equality". It was his decision, accepted it is true by the government, and on the basis of that decision the greatest historic friendship of all time began when France and Britain marched side by side through the generations that followed.
Surely there is a lesson for us today. Yes, there were horrors and there were terrors imposed by the troops of Napoleon, not comparable, it is true, with the stories that came out
[Mr. Drew.l
of Germany and out of German-occupied countries in the last war, but bad enough. We have seen the lesson; we can hope there will be friendship of that kind, and that hope should be justified by the wonderful contribution made to the life of our country by people of German stock who have come here to live and who are among our very finest citizens. What better evidence could there be that there can be no such thing as some fundamental weakness in the German strain than the fact that the President of the United States, who today is the most powerful leader of the western world, came only a couple of generations removed, direct from Germany. These are the things that give us hope, but there are also reasons for concern.
Those things should be borne in mind. There was every reason for France to show some concern, as she did. It would be appropriate in this house, a few days after France has ratified those agreements, to express our admiration of the men who did ratify them under difficulties that we simply cannot understand. After all, there were reasons why it was difficult for France to agree, which were not before our eyes when this decision faced us.
Across the whole of France are tragic reminders of German invasion in 1870, in 1914 and in 1939. Anywhere you go from the North Sea to Belfort on the Swiss frontier, anywhere you go from the Pyrenees to the northern frontiers, anywhere you go from Brittany or from the famous beaches of Normandy, you see those cemeteries which day by day remind the people of France of what German aggression really meant. I marvel that they were able to gain support for those treaties. They have done it, and from this house could well go words of admiration, of hope and of great confidence in a country which, with all that evidence before it, with millions of graves of two world wars in their own soil, have joined in this great and challenging act of friendship. But they were conscious of the dangers. They were emphasized during the debates; nor should we forget them.
Part of those Paris treaties that take the place of the European defence community deal particularly with the unification of Germany. I wish to speak on that. Chancellor Adenauer has made it clear that his primary purpose is to bring about the unification of Germany. That is an understandable ambition. In the declarations approved at Paris it was clearly stated that this must be by peaceful means. Germany, under the signature of Chancellor Adenauer, undertakes that

it will be by peaceful means, but Chancellor Adenauer will not be there forever. Therefore let us look at that situation for a moment.
What does unification mean? There is no doubt about the fact that it is constantly in the German mind. Just last week the Bundestag passed the appropriate measure to start rebuilding the Reichstag, which is not a hundred yards from the Soviet sector of Berlin, a fairly challenging gesture. It is intended to emphasize to the communists as well as to the west that Berlin is the capital of Germany. That is in their minds.
What happens when West Germany is rearmed? East Germany is substantially rearmed now. Is East Germany faithful to the communist cause? The answer is emphatically no. The answer to that question was given on June 17, 1953, when the food riots in Berlin sparked a series of outbursts in every city in Germany which amounted almost to open revolution. There was no integrated plan; it was a spontaneous outburst against communist control. I saw the official records of what had happened in those East German cities when I was in Berlin last August. I had no idea until I saw them that there had been great bloodshed in many cities, that tanks and armoured forces were required to put down the uprisings. That is how strongly the people felt.
I mention this because it may suggest what could happen when a rearmed East Germany and a rearmed West Germany stand side by side. Suppose something happened in East Germany which called for Russian intervention. Would a rearmed West Germany stand idly by? I do not need to answer that question. Or is it possible that the two forces might come together in some other way?
Many hon. members here will remember the ingenious device employed by von Rin-telin in the first world war to destroy allied ships at sea. It was a small lead tube about the size of a cigar and contained two chemicals separated by a thin plate. The chemicals gradually ate into the plate and at a given time met and an explosion occurred. I do not think it is unfriendly to West Germany to suggest that it is tremendously important that we recognize this danger which in turn could carry the spark which would involve communist forces beyond. Now is the time to make sure there is a clear understanding and a clear definition as to how this is going to be done; that there is no uncertainty, and that there should be agreement that there must be allied staff officers so closely in association with the troops of West Germany that there could be no reallocation and redeployment of troops preparatory to any
External Affairs
movement of that kind without the western powers being fully aware of that fact. These are realities; they are the kind of realities we must face if we are going to have peace.
When we talk about unification, just what do we mean? Is it unification of West Germany as we know it today and East Germany as we know it today? Most people think of it as the union of West Germany and East Germany which we see on the map, but the West Germans do not think of it as that. I wonder if it was sufficiently realized when a very important gesture was made last July to place Berlin in the German structure and members of the Bundesversammlung were flown into Berlin to elect their new president. The new president, Theodor Heuss, was elected in what is known as East Prussian hall. East Prussia is not in East Germany; East Prussia is well beyond the boundaries of East Germany.
In Berlin there are pictures which show the people there what they describe as the lost provinces. There are nine of them, but only three are in East Germany. I should think it would be important that we have a clear understanding of what they mean by unification, that there be a precision of definition because in any uncertainty about it there could be the makings of great trouble in the years ahead.
We have taken a bold and I believe necessary step in the western world in restoring sovereignty to West Germany, in assisting their rearmament, in extending the hand of friendship and widening the channels of trade. But let us not blind ourselves to those things which could cause difficulties in the years ahead unless they are understood and faced today.
I mention these because Canada with her 15 million people can never be suspected of aggressive intentions. Her voice can be heard. There is no government which is not willing and anxious to hear the opinions of the government and people of Canada in regard to matters of this kind. I would hope that perhaps we will contribute something to the understanding and solution of this problem, because I would be very sorry if in the years ahead we continued to be worried by uncertainties such as those which were associated with the Danzig corridor in years gone by, and other uncertainties of that kind. This must be done if we are to establish some sort of general stability in this period which we hope may be one of peace.
I leave my remarks in regard to the military situation there. I hope and pray that following the lessons of the past the good spirit of Germany may emerge triumphant in partnership with the west, and that we may

External Affairs
contribute much to the fellowship and understanding which will bring them wholly into our partnership. But I am sure the firmness of that friendship and the hope of peace will depend upon our frankness in facing issues and in pointing out dangers before it is too late to discuss them in reasonable and understandable terms.
We are going to have a period of coexistence whether we like it or not. We are in a period of nuclear coexistence. It is going to involve a lot of thought, a lot of discussion and a lot of very earnest effort. In the desire to attain peace there is certainly complete agreement within this house. May I say to my friends to the immediate left that if by inference I have been critical of any statements they have made, I certainly do not question the fact that within this house there is complete unanimity in the desire to achieve peace by the means that seem best to those who put forward arguments in different forms.
If we attain some stability and can gain time, then much can happen that we cannot foresee today. There was nothing in the arithmetic of war in the summer of 1940 to show how victory was going to come to Britain. They stood firm. Time was on their side, and God in his infinite wisdom followed a course which brought victory. And I believe it was Divine guidance, because it was the decent thing that prevailed.
If we in the western world will stand firm today in acceptance of the principles to which we subscribed at San Francisco in 1945; if we are patient in our efforts to maintain peace by the collective strength of the western nations, and if we do not abandon principle for expediency, then I believe that in this balance of terror which nuclear coexistence has brought we may see the birth of a real and extending peace. Precise definitions, strict adherence to principles, with all the nations of the world committed to the same principles of freedom, with patience in carrying forward the cause of peace, may still offer hope in the face of this dreadful terror.

speechtext:
All right, but why ask for a different standard for the communists? After all, he is a world statesman; he should be compared with other statesmen.
Mr. Speaker, one of the more curious phenomena of a debate on foreign affairs in this house is the unanimity with which the C.C.F. party attacks the United States, engaging gleefully in the seemingly pointless pastime of plucking the eagle's tail feathers. I say this phenomenon is curious because at first sight there does not appear to be any logical explanation. However, on reflection two possible reasons present themselves.
In the first place the United States represents the antithesis of the socialist ideal. It violates with impunity every tenet of the socialist creed, and moreover has the extremely bad taste to enjoy conspicuous material success while doing so. It must be galling to devote all one's waking moments and even one's dreams to contemplating the glories of a socialist utopia only to find that one's next door neighbour already possesses everything one could have imagined in one's fondest dreams and more, without benefit of the socialist's magic wand and, what is worse, under the aegis of that hated system, free enterprise. To realize that while the whole world is perilously balanced on the verge of bankruptcy this hated exemplar of free enterprise is able to provide the billions required to arrest the plunge into chaos; to have to accept favours from one's ideological enemy is gall and wormwood indeed.
The second reason is less tangible and probably springs from a vague ideological sympathy with the communist world. This sympathy probably springs from the common ancestry of socialism and communism. It should never be forgotten that Karl Marx was one of the earliest exponents of the socialist dogma in the western world. It is true that the Fabians, to whom our C.C.F. brethren probably profess a spiritual affinity, rejected the cold logic of Marxian conclusions and preferred a watered down version, more palatable if less logical. Nevertheless there probably remains a certain fellow feeling for the Russian branch of the family, as misguided and rather crude fellows, to be sure, but still repositories of the original, if now perverted, socialist gospel.
It is therefore quite natural that the United States should be regarded as the reactionary enemy of all things revered by the socialists. On the other hand while there is a vociferous and, I believe, sincere condemnation of the totalitarian aspects of Russian communism, nevertheless, in so far as the communist party line reflects the ideal of socialism, which it

does in some respects, it meets with approval and adherence from all socialists. This provides a plausible explanation, at least, as to why the C.C.F. party supports the cause of communist China and condemns the position of the United States in respect of the dispute over the status of Formosa.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in attempting to assess the role which Canada should assume in world affairs the primary and overriding consideration is full recognition of the general, central and elementary fact that the world, for the moment and for the foreseeable future, is divided into two hostile and irreconcilable camps. On the one hand we have a monolithic aggregation of power represented by the U.S.S.R. and the satellite countries, and opposed to it a bloc of the free nations of the world headed by the United States.
For practical purposes it has to be recognized that the United States possesses the only effective concentration of power in the free world capable of opposing the Soviet juggernaut. Consequently it is imperative in the interests of self-preservation that all the free nations, including Canada, give unstinted support to their real protector against the rapacity of Soviet imperialism. This does not mean a slavish obedience to United States domination in respect of over-all policy. We should reserve for ourselves freedom of expression through diplomatic channels on such matters as may involve our interests.
Throughout all this, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we must never lose sight of the one paramount consideration that the only effective force precenting communist world domination today is the United States of America. We must proceed on the assumption that the United States will not precipitate an atomic war, and on the equally certain assumption that if there was not a risk of effective retaliation the Soviet union would not hesitate to start such a war tomorrow. Truly, Mr. Speaker, we walk on the verge of the abyss, but I see no reason or no wisdom in the advice of those who would have us scorn the handrail.
In the world's continuing crisis the Eisenhower administration continues to exercise an admirable restraint, a refusal to be carried away by predictions either of inevitable war or of an easy peace. The communist enigma leaves us no choice but to prepare for the worst, but it does not commit us to accept the worst. We must not cease to explore whatever roads may lead us away from war. In this objective we can rest assured that we shall have the sincere and unqualified support of President Eisenhower. We should
External Affairs
not allow ourselves to be misled by the vapor-ings of certain irresponsible sections of United States public opinion. Such men are dangerous, and we may thank God that United States foreign policy is based on saner counsels.
In the welter of speculation on Soviet intentions that is going on in the world today one recognizes as valid Sir Winston Churchill's description, that they are "a mystery wrapped in an enigma". In this welter of speculation by columnists and editorial writers only one clear lesson emerges, that of the futility of speculation where the totalitarian mind is concerned.
The confusion of the experts in this connotation is strikingly apparent. The disgrace of Malenkov and the emergence of Khrushchev -or perhaps Marshal Zhukov or even Marshal Bulganin-as the major contender for Stalin's power merely emphasizes the danger of making absolute predictions of what effects may follow from communist causes. Other experts argue that Khrushchev is already too old to establish himself as Russia's absolute ruler. They point out that it was Khrushchev who nominated Bulganin for the premiership. It was Beria who. only two years ago, nominated Malenkov for the same post. These facts, it is claimed, point to a continuing struggle for power, and consequently the danger that Russia will take serious risks of war has decreased.
Similar expert disagreements exist over the question of red China's intentions in the Formosa straits. As we have reason to know from experience, a totalitarian world is one in which words are divorced from meaning, in which war can mean peace and peace war, and in which the objective has been abolished by decree. Whether or not Peking's bellicose words mean actual bellicose intentions, or whether in the face of United States force a de facto cease-fire will be permitted to prevail, is something no one in the west really knows.
In this atmosphere of confusion what may Canada do to promote a modus vivendi between these tremendous conflicting forces? It seems to me that we would do well to promote the mobilization of the British commonwealth of nations as a moral force for peace. Of course, the commonwealth is ill-equipped to enter the lists in a struggle where naked power is the criterion of effectiveness. Nevertheless if the commonwealth could be organized to speak with effective unanimity in world councils the moral effect would be incalculable. Maybe this is but an idle dream; but if any member of the commonwealth is fitted to play the leading role in such a rapprochement, surely it is Canada.

External Affairs
In view of the march and countermarch of conflicting ideas across the world stage, what possible conclusions or at least tentative guides to action exist? There are, of course, the obvious conclusions, the ones that have become cliches. The west must keep up its guard; it must remain strong and firm; it must turn its back on appeasement. With those statements it is impossible to disagree, for if we should forget them we are lost. But they are not enough. They take no cognizance of the possibilities for settlement by negotiation, slender though they be. They are not flexible enough to take advantage of opportunities for easing world tensions as such opportunities may occur.
If one might be permitted to paraphrase slightly an old watchword, the western nations should trust in God, negotiate and keep their powder dry or, perhaps I should say, keep their atomic nuclei fissionable.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. M. Fraser (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should first of all like to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the admirable exposition of policy which he presented to the house when he opened this debate. It was a most clear and comprehensive statement of the difficulties that face the free nations in the explosive area of the Far East.
I was particularly impressed by the skilful course which he charted through the shoals and shallows of the Formosa straits. If 1 may do so, Mr. Speaker, it is to the Formosan question that I should like to address my remarks tonight, and especially to the policy enunciated by the United States with reference to Formosa and the Pescadores. I do this because I think all hon. members will agree that that policy is fraught with

all-important consequences not only for the United States but for this country, and indeed for all the free countries of the world. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has so clearly put it, United States policy on Formosa is of vital concern to Canada.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that in order to set forth this policy we should go back to the statement made by President Eisenhower in his message to congress of January 24 of this year. It was in that statement that this policy was clearly enunciated. We should note also, I think, that this policy regarding Formosa is based upon the defensive treaty of last December between the United States and the government of Chiang Kai-shek, a treaty which was ratified by the United States Senate on February 9 of this year.
As I see it, the immediate objective of that policy was to prevent Peking from attacking Formosa, and to draw a line across which red China was warned she would advance at her peril. But we lose sight too easily, I think, of the other side of the picture, the second aspect of this policy. This policy of the United States not only warns Peking but it restrains Chiang Kai-shek from attacking the Chinese mainland. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this policy, by which the United States has put communist China on notice, is predicated upon the belief that the loss of Formosa to Peking would be a great disaster. If we consider the matter for a moment I think the soundness of this view is irresistible.
From the strategic point of view Formosa forms a vital link in that Pacific chain of defences which stretches from the Aleutians to the Philippines, and if Formosa were lost that chain would be snapped. Australia and New Zealand, sister countries in the commonwealth, would be in peril and indeed a break-out of the communist forces into the wide expanse of the Pacific would become a real possibility. Second, from the psychological point of view the fall of Formosa would be a very harsh blow to the confidence which the peoples of Asia are placing in the pledged word and the military strength of the United States. It would in particular, I think, undermine the confidence of the Chinese who are living in other parts of Asia, outside the mainland of China, and outside Formosa; in southeast Asia, for example. Such then, as I see them, are the main features of this United States policy.
I would next like to discuss the two main lines of criticism which have been directed against this policy. With the first of these lines I am disposed to agree. This first ground of criticism is that the line which has been drawn by the United States is too

blurred; it is not precise enough or definite enough, because it involves the offshore islands of Quemoy and Matsu as well as Formosa and the Pescadores, and because the United States has not definitely stated whether or not it will defend those two islands. Mr. Dulles, the secretary of state, has told us that they will not be defended as such, but they may be defended if the United States conceives that a red Chinese attack on them is a preliminary to an assault on Formosa and the Pescadores.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to agree with this view. I believe it would have been better if the line could have been drawn more definitely, more precisely. At the same time, however, I think we must try to understand the motives that lay behind the United States decision with regard to Quemoy and Matsu. As I see them, there may have been perhaps three reasons. The strategic reason, I think, was probably the least important of them. The position of these islands does, of course, enable a blockade to be maintained on Amoy and Foochow, and particularly enables supplies of jet fuel, for instance, coming by sea to be intercepted. This fact is of considerable importance, in view of the long haul across Asia from Russia, which is the only practical alternative.
More important, however, than the strategic reason is, I think, the diplomatic, the fact that the United States wanted to retain the freedom of manoeuvre, to use these two islands as a lever as it were with which to obtain the future acceptance of a ceasefire in Formosa. It may be claimed if such a pledge were made by Peking it might afterwards be repudiated, but in that case, of course, Peking would appear before the world condemned as a violator of the pledge. Then the moral case of the United States would be unassailable.
So much, then, for the first criticism to which United States policy has been subjected, a criticism with which, as I have said, I have a measure of agreement. The second ground of criticism is one which I cannot endorse. This is the ground which says that President Eisenhower's message to congress and the policy which is based on it mean a threat of war and are a provocation to communist China. I cannot agree with that, Mr. Speaker. In this connection, I should like to quote two or three extracts from the speech delivered by the President to congress on January 24, as reported in the New York Times of January 25:
The most important objective of our nation's foreign policy is to safeguard the security of the United States by establishing and procuring a just and honourable peace. In the western Pacific
External Affairs
a situation is developing in the Formosa straits that seriously imperils the peace and our security.
Not a word there about aggression, but rather defence of the United States and security. He went on:
In the interest of peace, therefore, the United States must remove any doubt regarding our readiness to fight if necessary to preserve the vital stake of the free world in a free Formosa, and to engage in whatever operations may be required to carry out that purpose.
Later in the same speech he added:
Again I say that we would welcome action by the United Nations which might in fact bring an end to the active hostilities in the area. This critical situation has been created by the choice of the Chinese communists, not by us. Their offensive military intent has been flaunted to the whole world by words and by deeds. Just as they created the situation, so they can end it, if they so choose.
The policy expressed in those words was overwhelmingly endorsed by the congress, in the House of Representatives by a vote of 409 to 3 and in the Senate by a vote of 85 to 3. I think it is clear, Mr. Speaker, from these quotations from the message on which the United States policy was based that that policy is not intended to threaten war but to safeguard peace, that its object is not to defend Chiang Kai-shek but to defend the peace of the world.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that any attempt to identify this policy with the defence of the Chiang Kai-shek regime appears to me an extremely superficial estimate of the situation in the Far East. It has been argued in this house that the Chiang Kai-shek regime is rotten, and that by allying itself with that regime the United States is allying itself with a government that does not deserve to exist but should be banished into exile, and that therefore the United States is pursuing a wrong policy. But as has been expressed by other speakers in this debate, and more particularly this evening by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), no matter what government were on Formosa the United States seventh fleet would still be defending that island today; because it is the island, not the government, that is of the essence of the question.
So far as that goes, though I hold no brief for Chiang Kai-shek nor for his entourage; though I admit they are no plaster saints, yet they do not in my mind compare unfavourably with the Chinese in Peking. I would not like to live under either of these governments, but if I had to choose I think I would choose the regime of Chiang Kai-shek.
In what I have said I hope I have succeeded in showing that the intentions of the United States have not been aggressive. I believe

External Affairs
the peaceful intentions of the United States have been convincingly demonstrated in recent months by several factors. First, let me recall to the house that the United States approved New Zealand's resolution in the United Nations security council, inviting Peking to discuss a cease-fire. The United States could have vetoed that invitation, but it did not do so. That invitation was allowed to go forward by Russia, as well. Yet on January 31 it was bluntly rejected by Peking.
Again, not only did the United States persuade Chiang Kai-shek to evacuate the Tachens and thereby relieve an explosive situation, but it actually provided its seventh fleet to help carry out that evacuation. Moreover, though subjected as we understand it to very strong pressure by the Chiang Kai-shek government, Mr. Dulles has steadfastly refused to comply with the repeated requests of Chiang Kai-shek to give an unconditional guarantee to defend Quemoy and Matsu as such-and I stress the words "as such". I believe also there are grounds for believing that Peking could have Quemoy and Matsu in return for a cease-fire, but up to now it has rejected all overtures for a cease-fire. There may even be indications also that the United States is moving-slowly, perhaps, but moving-toward acceptance of a two-Chinas principle.
Bearing all these things in mind I think we must agree that the United States, far from provoking war and far from taking an aggressive attitude, has gone out of its way to try to obtain a peaceful settlement of the Formosa question. In contrast, let us look at the attitude of Peking. First of all there was its rejection in very summary terms of the United Nations invitation to the cease-fire discussions. That rejection came on February 3. Likewise there was its intransigent reaction to diplomatic overtures which, we understand, have been carried out by the United Kingdom, by Mr. Nehru of India, and possibly also by Russia for a cease-fire in the Formosa straits.
We know, too, that the Chinese in Peking have been claiming that Chiang Kai-shek's withdrawal from the Tachens was a victory for them. And we are all too familiar with the repeated boasts emanating from Peking that the communist regime will take Formosa by the end of this year. Bellicose actions unfortunately are in keeping with the aggressive policy which Peking has been pursuing almost uninterruptedly since its intervention in the Korean conflict. Indeed, the Korean truce has been represented by Peking propaganda as a victory for communist arms. Likewise Peking has hailed the Geneva settlement of the Indo-Chinese war as a victory for herself.
[Mr. Fraser (St. John's East) .1
It does seem, Mr. Speaker, that these successes, or pseudo-successes, have intoxicated the Chinese communists with perhaps an exalted idea of their armed might. This mood in which they find themselves is very dangerous, because when men are intoxicated it is very difficult to reason with them. That. I think, is one of the reasons the situation in the Formosa straits is so terribly dangerous. The peace-loving governments must redouble their efforts to avert an explosion, to persuade Peking to adopt a more reasonable, more receptive attitude.
I am all in favour of unremitting negotiation, no matter how unlikely success may seem. Negotiation must be continued because the alternative is too horrible to contemplate; but negotiation must be accompanied by preparedness. We must not relax our vigilance; we must not drop our guard. A clear line must be taken, must be drawn and must be maintained. But if war does come-please God it may not-over the Formosa question, then as I see it the war guilt will not be with Washington but with Peking.
Now, as I have said, every possible effort must be made to prevent such a war arising. The immediate task is to negotiate a ceasefire. This would provide a breathing space, and we understand that efforts are being made to that end now. But a breathing space, though it is well so far as it goes, does not go far enough. A long-range solution must be found. Perhaps a beginning could be made by the cession of Quemoy and Matsu in return for a pledge from Peking to keep hands off Formosa; but a long-range solution must be of larger scope and in all modesty

for I know, of course, that the best brains in the armed services of all the countries of the world are engaged in this problem at present -may I make a tentative suggestion that might perhaps be worth considering.
I think, first of all, that long-range solution must be based upon some form of neutralization of Formosa, perhaps under United Nations guarantee. At the present time, of course, Formosa is in effect neutralized but by the United States. A United Nations guarantee might be more pacific, less dangerous; but I cannot agree with those who would suggest that Chiang Kai-shek be exiled along with his 600,000 soldiers. It is a difficult thing to exile 600,000 men. I confess I do not know where they might go. I think the nationalists should be permitted to retain Formosa, at least for the time being, if under a United Nations guarantee. Eventually there might be the possibility of a plebiscite among Formosans themselves, not yet I think because I doubt very much whether they have reached

the stage when they are capable of selfgovernment, and to hand over a strategic island to the administration of inexperienced hands at such a dangerous juncture would be most imprudent. But eventually training might precede a plebiscite.
You will notice I have not mentioned a trusteeship, because a trusteeship would suggest grave practical difficulties. It is all very well to speak of United Nations trusteeship. Who is to be the trustee? Who is to administer the trusteeship? I confess I find it hard to see that there could be agreement on a trustee at the present time, and collective trusteeship would very probably lead to friction and disagreement among the trustees themselves. The old question would arise, quis custodiet ipsos custodes? Eventually, too, there might be the possibility of enabling communist China to give sufficient proof of her good intentions, of a change of heart and then the question of her admission to the United Nations might be reconsidered.
Together with these purely political suggestions, Mr. Speaker, there must of course, I fully agree, be the provision of economic and technical assistance along the lines of the Point Four program and the Colombo plan; and even more important, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out in his speech, there must be a wholehearted
External Affairs
and sympathetic effort to encourage the peoples of southeast Asia and Formosa to develop democratic governments of their own under which they can live in peace and freedom. Only by these methods, military, political, economic and social, shall we be able to build up a true resistance to the onset of communism in the Far East. That must be done; otherwise, Mr. Speaker, the world balance of power might be upset, to the grave disadvantage of the freedom-loving nations.
If Formosa and southeast Asia were to fall under communism, either by invasion or by infiltration, then indeed the frontiers of freedom would be perilously narrowed.
On motion of Mr. Nesbitt the debate was adjourned.

1.	Is any research being carried out by the Department of National Health and Welfare regarding the harmful effect of atomic radiation on humans?
2.	Is any research being done in respect to radiation effects in Canada resulting from atom bomb tests that have taken place in the United States of America?
3.	Do researchers know anything about the genetic effect on humans of such radiation?

1. Yes. Radioactivity, of course, is not a new phenomenon. Since life first appeared on this planet, living beings have been exposed to cosmic and natural radiation. Thus it is not an essentially new influence which is being considered, but an increase in the intensity of an influence which has never been entirely absent.
It was not until the discovery of radium and X-rays over half a century ago that the possibility emerged that some human beings would be exposed to greater amounts of radiation than naturally occur in the everyday environment. Since that time, scientists have shown a continuing concern for the possible harmful effects of uncontrolled radiation. A system of protection has slowly developed, as is manifest by the precautions observed in the use of X-ray and radioactive materials and in the regulations governing the use of isotopes in this country since the war.
Problems associated with radiation have engaged the attention of officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare and of a number of other government agencies for more than ten years.

Experience gained during this period enabled Canada to pioneer in developing a promising advance in the treatment of cancer-the cobalt 60 beam therapy unit-which has since brought new hope to thousands of cancer victims and has received world-wide recognition. Many industrial uses of radioisotopes have also been developed in Canada, ranging all the way from testing the welds on enormous metal castings to controlling the thickness of paper as it comes through the paper-making machines. These isotopes have also been made available to other countries.
As a result, Canadian scientists have gained firsthand experience in the study of radiation effects and the development of adequate safeguards against them. On March 14 of this year, a reply was tabled which outlined some of the activities carried out by the department for the safe handling of radioactive materials.
The interest of the department in radiation, however, predates these more recent developments by several years. For example, since 1951 the department has accepted responsibility for the supervision of the use of radioactive isotopes in university and hospital laboratories and in industrial operations.
In carrying out this responsibility, a film monitoring service is maintained for the protection of persons working with radioactive isotopes. Advice is also provided during the planning stages of radioisotope laboratories in order that arrangements can be worked out for the safe handling of radioactive materials and for the disposal of radioactive waste in such a manner that there will be no danger of contamination. In addition, it is planned to provide training courses emphasizing the safe use of radiation.
Anticipating an increasing use in this country of radioactive materials for industrial and medical purposes, arrangements were made some time ago to send a senior physicist of the department to the United Kingdom for special training.
There is at all times continuing consultation between the Department of National Health and Welfare and other government agencies such as the national research council, the defence research board, and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, having an interest in this field.
As a result of all this joint effort, there is every reason to believe that the measures taken in this country for the protection of those persons who are likely to be exposed to radioactive materials are fully as effective as those carried out anywhere.

2.	Yes. This research is carried out, not with particular reference to experiments being undertaken in any one country, but with reference to the effects of radiation, from whatever source it may come, occurring in the different regions of Canada.
3.	Yes. The biological effects of increased radiation may be divided into two categories -the somatic effects, or those which lead to disease in the exposed individual; and the genetic effects, or those which cause changes, usually adverse, in his descendants. Any somatic effects which might arise would affect only the generation irradiated but genetic effects would show up in future generations.
As to somatic effects, it is the opinion of medical scientists that the most important results might be an increase in the incidence of certain malignant conditions, but these usually result from much higher radiation exposures than those which are now being considered.
With regard to the genetic effects, it has been established by experiments on certain rapidly-breeding lower forms of life, such as bacteria, plants, insects and small mammals, that genetic changes can be produced by exposure to radiation.
It is pointed out by geneticists that the characteristics transmitted from parents to offspring are determined by the structure of the genes. Certain genes produce certain characteristics, such as the colour of the eyes and so on. A particular gene may also be related to a physical or mental defect. It so happens that genes are capable of mutating or changing and that all such mutations, being permanent, are carried on in later generations.
In the exposure of experimental animals to radiation, there has been observed an increase in the rate at which these mutations occur. Usually no harmful effect shows up until, at some future time, mating takes place between two animals carrying the same mutated gene. Since a study of genetic changes in humans would inevitably take several generations, the belief that radiation might cause genetic damage in humans is based mainly on the evidence that it does so in other forms of life.
In determining genetic effects on man there are two principal difficulties. First, most mutations will remain hidden until one individual receives the same mutated gene from both parents. Secondly, naturally occurring genes for recessive defects and abnormalities are already numerous in the population. Neither these naturally occurring mutant genes nor those that might be induced by radiation are likely to produce an effect in
Questions
the children of the individuals carrying them unless the parents have received the same defect from a common ancestor.
In general, there has been much misunderstanding between the possible hazards to human health arising from weapon trials and those that would result from nuclear warfare, with the result that some of the more sensational statements made on this subject have been confusing.
Since there remain a number of unanswered questions in this field, there is a need for continuing research and investigation into the genetic problem. Increasingly large numbers of people are being exposed to increasing amounts of radiation because of the wider use of radioactive materials in industry, research and medicine. In addition, there has been a slight, though appreciable increase in radiation all over the world as a result of the weapon tests.
However, the best scientific evidence available, indicates that it is most unlikely that any significant genetic effect would result from the increased radioactivity that has occurred.
Canadian scientific experience in this connection is confirmed by that of research scientists in other countries. For example, in a statement in the British House of Commons on March 22 last, the minister of health, the Right Hon. Iain Macleod stressed these points:
(1)	Radiation does produce genetic effects and the radioactivity of the planet has increased slightly as the result of nuclear bomb explosions.
(2)	Present knowledge is insufficient to fix precisely the level of radioactivity above which genetic damage would significantly affect the well-being of populations.
(3)	Research in genetic changes is necessarily and inevitably slow in producing conclusive results.
(4)	It is extremely unlikely that the increase in radioactivity which has appeared up to the present will have any appreciable genetic effect.
While the genetic problem is exceedingly complex, the important factors are known and Canada possesses at the present time the scientific potential to carry on continuing investigations in this field. The Department of National Health and Welfare is pursuing research efforts with a view to the further development of a long-range program for the collection and study of human data that will aid in the assessment of this problem.
The department is carrying out a systematic and continuing examination of all evidence available in order to ascertain all of

Motions for Papers
the facts in connection with increased radiation. As the program develops further, it will involve, among other things, the constant examination of a variety of materials to determine the level of potentially dangerous radioactivity.
In furthering this project, full advantage will continue to be taken of the experience of outstanding Canadian scientists who have a particular knowledge of this field and every effort will be made to co-ordinate this longterm study with Canada's over-all public health program.
The government is fully aware of the problems posed in the field of public health by atomic developments and will continue to take proper steps to assess progressively the possible hazard to human health of increased radiation background.
