subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to give the committee this afternoon a fairly full explanation of what it is desired to accomplish under this resolution.
In introducing this resolution I make no apology for the fact that it is the second one under this heading recommended to this house in a period of less than 12 weeks. This measure today is by no means an afterthought of the one I presented in January. Instead, these and the January amendments are all one of the same piece. The reasons why I did not bring these forward in January were, first, that we wanted still more time to study the larger changes represented by this resolution before presenting them to the house. We wanted parliament to have ample opportunity for a full and detailed consideration of the proposed larger changes, after they came to this house. We wanted the item related to the improved supplementary benefits to go into effect in January so as to make its impact upon this winter's serious unemployment, which it has. So, in the light of those considerations, the only way I could see was to divide the task into two parts when seeking the necessary legislative approval. If and when the bill, based upon this resolution, receives royal assent, then the January amendment will have been absorbed and will be administered as part of the new consolidated act. As study

on these matters was in progress I was curious to see what was in the minds of those who were here when the present act was passed through the various stages of this parliament.
I found it very interesting and, I think, useful reading. The first resolution, corresponding to the one we have here today was introduced by my predecessor, Hon. Norman McLarty on July 16, 1940.
I am going to quote from part of that resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to enact a scheme ol national unemployment insurance to be administered by a commission appointed by the governor in council, and to create an unemployment insurance fund from contributions from specified persons and from moneys provided by parliament for the payment of insurance benefits, to be administered by the commission . . .
That was the main part of the resolution. There are patches of Mr. McLarty's speech that I find of special interest:
It has received in principle the approval of every section of this house. It has received the consent of every province in the dominion. It passed the parliament at Westminster within the last two weeks in less than nineteen minutes of debate.
Then further on:
At the time the resolution was passed asking the parliament at Westminster to confer the necessary power to enact this legislation, we were at war. We are at war today; but I suggest that the particular occasion has not changed in so far as the desirability of this measure of social legislation is concerned.
I am sure it is very difficult for us today to put ourselves back into the dangerous atmosphere of that 16th day of July in 1940 when Mr. McLarty was talking about that first resolution. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) said Friday evening:
There was nothing in the arithmetic of war in the summer of 1940 to show how victory was going to come to .Britain.
It is inspiring therefore to read how under the dangers of that summer this government with the unanimous backing of parliament was clearing the ground by amending the British North America Act and introducing a resolution that made possible what Mr. McLarty called "this measure of social legislation". I have read the debates of that day and there are enlightening passages. One is greatly tempted of course to quote at length but I shall refrain from doing so and read just a few extracts at random. Mr. McLarty said:
The total number of workers in 1941 who will be under this act is 2,100,000.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The figure today is of course around 4,000,000. Then he went on to say:
It is almost trite to suggest that an unemployment insurance measure does not exercise its full benefit at a time when employment is at a low level. Necessarily the fund which must be created can best be created in a period of high employment. On July 1 this year employment in this country was higher than it has ever been at any time in our history.
Hon. R. B. Hanson, then leader of the opposition and representing in this house the great constituency of York-Sunbury, is reported on page 1562 of Hansard as having said:
This scheme must be on a sound actuarial basis, and we must have concrete evidence that such is the fact. It will not do to adopt any scheme or plan which is simply a device for transmitting money raised by general taxation or borrowing.
And again:
There is a class of workers in this country who may be called "safe" employees. Perhaps that is not very well put. There are those in "safe" employment in this country who, under any scheme, if they are brought under the act . . . will be taxed for the benefit of those who are engaged in what might be termed the "exposed" positions.
Mr. Hanson here outlined the whole idea behind the insurance plan. Then the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Mac-Innis) is reported at page 1658 of Hansard, still dealing with unemployment insurance, as saying:
I have always supported it, not only on this occasion but every time it has been brought up in the house. As a matter of fact, as a member of organized labour of long standing I supported this principle long before it was accepted by many in this house. But to say that it is not a cure for all our social ills, and even to say it is not a cure for unemployment, is only stating a fact. There is something it does; as far as it goes it is a planned and orderly way of dealing with a social problem and to that extent I think it should have the approval of everyone who believes in dealing with these matters in an orderly, planned manner.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han-sell), speaking for the Social Credit party, is reported on page 1662 of Hansard as follows:
I do not believe that our group will be found in opposition to this legislation. Broadly speaking, under the present economic setup, it will help to some extent to relieve unemployment so far as financing the unemployed is concerned.
I need not go on to repeat what was said about monetary policy. Finally I should like to give this summary by Mr. McLarty:
The surest foundation on which to base democratic government is a happy and contented people. Nothing militates more against happiness and contentment than fear.

Unemployment Insurance Act
Then referring to the passing of the act he said:
This done, it will be recorded of the present generation that . . . we were not unconscious of our duty and our obligation to promote the welfare and happiness of our own people.
That ends my quotations. All of this was under 15 years ago. Ever since then I am glad to say that this contributory social measure has retained the full support that it had in 1940 of all parties represented in this house. It was a new plan and new and difficult ground had to be broken, but whenever it became quite clear that it could be improved to meet more effectively the conditions experienced by our Canadian workers this government has recommended that such improvements be made.
So the present act was passed in its original form by parliament on August 7, 1940. The original measure set an upper limit on salaried workers coming under the plan of $2,000 and provided these benefits:
A weekly maximum for a single person of $12.24 and for a person with a dependent a weekly maximum of $14.40.
I should like to indicate the principal changes which have been made and the years in which they were made. I refer to them because they were important changes. The Hon. Humphrey Mitchell in 1943 brought in changes that eased the conditions for requalifying in a second benefit period; raised the insurable limits for salaried workers from $2,000 to $2,400 a year; and brought under insurance all workers paid by the hour, day, piece or mile, regardless of the amount of yearly earnings.
In 1946 Mr. Mitchell again brought in changes which broadened the interpretation of a dependent; increased the allowable subsidiary earnings for claimants from $1 to $1.50 a day; and extended the coverage to seamen-both deep sea and inland waters.
In 1948 Mr. Mitchell brought in changes which added a higher contribution class and increased maximum weekly benefits to $14.40, single rate, and $18.30, dependency rate; again widened the definition of a dependent and raised the ceiling for salaried workers from $2,400 to $3,120 a year.
In 1950 during the illness of Mr. Mitchell these changes were brought in by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). They were important changes because they incorporated a completely new provision to help take care of the difficulties arising from our Canadian climate. The changes in 1950 added still

further contribution classes and again increased maximum weekly benefit rates to $16.20, single rate, and $21, dependency rate; provided for supplementary benefit payments in the winter months, January 1 to March 31; raised the ceiling from $3,120 to $4,800; and extended coverage to the logging industry in all parts of Canada.
In 1952 I brought in changes which increased the maximum weekly benefits to $17.10, single rate, and $24, dependency rate, and reduced the waiting period from eight days to five days.
In 1953 I brought in changes which provided for continuing benefit payments to persons who become incapacitated after starting to receive unemployment benefits.
In January, 1955, changes were introduced which increased the duration of supplementary benefit payments and brought up the rates to the level of regular benefits; and now we are proposing further changes in the plan.
Mr. Chairman, in all the changes and amendments I have mentioned above, several objectives have constantly been kept in view. One of them is that the insurance plan shall be maintained on a sound actuarial basis; that both the employment and insurance phases of the plan shall be adapted to meet Canada's special conditions; that the bulk of contributions be paid by the two parties directly benefited-workers and management -with the taxpayers at large making the minority contribution and bearing administration costs; that higher benefits be provided a worker with a family, compared with those to the worker with no dependents; that the benefits designed to alleviate the hardships of unemployment should not be of a nature that would lessen the incentive to work when jobs are available; and that an important accompaniment of the plan is to help workers find suitable jobs through the national employment service, and management find suitable workers.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that Canada can take a good deal of satisfaction out of the effective way in which this plan has been working out for the benefit of Canadian workers. Since Mr. McLarty's time about an average of 3,500,000 workers have come under it. It has also been to the advantage of the 250,000 employers who participate in the act and it has also been of great advantage, to my mind, to all the rest of us.
Benefits from this plan, payable to the unemployed workers entitled to them, regardless of their other resources, have helped to maintain purchasing power and greater stability in local labour markets especially during periods of temporary unemployment.

They have taken some of the burden of relieving the unemployment costs of the municipalities and public welfare agencies.
This has been done by a method that preserves the self-respect of the worker, because when he is out of a job he gets a weekly benefit that is not charity but something he has helped pay for himself.
During the immediate past fiscal year, for the first 11 months some $210 million was paid in insurance benefit, with $35 million in February last.
All told, from the inception of the scheme to the end of February of this year insured workers have received almost one billion dollars.
The plan has done something more, and, of primary importance. It has made available, through the national employment service, facilities for enabling workers to find jobs and for employers to find workers.
This is a service that is free, that is available to insured and non-insured workers alike, and that is given without any discrimination because of race, colour, national origin, politics or religion.
From July 1941 to the present date the employment service helped to place nearly 14 million Canadian workers.
However, over the years the act in its present form has become somewhat complicated. Simplification has been needed that workers and employers might more readily understand its terms and that the administration by the commission might be facilitated.
Experience has shown that the amount of protection at present given to certain groups of workers is not enough.
Unemployment Insurance Act
This is particularly true of young workers who have not been in insured employment very long and of workers who are not able to secure steady employment.
Also, some benefit rates are no longer in line with earnings and they need to be raised.
The new seasonal benefits initiated in January last should be made to apply to future winter seasons.
There did appear to be the need of providing for a better income maintenance plan.
It is also desirable that the amount of work it puts upon employers should be kept to the minimum necessary, and that efficient and economical administration should be possible.
These objectives have been kept in view in the proposed revision of the legislation.
The most important changes concern the contributions and benefits.
The contribution rates and the basis on which they are paid have both been revised. At present, workers made their contributions to the fund on a daily rate basis.
In the lower wage brackets these rates are a considerably larger percentage of the worker's earnings than in the higher brackets.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask permission to insert some tables in Hansard, if I have unanimous consent to do so, because it will be seen more clearly by hon. members if it is tabled.

It is proposed that future contributions be made on the basis of weekly rates of about 1 per cent of earnings, with a like amount contributed by employers.
There will be nine earnings classes and the scale of contributions will run from 16 to 60 cents a week. This just slightly exceeds 1 per cent of average earnings in every contribution class. It thus makes the contributions more equitable in that the rate of contribution as a percentage of earnings shows much less variation than the present scale. This will be seen more clearly by referring to the table I have just now tabled.
Generally speaking, the contribution payable by a worker will be lower than that now required for the corresponding earnings class. At the same time the regrouping of the contribution classes will provide additional classes in the higher earnings ranges, so that additional and higher rates of benefit will be available to workers in those earnings classes.
At present, the maximum contributory bracket is reached when a person earns $48 or more a week. The new scale provides for three further classes, which carry on up to earnings of $57 or more a week, as indicated in the tables.
The change from a daily to a weekly rate of contribution will help also to simplify the administration of the act. It will reduce the work involved for employers where contributions are made through the use of stamps,

since six daily stamps will be replaced by one weekly stamp. The contributions will be based on earnings without reference to any specific number of days. The stamp placed in the book will represent the actual earnings in a week whether the period being worked be one or more days. If there is more than one employer in a week, two or more stamps will be placed in the weekly space up to the maximum contribution required of 80 cents from the worker and 60 cents from his employer. All the stamps acquired in a week will be counted as one week's contribution and the worker will be given credit for the total contributions made so far as benefit rate is concerned.
The benefit rate will be determined by the average rate of contributions in the last 30 contributory weeks. Where the earnings in a week are in a very low range provision is made for crediting only half of a stamp, to avoid penalizing a claimant by lowering his average weekly contribution rate unduly. The present insurance book and contribution records will be retained with suitable modifications to fit in with the revised proposals previously outlined.
As to the benefit features, there are several material changes. I give, first, the reasons for them. Experience has made it clear that the present act does not give sufficient protection to workers who are just entering insurable employment and those who by force of circumstance are not able to find steady

work. At the same time it provides longer protection than is required for the vast majority of workers. We have found that although about one-third of all those establishing benefit rights are entitled to 180 days or more under the present act, only about one-twentieth actually draw benefits for a period longer than 180 days. Many of these one-twentieth are married women and elderly people for whom alternative social security programs would seem to be more appropriate.
We feel that it is particularly important to provide better protection for young people just entering insurable employment and for those workers who can do little more than meet the minimum contribution requirements because of the effect, for instance, of seniority clauses in collective agreements. These clauses mean that when lay-offs do occur, substantially the same group of workers lose their jobs each time, thus interrupting the build-up in their contributions and reducing their benefit entitlement. In other words, the very workers who have needed protection the most have often found their opportunity to earn it is severely limited through no fault of their own.
For these reasons, we are proposing that the benefit formula be changed so that a greater amount of protection is made available to workers who have not been able to find steady work. The present formula provides a minimum of 6 weeks' benefit and a maximum of 51 weeks' benefit, depending on the length of time for which an insured person has contributed. To qualify for the minimum of 6 weeks a worker must have made, in the two years preceding his claim, 180 daily contributions, or the equivalent of 30 weeks' contributions.
The new benefit formula will provide a minimum of 15 weeks of benefit, instead of 6, for all workers who have made 30 weekly contributions in the two years preceding a claim for benefits. It will be possible for workers to earn additional weeks of benefit by additional contributions on the basis of one week's benefit for two weeks' contributions that have been made within the two years prior to the claim.
The maximum regular benefit will be 30 weeks. For the increased number of workers who will now qualify also for seasonal benefits the maximum total of regular plus seasonal benefits will be 45 weeks. I will outline the seasonal benefits later. I might indicate here, Mr. Chairman, that the reason the name "seasonal" is proposed instead of "supplementary" is because it was felt it was a better name for the benefits referred to.
4. 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act
Approximately 95 per cent of all claimants now draw less than 30 weeks' benefit. The new benefit formula will therefore take care of the great majority of persons who ordinarily work in insurable employment. At the same time it will provide much greater protection to those who do not have long and steady employment by lowering the maximum entitlement available, which has been made use of by only a small number of workers, and by increasing substantially the minimum amount of benefit available. The total effect of this change is to redistribute the amount of protection so that a greater proportion of it can actually be taken advantage of by insured workers who become unemployed.
The actuaries have estimated that, if these provisions had been in effect a year ago, the net result of lowering the maximum and increasing the minimum entitlement as now proposed would have been an increase in the number of benefit days available to claimants of approximately 4J million, or an increase of about 6 per cent. The changes as a whole will mean that fewer claimants will exhaust their benefit before finding work. In the past the majority of workers using up all their benefit rights were those whose entitlement was less than 15 weeks. The new act will in practice give greater protection to a greater number of workers and will tend to concentrate that benefit where it is most needed.
At this point I should like to say, however, that we were concerned as to the existing equity of those workers who are under the present plan in making the proposal that the duration of the maximum regular benefit be cut from 51 to 30 weeks. To take care of that matter we are here proposing the following. In view of the reduction of the maximum duration of regular benefit from 51 to 30 weeks, it is felt desirable to provide for a transitional period during which those who have accumulated credits under the present act might be eligible for more than the maximum of 30 weeks of regular benefits under the present proposal. Although the new act will provide better protection for the great majority of workers, we have felt it is important to ensure that no one loses any equity which a presently insured worker may have built up over the years under the present act prior to these amendments. This objective will be accomplished by providing for a transitional period of three years from the time the new act comes into force.
During these three years, all workers who exhaust the benefits available to them in their first benefit year under the new act

Unemployment Insurance Act will have their contribution record reexamined to determine whether or not they might have received more benefits under the old act. In the great majority of cases they will already have exceeded the amount of benefit protection they would have received under the old act. However, if it is found that they would have received more protection under the old act they will then be given the additional benefit coming to them on the old basis. In this way no worker will lose any equity which he may have built up over the years, while the great majority will receive a much greater protection under the new arrangement.
The adoption of a weekly contribution basis rather than a daily one will make it easier for workers to build up contribution rights, particularly if they are forced to accept short-time employment. For example, if a person ordinarily working on a five-day week goes on short time of four days a week, under the daily stamp system he would receive four daily stamps for his week's work rather than one weekly stamp. That meant that, if the short-time condition lasted for three months, under the old daily plan he would be credited with 52 days or 8J weeks. Under the new weekly plan he will be credited with 13 weeks.
In order to requalify after a benefit period has terminated, a claimant will have to acquire additional credits by building up eight weeks of contributions in insurable employment since the commencement of his previous claim, and have at least 30 contribution weeks in the previous two years. Contribution weeks more than a year old at the time of a subsequent claim, if they have already been used on a previous claim, cannot be used a second time to qualify either for rate or duration.
With respect to benefits, we are proposing to increase the weekly benefit rates. The new maximum for a person with a dependent will be $30 per week in place of the present $24 per week, and for a single person it will be $23 per week instead of $17.10. The scale from there down is shown in the tables which I have filed. When the act first came into operation the scale of benefit rates was designed to preserve a certain relationship between the ordinary rate of earnings and the benefit payable. This relationship has been impaired as a result of the rise in wage rates and, as a large number of insured persons have moved into the top benefit class, the ratio of benefit to average earnings has dropped considerably. By a revision of the earnings classes it is intended to restore the proper relationship between benefit and ordinary earnings, so that this will not result

in over-insurance in the lower earnings ranges or in under-insurance in the upper earnings ranges. This is shown in the tables.
Another very important feature is the provision of what will now be known as seasonal benefits. These seasonal benefits will replace the supplementary benefits in the present act, and will incorporate substantially the changes recently made during this session. It is proposed that seasonal benefits be available to the same two classes of workers as at present, namely, those who exhaust their regular benefits after April 15 of any year, and those who do not have sufficient contributions to qualify for regular benefit but have made 15 weekly contributions subsequent to March 31 preceding their claim. Like the supplementary benefits, these seasonal benefits will be available from January 1 to April 15 of each year. They will provide the full rate of benefit for 15 weeks in the case of those who exhaust their benefit rights and for from 10, formerly 3, to 15, formerly 6, weeks in the case of those who have at least 15 but not 30 weeks of contributions.
The protection offered by these seasonal benefits is the same and in some instances better than that now available from supplementary benefits after the amendments made last January. The present method of paying benefit on a daily basis, under the act as it now stands, is involved and leads to a number of difficulties where holidays and short-time employment are concerned, particularly where some claimants are on a five-day week and others are on a six-day week. In addition, the provision that the first day of unemployment shall be non-compensable and also the provision with regard to earnings from subsidiary employment are misunderstood by claimants and, I might add, by a great many other people. To overcome this, the new plan proposes that the non-compensable day be eliminated and that claimants be allowed to earn a specified amount during a claim week without reducing their benefit. Earnings above this amount will be deducted from the benefit payable.
It will be immaterial whether the allowable earnings are from subsidiary employment carried on outside of the claimant's usual hours of work or from any other type of employment. This new provision will simplify the computation of benefit and will provide a greater measure of protection to workers who can find casual employment or who are working short time. It is not proposed to make any change in the effect of the waiting period, but a minor change is proposed. The waiting period at the beginning of a benefit year can now be deferred to

a later date in order to prevent hardship when a new benefit year commences after a claimant has been unemployed for some time. It is now proposed that the waiting period in such cases be waived entirely, if this has not already been done within the preceding year.
A number of other amendments of a minor character and a general rearrangement and consolidation will be found in the bill. It will be complete in itself, incorporating all the required sections of the existing act whether amended or unamended. I shall ask that the bill be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations after second reading.
When the unemployment insurance advisory committee met on December 14 last to review the amendments regarding seasonal benefits, it was of course necessary for the committee to have before it the views regarding this general revision as they were then held. Later when plans had further crystallized to the point where they were nearly the same as the amendments now proposed, a further meeting of the advisory committee was held on February 15. In order to review these final recommendations, as reflected in the actual bill, the committee has called a further meeting for tomorrow, April 5.
I think it would be in order on this occasion for me, as the minister responsible for the time being to the government and to parliament for reporting on the operations of the unemployment insurance commission, to say a word or two about those who are responsible for the carrying out of the will of parliament in the administration of this legislation. The commission is a semi-autonomous federal government agency. It is proposed that its status in this regard shall remain unchanged. It is an agency with large, far-flung central, regional and local offices whose workers have a very intimate contact with the lives of fellow workers in private industry throughout the country. After the first of the year the unemployment insurance commission workers were called upon to superimpose the new seasonal benefits upon their administrative machinery. This was done without hitch or fuss and with no delay in service to their customers. Both employment and insurance workers in those offices have now just passed a peak work load that has had more stresses and strains this winter than at any time in the past.
Mistakes have been made and I know that complaints have been received by hon. members. Yet with all that a great deal of evidence has come to me this winter to indicate that our staff has been coping with the situation in most commendable fashion. Further,
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act in spite of the pressures they have continued to apply the provisions and the benefits of the act with the whole accent constantly placed on the factor of human need. For that I wish to express appreciation this afternoon.
It will be apparent from what I have said, Mr. Chairman, that what the government is here proposing is not merely a series of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is something much more fundamental than that. We are undertaking, in fact, the most far-reaching revisions of our unemployment insurance program that have been attempted in the decade and a half of its existence during the course of the seven times the legislation has been reviewed by the house.
The act since 1940 has served as the steady bulwark of protection in times of unemployment for an average of 3,500,000 Canadian workers and their families. During this time, it has proved a flexible and effective federal instrument of social security. This was the first of the comprehensive nation-wide social security measures which marked, in the postdepression years, the emergence of a new sense of social responsibility on the part of the Canadian people.
Born out of the suffering and the hardship of the great depression, the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 established a new dimension of social statesmanship to which all our subsequent social legislation-family allowances, the new veterans charter, old age security, the national health program, rehabilitation of civilian disabled, have faithfully conformed. It was the passage of the Unemployment Insurance Act which enabled my predecessor, who introduced it, and all his fellow countrymen, for the first time to speak of "a Canadian social security program".
The system which has developed from those first beginnings owes much to the pioneering spirit of those who brought in this enactment. In a very special sense it has been called a twentieth century bill of rights for the Canadian worker.
What we are doing today, in the new legislation which I have the honour to introduce, is adding a worthy addition to the steadily-growing structure of social security that we have been building in Canada. Approval of these proposals will go far to provide an answer to the problems of the large number of our workers who undergo short periods of unemployment such as has been experienced these past few winters.
I have every confidence that on the basis of this sound foundation, supplemented by whatever additional measures will be worked

Unemployment Insurance Act out in the forthcoming co-operative discussions with the provinces, the Canadian wage earner will be able to look forward with confidence to a new era of incentive, security and opportunity better than anything that he has yet known.
I commend this resolution to the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It has been indicated that the hon. member for Fort William wishes to ask the minister a question.
I was wondering if it would be possible for us to have this bill to take with us during the recess, as it is most important that we should have time to study it.
The bill is ready. What the hon. member suggests, of course, will depend upon the discussion taking place in the house.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I had not intended to go in any detail into the history of the Unemployment Insurance Act. However, inasmuch as the minister has made quite a point of tracing back the origin of the act of 1940, and inasmuch as at the close of his remarks today he has referred to this act as the first, to use his words, of the comprehensive nation-wide security measures-and there was much more in the same vein-I feel it would not be proper for us to proceed with the discussion of this measure without bearing in mind that it was on February 12, 1935, that the late R. B. Bennett, who was then prime minister of Canada, introduced to the House of Commons the first unemployment insurance scheme.
Which the courts disallowed.

Which the courts disallowed, as the hon. member for Spadina has said, and quite rightly. And why? Because the Liberal government which followed the government of Mr. Bennett in that same year made it a point, as one of its first items of business, to throw that act to the courts, in the hope that it would be disallowed, instead of seeking the co-operation of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is this an attack on the courts?

No, this is an answer to some of the truck that has been thrown into the debates in the House of Commons for many years. Certainly since my entry to the house I have had to listen to it; and I am not going to listen to that sort of stuff any longer.
I suppose there is rarely a piece of legislation introduced that does not have some flaws in it. Granted that, at the time the legislation was brought down, it probably did

not have the support it should have had from the provinces, still it would have been a simple matter to have obtained that support, had the government so wished. But the government did not.
They did not wish it.

They did not wish it to have any support, and they made no effort to get the support of the provinces. And so, rather than implement a piece of legislation brought in by a Conservative government, the Liberal government of Mr. King sought to destroy that legislation and, indeed, succeeded in destroying it, although six years later, having delayed the protection which was due to the workers of this country for that period of time, the Liberal government then brought in what was basically the same legislation.
Now, in 15 years conditions change.
Under a Liberal government.
They change for the worse.
I might add they also changed after 1921. But memories are short. I remember back to 1921. I was one of those out of work in 1921, as I was in 1931.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: When the hon. member says that, she disillusions us.
She must have been only a kid.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: She was a little girl then.

Anyone who comes to the House of Commons has no right to have any illusions.
As I was about to say, there have been many changes since this act came into force in 1940. Wage rates have doubled. Hours of work in some instances have been almost cut in half. Certainly several of the provinces have introduced legislation respecting maximum hours of work, and labour itself has negotiated for an even shorter work week than that dictated in much of the legislation on the provincial statute books.
All this has created an entirely different labour picture from that in effect in 1940. In 1940 and 1941, when this act began to operate, the economic conditions in the country were entirely different. As the minister said, when quoting Mr. McLarty, we were in the midst of war. It is to be expected that over the years coverage would be extended, and that there would be changes in the act. The official opposition has supported the government in respect of most of those changes, and has even made suggestions for what it considered to be a broadening of the provisions of the act.

In the meantime the fund has grown steadily. Within the last nine years it has more than trebled. In the thirteenth annual report of the commission I find that on March 31, 1945, the fund stood at $268 million. On March 31, 1954, one year ago, the amount in the fund was $881,225,000. The latest figures which are available, namely those of February 28, just a little over a month ago, show that the fund stands at $869 million, which is slightly below the amount at which it stood on March 31, a year ago. There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Chairman, that when the figures are available at the end of the current year they will show that the fund is lower than that because the calls which have been made upon it have been particularly heavy this year. However, in spite of this reduction it is a fact that the fund is still running in the neighbourhood of $900 million. This in itself is a sign that the plans which were laid and the alterations which have been made in the act over the years have in no way injured the fund, and we now ask ourselves whether it is too large.
After what we have been through this year,
I do not think many of us would want to see it depleted, but we certainly do not think it was ever contemplated that the fund would reach unwieldy proportions. In each instance, when the minister has brought suggestions to the house for alterations in contributions-I recall when the supplementary benefits were put into effect and when the one cent a day increase was brought in-we all thought that the supplementary benefits would eat up the additional contribution, and probably the payment of the supplementary benefits would deplete the fund in spite of the additional contributions made to it. That did not prove to be the case, and time went on. As I said, we now have a fund of approximately $900 million. This brings up the problem of just where we are going and whether the workers of this country have the coverage to which they are entitled. There are still several classes of workers who are not covered, and some of those classes have repeatedly asked for coverage. I am not going to try to deal with them all. I should like to mention one in particular, namely, the coverage to be afforded to fishermen.
In January of this year, when the former amendments to the act were under consideration, to which the minister referred, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich made a plea for fishermen and men who are connected with the fishing industry. He referred to tradesmen who were employed by fishing companies and who were in employment which is deemed insurable. I think I could do
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act no better than to read this short description which he gave, when he said, as reported at page 77 of Hansard:
There are certain companies which are engaged in the fishing industry and which employ a large number ol men who are not actual fishermen in that they are not employed in the catching of fish but they are connected with the lifting of fish from various fish traps which are established legally in the strait of Juan de Fuca. I refer particularly to men who are employed in such companies as the Sooke Harbour Fishing and Packing Company as pile drivers, and men who are employed in the repair of the leads which guide the fish into their traps. These men are not fishermen in the ordinary sense of the word. They do not go out in boats to catch fish. They are employed in the fishing industry, but they are very definitely tradesmen of another classification.
The hon. member was speaking of fishermen in general and of tradesmen employed in the fishing industry as well. I would think, Mr. Chairman, that no one who knows anything about the problem of fishermen being considered eligible for unemployment insurance will minimize the complications which are involved in finding a basis, under the act as it now stands, by which assessments to the equivalent of the contributions of wage earners and employers could be collected from fishermen. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, as I quoted, described some of the anomalies that exist on the west coast. It is also a fact that the west coast fishing is very well organized. There should be no difficulty, I would think, in producing a formula for coverage of employees in that industry. Likewise, in Ontario, fishermen have become well organized in associations and co-operative marketing and I would think that they could quickly rally to any realistic requirement that would enable them to contribute and benefit from the unemployment insurance fund. Everyone knows of the large and successful Quebec united fishermen's co-operative, which could readily bring about the means of enabling fishermen and the buyers of the products of their labour to contribute to the unemployment insurance fund so that the fishermen could reap the benefits therefrom. I do not think there is any doubt that the organized fisheries industry, the strong co-operatives and the private corporations which exist in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick could quickly agree to meet the requirements of regulations designed to enable the fishermen to gain the benefits of unemployment insurance. Nova Scotia has never been backward in reaching out and claiming just deserts for her sons, and I am sure that the industry in that province likewise could be quickly organized to participate in this scheme.
The production of the labour of by far the majority of the fishermen in Newfoundland, I understand, is marketed under the administrative direction of the federal government

Unemployment Insurance Act fisheries board, and it has contracts with an exporting organization of dry salted fish known as the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited, better known to us as NAFEL. Between this federal government board and the exporting agency, I would think that the administration machinery is available through which to implement an assessment on the product of the labours of fishermen in that province as a means of admitting them to eligibility under the unemployment insurance scheme.
With respect to Newfoundland in particular, Mr. Chairman, I think a great many promises were made during the election campaign of 1953, which I hope the minister is now prepared to fulfil within the framework of the revised Unemployment Insurance Act. It is advisable that the coverage for unemployment insurance should be as wide as possible, and should embrace as many categories of workers as possible. I am not without some knowledge of the difficulties that appear in certain classifications, and I realize that some of our workers might never find it possible to participate in this scheme. But on the other hand there are some, such as those I have just mentioned, who, with a little ingenuity on the part of the government, could be included in both the contributions to and benefits from unemployment insurance.
The labour force, as reported on February 19, was 5,391,000. According to the report of the unemployment insurance commission, to which I referred a few minutes ago dated March 31, 1954, the coverage of paid workers was 61-6 per cent. Surely, Mr. Chairman, in a country as broad as Canada, which the labour department and the unemployment insurance commission have reputedly so well organized, a larger percentage of the labour force could be included, now that the foundation has been laid, now that 15 years have gone by and various amendments have been made to the act from time to time.
I call upon the minister when he is discussing this bill with the advisory committee, which I think he said would be tomorrow, to discuss this phase also because it would seem to me that in the time which has elapsed since the last survey was made, of the fishing industry for instance, some four years ago, the advisory committee must have more information available.
Then with reference to the amendments to the act in general: In January when this was first mentioned in the speech from the throne a number of articles appeared in the newspapers, I think mostly Canadian Press dispatches, which sought to guess at the type of amendment which would be forthcoming. The main guess at that time was that the
[Mrs. Fairclough.l

recording of contributions by stamps in books of employees would be discontinued and a method substituted of a 1 per cent deduction matched by the employer, the employer to remit these funds monthly to the unemployment insurance commission.
But as time went on we heard no more about that. Now the minister is bringing down his bill and has made his announcement with reference to the changes. I noticed that two or three days ago the newspapers had pretty much the same material which the minister gave to us today and it became apparent that rather than have a 1 per cent levy the stamp system would be retained although in a more easily handled way. I must say that now that this report has been corroborated by the minister it is apparent from some of the changes he has mentioned that they will undoubtedly smooth out some of the administrative difficulties, not only from the point of view of the department but at the employer level as well.
There is no doubt that the perforated stamp system in use was a complicated method of recording the days worked and frequently resulted in the elimination from the benefits, or the disqualification from benefits, of employees who had worked as much as 175 of the 180 days within the required period of eligibility. Some of these people found that rather hard to take.
As I understand the new scheme, there will be a weekly stamp and a requirement of 30 weeks of contributions rather than 180 days. It will be possible for an employee to benefit if he has had any work at all in the 30 weeks regardless of whether it is one day or five days. I think that that is all to the good.
Some of the other amendments which are suggested, I take it, will reduce the rate of contribution for those in the lower wage brackets and provide benefits at a higher rate for those workers in the higher wage brackets. All of which is likewise to the good.
Whether the average which has been struck by the department will prove to be sufficiently high remains to be seen. I realize the difficulties under which the department must labour in trying to strike a balance which will provide sufficient benefits for the employee without making work completely unattractive to those who consider that receiving benefits is better than working. I think that those are definitely in the minority, that most of the workers in this country would prefer to work at their regular jobs no matter what the benefits were.
There are some things about the references which have been made that concern me. I am very much concerned about the reason

for the curtailment in the number of benefit days whereby the maximum is reduced from 51 weeks to 30 weeks. I realize that the minister has said that during the transition period care will be taken to see that a worker who has built up a reserve will not suffer. However, this is going to go on for some time and the day will come when people who are retired either voluntarily or compulsorily will find that they cannot claim the benefits which they have built up over many years of working.
Certain it is that many people in industry today are compelled to give up their jobs to younger workers at as early an age as 60 years, with 65 years being the popular age. We talk about the benefits which have been made available to workers and we do a lot of bragging about our old age security scheme and our old age security program which are in effect in Canada, but it seems to me that there is a wide gap between the age at which a man may be forced to retire and the age at which old age security payments would become available to him. In those intervening years one thing which has helped the average worker in forced retirement has been these 51 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits.
It is all very well to assume that these benefits are not in effect insurance benefits but are a sort of pension for these workers who have been retired, but I maintain that regardless of the reason for the severance from employment, a man who has contributed for many years to unemployment insurance is entitled to the full benefits. The fact that his severance from employment is due to an industrial ruling which throws out of work all people over a certain age in a given plant should not mean that he will not receive the benefit of the contributions which he has made over the years.
This thing will hit those very people who have been the backbone of the unemployment insurance scheme, that is those people with steady jobs who work along day after day, week after week and year after year without any hope of benefiting because they never expect to be unemployed. True enough, their first unemployment is when they are forced to retire. Many of these people are capable of taking employment. They go to the unemployment insurance office and register for employment but there is none available because of their age.
It would appear that in these amendments it is proposed to cut down their benefits from the 51 weeks which were available to them previously to 30 weeks. If I am to understand that, from what I heard the minister say and from what I have read in the newspapers, then we will oppose it because it is
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act not proper that these people should be refused benefits at the very time when they need the benefits to which they have contributed for many years.
I should now like to say a few words with respect to allowable earnings. I was interested in the minister's remarks. I hope that in the regulations governing this amendment the worker will be permitted to glean his allowable earnings from whatever source he pleases. That was the construction that I put upon the remarks made by the minister. It has certainly been the case heretofore that if the worker had employment which paid him $2 a day he forfeited $4 of unemployment insurance benefits which is little enough incentive to work.
I know of one man who obtained night employment which paid him $16 a week and because of that he lost his unemployment insurance benefits of $24 a week. The only solution was for him to work for less money. Eventually he decided to retain the same job but suggested to his employer that instead of being paid $16 a week he should be paid $10 and this was done. By reason of having the earnings derived from his subsidiary employment reduced to less than two-thirds of their value he was able to retain his unemployment insurance benefits. The alternative course would have been for him to stay at home, not work at all and collect the $24 on which he could not live anyway.
One of the outcomes of this system was demonstrated in Hamilton last week. We had a snowstorm-not as severe a storm as we had in Ottawa, but quite a heavy snowstorm-and it was impossible to obtain the men who were needed for snow shovelling because if they took this type of work, which they knew would last only for a few days, their position with regard to unemployment insurance benefits would be jeopardized. It is a foolish law which inflicts conditions like that upon men who are otherwise willing to work. I do not think it should be necessary for a worker to be confined to subsidiary employment. If he can obtain a little employment in his regular field I think he should be permitted to take it. I hope that the minister has borne that in mind when bringing in the amendments and that provision for this will be made in the revised act.
We had something to say earlier this session, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the terminal date for payment of supplementary benefits. The minister has now made some remarks which would indicate that the term "supplementary benefits" is to be removed from the act and that we will still have
2668	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act the supplementary benefits but under a different name; a case of a rose by any other name, I suppose.
I should like to speak for a moment about the need for extending not the benefits themselves but the period of the payment of those benefits. April 15 is practically upon us now and while the sun has been shining for a few days and the snow is melting, the type of work which is available to many of these men has not yet opened up. We had the same situation last year; it is not a new situation. It would seem to me that rather than placing in the act a specific terminal date there should be some flexibility to the termination of the supplementary benefits, or by whatever name you may call them.
In certain parts of Ontario where the weather does not open up as quickly as it does in southern Ontario it might be necessary to extend the supplementary benefits even to the 1st of June, but whenever conditions demand it I believe there should be sufficient provision under the act for taking care of these people, even if it has to be done by regions. It might be that rules would have to be laid down according to the weather which is encountered in the various parts of Canada.
A few days ago an hon. member of this house asked the minister if any consideration had been given to the extension of the date for this year and his reply, as I remember it, was that the government had not yet decided. There are many problems which need to be solved and which are brought up by speakers in this house in various debates from time to time. There is the problem of the young people who enter the labour force and are unable to secure work; or, if they secure work, who work for a short time and then are unemployed and have insufficient contributions to qualify for unemployment insurance. I know the minister has made reference to that in his remarks and has said that the new regulations which he proposes to bring in will help cure that situation. Whether or not the new regulations will be broad enough to take care of this situation remains to be seen and it will be interesting to see precisely what he has in mind. There is also the matter of immigrants who come to this country, who work for a while and are then thrown out of employment before they have made sufficient contributions to qualify for benefits. I am sure the minister is aware that it has been a matter of contention in various parts of the country as to who is responsible for these people and whether they should be looked after by the unemployment insurance 

commission or whether they should be a charge on the department of immigration. If the minister is not aware of the fact, I think he would be interested in knowing that there are several different opinions on that score. In some centres the immigration department takes charge of these people quite gladly and in others they wash their hands of them and say they can do nothing for them. Whether this means that the two departments should get together and formulate a policy concerning these specific workers as a matter for government consideration I do not know, but I commend it to the minister for his consideration.
There are those workers, Mr. Chairman, who are taken ill or who suffer disability between the time of their severance from employment and the date on which they apply for benefits. This too creates an anomaly since the worker who is taken ill subsequent to receipt of the benefits has been taken care of now for a couple of years or so.
I had one case not long ago when a man called me up and said that he had been laid off on a Friday night for an interminable period, or so he was led to believe. On Saturday, of course, the unemployment insurance offices were closed, and Monday was a statutory holiday. On Monday he took his family out and succeeded in injuring himself; he broke his arm. Therefore he was declared ineligible for benefits by the unemployment insurance commission. Well, it is quite possible that these things happen particularly on a long week end. The papers are full of stories about the number of accidents which occur during the course of a long week end. However, if some of these unfortunate people are in the position of having been laid off on the previous Friday then they are automatically disqualified for benefits. This is another matter which I think the minister has had under consideration and is rectifying in the current bill.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I know that the minister would be very disappointed if I did not mention once again in my remarks on any unemployment insurance measure the matter of regulation 5A (1). I could not let this opportunity go by without assuring the minister and the house that whenever there is a debate at any time on unemployment insurance you will hear about it until it has been removed. This clause was not put into effect until 1950 and it affects only married women. I have followed the questions which have been asked because they are published in some of the trade magazines. It is amazing how frequently there is a question asked with reference to the

circumstances under which a married woman can qualify for unemployment insurance. I picked this one out because it is typical. The question which was asked, and which I understand is answered by some official of the department, is this:
Why am I disqualified for not having 60 contributions since marriage when I worked six months after I was married?
The answer was:
The regulation says that you must have 60 contributions since your marriage if you were unemployed at the time you were married. On the other hand, if you continued to work after you were married, you must have 60 contributions after your first separation from employment following your marriage.
Of course, I suppose the answer to that is that anyone contemplating marriage should just quit her job and say, "I am now unemployed", and then immediately after marriage go back to work; in two months of work after having resumed her position she could qualify. I suppose these people never thought of that. I throw it out to them as a suggestion.
I would not feel so strongly about this particular regulation if it were not for the fact that it is the only one of which I know which is definitely discriminatory against one class of worker. The minister knows as well as I do of various classes of workers who at times make a run on the unemployment insurance fund. They find out that they can have a couple of weeks of holidays. If they handle it discreetly it will be made to appear that they have been laid off for lack of work. Then having received their benefits, after a while when they have had a little holiday, they can go back to their employment again.
That is something that has happened not once but several times. I am sure the minister is perfectly well aware of the classes of employment in which it occurs. Yet this one group of workers is the only one which is mentioned in the regulations, to my knowledge, or which has a definite regulation governing the matter of availability for employment. I urge the minister once more to have it removed. I think it is ridiculous. I do not know why it was ever put in there in the first place except that, having had some instances of married women claiming unemployment insurance where probably it was thought they had no intention of rejoining the labour force, it was felt that this regulation would stop the practice to which I have referred. I might say that I have much the same sort of feeling with reference to the proposed amendment to the act of which I spoke a few moments ago with reference to those people who are retiring from industrial
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act work through no fault of their own. If that is the case, I intend to oppose that amendment as well. I ask the minister now, when he is making amendments to the act, to see that this regulation 5A (1) is taken out of the regulations.
While we talk about unemployment insurance and while we try to build up the fund to take care of emergencies which arise in the industrial life of this country, it seems to me that we cannot allow to pass the opportunity to examine slightly the causes of unemployment. I have no intention of taking up the time of the committee by going fully into this matter in which I am keenly interested but I want to say just this.
We hear quite a bit of talk about proposals which are being put forward more and more by union members for what is called a guaranteed annual wage, guaranteed employment and various other names. I would suggest that there is hardly an industrialist in this country who would not be delighted to have his plant work 52 weeks of the year and to have all his employees employed 52 weeks in the year. In my estimation, industry is ready and willing to co-operate in the matter of year-round work, but the situation is not entirely in their hands. I ask the committee to consider for a moment this situation. If one industrialist attempts to spread employment he places himself economically in a position where he is unable to compete with his rivals in the same line of business. He may say, "I can cure this matter; I can call in my competitors and we can agree that we will take a certain line of action which, true enough, may raise our costs a little bit but it will give to these people employment for a full period each year." Then what happens to him?
He calls in his competitors. They confer together. They are willing to adopt the same system that he is willing to adopt in order to give steady employment. Then the Minister of Justice steps in and says, "You cannot do this. You have connived together to raise the price of your product and therefore you are guilty under the Combines Investigation Act". So he is left right back where he started, except that he may have had a nice fat fine slapped on him also.
Clearly, Mr. Chairman, it is a problem in co-operative action between industry and government. Surely we can give to industry some of the benefit of the doubt that they take this action with good intent and for a purpose of supplying work for their employees. Surely the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Justice and any othei members of the cabinet who may be interested can get together and try to find
2670	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act some way of solving this employment problem. I submit to this committee, Mr. Chairman, that it is a problem which can be solved. Before this bill has been approved by the house I trust that all these things I have mentioned and many others will have had full and proper consideration not only by the standing committee on industrial relations but also by every member of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to the extent that the bill forecast by this resolution makes provision for some real improvements in the Unemployment Insurance Act, we welcome it. We also welcome the fact that it is the intention to refer the bill, after it has had second reading, to the standing committee on industrial relations so that it can be thoroughly examined by the members of that committee. The committee has the power to send for persons, papers and records and I am sure that it will exercise that authority.
In thinking of what I would say, Mr. Chairman, I have decided to pattern my remarks after those of the minister, in this sense. As I see it, he dealt with the subject under three headings. In other words, like Gaul, his speech was divided into three parts. The hon. member for Hamilton West seemed to feel that all the gall was in the third part. In the first part of his speech the minister gave us something of the history of the enactment of this legislation in 1940. In the second part of his speech he outlined the changes being proposed in the bill to be based on this resolution. In the third part of his speech he asked us to see this resolution in the context of a reputed over-all Liberal social security program. It was there that the hon. member for Hamilton West felt that the gall came into the third part of the speech. However,
I shall have something to say about that matter when I reach that portion of my own remarks.
The minister started off by saying he had found it extremely interesting to go through the debates of 1940. It so happens I spent the week end doing the same thing. I found it interesting to read the debates not only on the resolution and the bill respecting unemployment insurance itself but also on the motion for an address to Westminster for an amendment to the British North America Act to make unemployment insurance possible. I found in the course of my reading that Mr. King had strongly recommended to members of the house that they peruse sessional paper No. 152, tabled on June 25, 1940, which contains the correspondence between the federal government and the provincial premiers leading up to the
[Mrs. Fairclough.l

general agreement that the British North America Act might be amended so as to write unemployment insurance into the British North America Act as class 2A of section 91.
What interested me particularly as I read the debates of 1940 was that there seemed to be more attention paid to the constitutional aspect of the matter, more attention paid to the question as to whose was the responsibility for unemployment insurance, than there was to the actual details of the bill itself. The hon. member for Hamilton West has drawn attention to the fact that the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 was not the first one presented to parliament but rather that there had been one introduced in 1935 by Mr. Bennett which had been referred by the succeeding Liberal government to the Supreme Court of Canada and then to the judicial committee of the privy council. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-since the hon. member for Hamilton West has suggested that the history of this act should go back beyond 1940 I suggest it should go back considerably beyond 1935. As a matter of fact it was during and after world war I that the trade union movement of this country first began to advocate and call for the enactment of unemployment insurance. I suppose it was not unnatural, in view of the popularity which the labour people of the country were giving to this idea in those years, that the Liberal party at its famous 1919 convention included in its platform a plank calling for unemployment insurance. Of course the fact that it was written into the platform in 1919 did not mean it was to be brought into effect overnight, any more than the health insurance which is talked about by my hon. friend across the way, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but at least unemployment insurance was achieved in 21 years.
In the meantime, as hon. members will recall, the matter was discussed in the House of Commons a great deal, frequently on the initiative of my predecessor, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre, the late J. S. Woodsworth. Hon. members will recall the

very famous exchange of letters in the year 1926 that had to do with old age pensions. At least, hon. members will remember mainly the old age pension part of that correspondence between Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Heaps on the one hand and Mr. King and the other party leaders on the other. I remind hon. members that old age pensions were only one subject of that famous letter and of Mr. King's reply. Concern for the unemployed was the other subject. Likewise, in 1928, and very largely because of the pressure exerted in parliament by Mr. Woodsworth and others associated with him, the select committee on industrial and international relations was given this instruction: That in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
That committee made a report approving in principle of unemployment insurance but drawing attention to certain constitutional difficulties. The matter came up again in 1929. That would be ten years after it was written into the Liberal platform in 1919. Mr. King still stalled on the ground that there seemed to be some problem of a constitutional nature. Hon. members are aware of what happened from then on. Mr. King did nothing while he was in power up until 1930, but in 1933, while in opposition, he pledged that if the Liberal party came back into power after the next election they would take the necessary steps and conduct the necessary negotiations with the provinces to bring about a nation-wide scheme of unemployment insurance. Then there followed Mr. Bennett's legislation of 1935 which, as has already been said, was referred to the courts in 1936 and declared ultra vires both by the Supreme Court of Canada and by the judicial committee of the privy council.
In 1940 the act which is now on the statute books was brought in. Before it was brought in there was a resolution, which was debated in the house on June 25, 1940, calling for an address to Westminster so that the British North America Act might be amended. As I say, that debate was extremely interesting and some of the arguments advanced during its course carried over into the debate on the unemployment insurance legislation itself. I found particularly interesting the position taken by Mr. King, by Mr. McLarty, who was then the minister of labour, and by Mr. Lapointe, who was then the minister of justice. All three of these late gentlemen figured very prominently in these debates.
They made the contention very strongly that what they were seeking was not just a clarification of a somewhat ambiguous position. They did not go for the idea that there
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act was any uncertainty, that maybe unemployment was a provincial matter, maybe it was a federal matter, maybe it was half and half. No, they took the position that as from 1867, as from the adoption of the British North America Act, unemployment had clearly been a provincial matter. They did not argue with that at all but they took the position, and Mr. King said this particularly on second reading of the bill, that Canada had moved a long way since 1867 and that in 1940 the time had come to make a clear-cut and definitive change. The time had come to say that industrial and economic conditions were such that we had to transfer concern over unemployment and responsibility for dealing with it from the provinces to the federal parliament.
Mr. King insisted that the federal parliament had the right to request Westminster to change the British North America Act without getting the consent of all the provinces, but at the same time he said, "This matter is so important I think we should get that consent." One of the reasons he gave for the considerable delay in connection with the matter was that it took time to get the consent of all the then nine provincial governments of Canada. He made a great deal out of that in the debate both on the resolution respecting the amendment to the constitution and in the debate on the legislation itself. Through all of this runs the theme that parliament was being asked to make a specific change, to transfer to the field of federal authority what had clearly been a provincial responsibility under the British North America Act from 1867 down to 1940. Without getting into the argument that went on here a while ago between my Conservative friends to the right and the Liberals across the way, I think even my friends to the right would agree it is a good idea that the British North America Act was amended and that it is now clear beyond any doubt that the responsibility for insuring against unemployment is a federal matter.
One of the points Mr. Lapointe made in the debate on the resolution addressed to Westminster was that no unemployment insurance act, no matter how well drafted, could be perfect for all time, and that amendments would have to be made as time went on. So he insisted that if any attempt were made to establish unemployment insurance on the basis of consent as between the provinces on the one hand and the federal government on the other, or if any attempt were made to establish such legislation on a concurrent basis, then certainly difficulties would be encountered just as soon as any amendments had to be made to the legislation. He indicated
2672	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act it was not enough just to get concurrence; you would have to hold that concurrence through future years. Therefore it was imperative that the matter be transferred once and for all to the federal authority.
I take no exception to the position taken by Mr. Lapointe, by Mr. King and Mr. Mc-Larty in that debate, but I think the government should recognize what flows from the decision made at that time. All the provinces agreed. In due course the resolution passed this House of Commons and the other place unanimously. I think some reference was made in the debate later on to the fact that it took only 19 minutes for Westminster to agree to the requested amendment to the British North America Act. In other words it was agreed all round that unemployment insurance is clearly and exclusively a federal matter. I submit it flows from that that the federal authority is the one that has the responsibility to insure against unemployment, not only by means of a particular statute that might be called the Unemployment Insurance Act but by whatever means are necessary to see to it that unemployment is minimized, or that the suffering which flows from unemployment is mitigated so far as those who are unemployed are concerned.
So I submit that what Mr. King said in the debate on this matter in 1940 is even truer today. He said in 1940 that we had come a long way since 1867 in the economic and industrial conditions of this nation, and that we had to make a change. Well, the change was made. And we have come a long way since 1940, Mr. Chairman. We used to hear the words "technological improvement" and "technological advances". Those words have now been replaced more or less by the new word "automation". To some extent it may be the same thing, but at a much higher speed. It may be that the difference is so great that it is one of kind rather than of degree.
In any event I suggest that in 1955 the problem of unemployment has become as much greater than it was in 1940 than that of 1940 was greater than the problem of 1867. There is no constitutional argument any more. The Liberals made sure of that. They said they had to be sure of it, and that there had to be no argument about it in future. It is all there, particularly in the words of Mr. Lapointe and Mr. King on June 25, 1940. All right, they have the authority; they have the responsibility. I am talking about the federal government, these same Liberals who sit across the way today. And I submit there flows from what was done in 1940 that this 

federal government now has complete responsibility for the problems that arise from unemployment.
We are glad to have a bill like this brought in at the present time, containing the improvements indicated by the Minister of Labour. But I suggest that under that heading of unemployment insurance, which I prefer to put in its other form as insurance against unemployment, the federal government has a responsibility which calls for far more than is presented to us in the legislation laid before us today.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend will agree that that may or may not be the case. We will not argue that at the moment. But there is no question that the amendment obtained in 1940 was to enable the federal government to pass a measure which would permit it to require contributions from various groups for the purpose of bringing into being the Unemployment Insurance Act. And that was all that measure did. The question my hon. friend is now arguing is apart from the point altogether, although admittedly it is a very important question.

There goes the orderly
