That was Mr. King. He
said in 1940, when the house was dealing with unemployment insurance, that this was part of the Liberal government's chart for an over-all social insurance program. Perhaps I should read one more sentence from the late and great Mr. King.
It took time to gain that end.
Some others who took part in that debate are still with us. I refer in particular to my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and my colleague the present member for Vancouver-Kingsway, or for Vancouver East as he was then. They had contended that at a time when parliament was asking Westminster to amend the British North America Act to include the authority for unemployment insurance, parliament should go further and ask for authority for social insurance. Mr. King felt he had to make some reply to what my leader and my colleague said, and this was it. At page 1118 of Hansard of June 25, 1940, he had this to say:
As the correspondence will show, one of the circumstances which enabled us to get the approval of all the provinces was the fact that we were asking for only one amendment, specifically related to unemployment insurance. I imagine the provinces have felt that they would like to wait and see just how that amendment works out before they give their consent to amendments of wider scope.
There is a typical Liberal approach. In 1919 you lay down an over-all program for old age pensions, for unemployment insurance, for sickness insurance and all those other social benefits. You bring it in step by step, very slowly. In 1940 you face the fact that to go any further you need an amendment to the British North America Act; but no, you do not ask for an adequate amendment to cover the whole field, you just ask for one point and leave it to the provinces to tell you later on whether they are satisfied. Well, we have had 15 years since that time, and still no suggestion comes from the other side that if it is necessary to obtain another amendment to the constitution to make possible a nation-wide program of

health insurance, that anything along that line is being done, despite the fact that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare himself said in July of 1940 that unemployment insurance is not enough, but that we must have other measures including health insurance.
Perhaps in what I have said, Mr. Chairman-and I thank or blame the Minister of National Health and Welfare if this speech is not set in the three water-tight compartments that I intended it should be at the start-I have been dealing with history and the gall of the Minister of Labour all mixed up together. But I think the history of this matter is interesting, and I would hope that hon. members might be prompted to read some of the history behind this legislation; for it does make it crystal clear that what this Liberal government wanted was a clearly defined, unanswerable, unassailable authority for unemployment insurance. I submit that if this government has taken that authority by getting an amendment to the British North America Act, there goes with that authority the federal responsibility to deal with the whole problem of unemployment, including full responsibility for the employable unemployed, whether covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act or not.
Incidentally, one of the arguments put to the provinces when they were asked to agree to the amendment to the British North America Act was that it would save them money in terms of unemployment relief. Here, for example, is a paragraph from Mr. King's letter to Hon. Adelard Godbout, premier of Quebec, written on January 16, 1940. This is contained in sessional paper No. 152, tabled on Tuesday, June 25, 1940. Mr. King said this:
In asking for the view of the Quebec government, at your early convenience, I should perhaps add that the establishment of a national scheme of unemployment insurance should, it is anticipated,-
No one can doubt that this is Mr. King's language. I continue:
-have the effect, once the scheme is in full operation, of reducing substantially the financial burden which now falls on the provinces for the provision of unemployment relief.
Mr. King made that point in every letter which he wrote to an industrial province. I point out-to his credit-that the letters he sent to the various premiers were not carbon copies of the same letter, but they were written in the light of the circumstances in each of the provinces. Well, that was part of the bargain; that was part of the arrangement that was made with the provinces in 1940. The federal government said, "You give us this authority and we shall be lifting the load from the provinces so far as unemployment is concerned".

I might point out, Mr. Chairman, that in effect what has happened is that the federal government has taken over the responsibility for the easier part of the unemployment problem, that part that can be insured against, the part that can be covered by contributions, but the federal government left with the provinces the residual part of the problem, the hard core. I submit that is most unfair, and that it is not in keeping with the spirit of what was done in 1940 when the federal government insisted upon and got for the parliament of Canada full control over unemployment insurance or as I put it, and I think justifiably, insuring against unemployment. I submit that as this problem becomes greater in these days of automation we have to have a great deal more than is contained either in the legislation we have had thus far or in the proposals brought forward today by the minister.
Some of the possible angles of approach have been indicated already by the hon. member for Hamilton West, although she did not align herself too closely with one I have in mind, namely the guaranteed annual wage. The guaranteed annual wage has to come; and while it is a debatable point whether it should be enmeshed with the Unemployment Insurance Act or provided in some other way, it has to come just as surely as night follows day.
I know there are those who will reply that you cannot do that without encouraging people to look for the day when they can receive an income without working, but let me read to the minister some words that he uttered on a certain occasion. I have in my hand a booklet entitled "Employer-Employee Relations Conference, eighty-first annual general meeting Canadian Manufacturers Association, Royal York hotel, Toronto, May 28th, 29th and 30th, 1952." One of the guest speakers on that occasion was the Minister of Labour. The minister made quite a speech, and on page 5 of this printed report he was dealing with the problem of seasonal unemployment. He was pointing out to the manufacturers association that it would be in their interests as well as in the interests of everyone else if seasonal unemployment could be minimized. He had this to say:
There are also business costs involved which could be avoided through a greater degree of employment stability. In many firms when operations are seasonally curtailed there are, as you know, continuing overhead charges. Such fixed charges include taxes, rent, insurance, depreciation and maintenance of equipment. The salaries of executives have to be maintained and it is often not feasible to discharge salesmen at such times. The office staff is usually kept on at something approaching its normal strength.
If there is a fundamental point at which we in this group have an approach that is

Unemployment Insurance Act different from the approach of other groups in the house it is right there. The Minister of Labour is not unique in this, because he speaks the mind of a great many hon. members of this house in other parties who accept it as axiomatic that of course the salaries of executives have to be maintained and that it is difficult to discharge salesmen, and indeed that you must maintain office staffs the year around. It is accepted as axiomatic that fixed business charges such as taxes, rent, insurance, depreciation and maintenance of equipment have to be met, but the attitude of the Minister of Labour and of many hon. members of this house stops there. I am not taking this out of its context so far as the minister's speech is concerned, because he goes on to another subject in the very next sentence.
Our contention is that the worker has just as much right to year round maintenance as has equipment. Our contention is that the worker has just as much right to a guaranteed annual wage as has the executive or any other of the highly-placed people in business and in industry. As I say, this is the point about which we feel most strongly and where there seems to be a difference of approach between us and other sections of this house.
But I say to the minister and to the government that they are going to have to do something about this question of a guaranteed annual wage. I say to them that philo-' sophically and socially it is sound and justified, and I say to them as well that a facing up to the guaranteed annual wage is called for under section 91, class 2A of the British North America Act, which gives the federal government authority to insure against unemployment.
There are other things that can be done. A shorter work week will have to come. It is also becoming more and more evident that as automation progresses, just as was the case or should have been the case with technological advances, its benefits must be distributed among the community as a whole. That is where we come in with wider social security legislation such as health insurance as suggested by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in 1940, and all the other proposals that can be enacted to distribute among all our people the advantages of an industrial age that has moved on to the point where under automation can now produce goods and services to an unlimited extent.
I call upon this house to face this matter in its broader terms, to face the tremendous issue that we are up against in this day and age. It is akin to the industrial revolution brought about by the introduction of steam power. There lies ahead of us either economic

Unemployment Insurance Act dislocation and misery if these problems are not solved, or what might be called a golden age for our people if we can see in the conditions which now face us a chance to distribute among all our people the advantages of the great wealth of goods and services we are now able to produce.
I should like to say a few words about some of the details outlined by the minister in his remarks. I refer to the detailed changes that he says will be made by this bill. First of all I am glad to note that we are to be given not just a bill to amend the act here and there, but rather a complete consolidation of the act. So many changes have been made since 1940 that it is desirable there should be a new act with all the legislation in one place.
We welcome the increase in the benefits. Also, I think it is a good move that the contributions and benefits are to be on a weekly rather than a daily basis. Likewise I think it is a good move that the amount which a person on unemployment insurance benefits can earn is being put on a weekly rather than a daily basis. Most of us know of many cases where there seemed to be unfairness because of the application of this provision.
I welcome the fact that the minimum number of weeks for which benefits may be drawn is to be increased from 6 to 15, but there is a question in my mind regarding the reduction of the maximum from 51 to 30 weeks. I shall not press the point now, but I will wait until there is a chance for questions to be answered. However, that does seem to be quite a substantial reduction. The minister has pointed out that by the addition of 15 weeks of supplementary benefits the 30 weeks could become 45, but if I correctly understood what he said it would seem that that would follow only if the 15 weeks came in a period of the year when supplementary benefits are payable. That being the case, it seems to me that we are going to have to look into that question, either in committee of the whole when dealing with the resolution or when the bill is before the standing committee on industrial relations.
I want to join with the hon. member for Hamilton West in urging that something yet be done about the discrimination against married women. She pointed out correctly that this did not come into effect in 1950. As hon. members will recall, when an amendment was made to the act in February, 1950, there were a number of provisions in the bill that we had been crying for at the time, but some that we had not asked for were also tucked in. Some of them, if I may say so, turned out to be "jokers". Some were provisions the significance of which we did not really grasp at the time. One was an amendment to the


act making it possible for the commission to pass regulations dealing particularly with married women. It was under that provision which was put through the house in February, 1950, that later all the damage was done by regulation 5A. I recognize, because I have had the opportunity of discussing the matter with-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: All right, Mr. Chairman, I shall sit down and come back at it later. The minister knows what I think on that as well as on the other points that have been raised. Such improvements as are forecast by this resolution are welcome; but as the Minister of National Health and Welfare said in 1940, there is a long way to go yet in dealing with this tremendous problem of unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, in my first words I would like to compliment the minister for doing something I had hoped a great many other ministers might have done when they were delivering complicated statements preceding the introduction of bills in this house. I received from the minister an advance copy of what he was going to say, so while he gave his statement I was able to follow it page by page and mark those passages which should receive emphasis and which I should stow away in my mind. I think it is an excellent idea, and I express the hope that some of the minister's colleagues will follow his example when making statements in the house in future, particularly with reference to technical legislation of the kind we are now considering.
I am always grateful-and I am sure I speak for my colleagues1-when I see the government bring in improvements to existing laws, particularly those laws which have to do with human welfare. It may be argued, of course, that all laws are of that nature, but I will pinpoint it a little more specifically by saying legislation concerning social welfare, providing the laws are based on sound principles.
The bill that is to be introduced after this resolution has been approved promises to be one which will make a number of commendable improvements in the unemployment insurance law. I was not here when the act was passed by this house in 1940, but if I had been here I feel sure that I would have supported it. I was at that time in the Alberta legislature, and I there supported the granting of provincial consent which was required before the present federal act could be passed by this parliament and made law.

For this reason I say I am quite certain I would have supported the act, perhaps making some criticisms of it. However, the Social Credit group in this house did support the bill in 1940, and we support it now.
Over the years we have felt that changing conditions and a broader understanding of the problem have made changes in the first legislation most necessary. We have felt all along that unemployment insurance is not enough by itself to provide what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to as insurance against unemployment. I believe that my colleagues in the house pointed out that fact in 1940 when the Unemployment Insurance Act was being considered. We have always been most concerned about changes in our whole economic policy that would be effective insurance against unemployment.
When I see unemployment insurance legislation brought into this house at any time, whether or not it is designed to improve the existing law, I feel that the government is demonstrating a lack of faith in its own economic policies. Unemployment insurance, Mr. Chairman, is simply a pair of crutches to me, rather than a good healthy body. We would prefer, of course, to see a sound condition in the economic policies which would make it possible for us to get along without crutches. I think everybody would agree with this. We are glad, however, that the unemployment insurance legislation is on the books, and we say so because the government is not living up to the promises it made to the people.
In 1945, when I took part in my first election in the federal field, billboards from one end of the country to the other were plastered with huge signs that promised jobs for everyone if the people would vote Liberal. I think everyone in this house remembers that slogan; if the people would only vote Liberal there would be jobs for everyone. Well, the people' did vote Liberal in 1945, in 1949 and again in 1953, and I ask you to seriously consider whether or not they got what they were promised. I do not have to make accusations; my hon. friends on the other side of the house, if they will just think about it honestly, will realize that the people did not get what they were promised.
What did they get? Unemployment insurance. That does not provide insurance against unemployment at all but is merely a palliative to bolster up an ailing economic structure. Whenever you see such legislation placed on the books or being used it is a sign of economic illness. What we are considering today is a medicine which the government hopes will cure the ailment. We have not

Unemployment Insurance Act been given a prescription telling us how to build a sound, healthy body. It is unfortunate that we do have unemployment developing. Of course it is fortunate that we have an unemployment insurance program to help in some measure at least when unemployment presents itself, and so we welcome the changes and improvements promised in the legislation which is to follow this resolution.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre mentioned the necessity of facing up to the situation particularly in regard to the requirement of labour generally for an annual wage.
I think he referred to a guaranteed annual wage. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this country must soon face up to the question of a guaranteed annual wage, because it is going to become a most important issue much sooner than is thought by many people. I believe we have to give it serious consideration and think the matter through, rather than being guided solely by our emotions in respect to it.
I do not know just how in the world those who are promoting the idea of a guaranteed annual wage think it can be paid without a serious increase in the cost of production. I cannot quite follow how they propose it can be done without creating a serious increase in the cost of production which will have to be borne by a comparatively small proportion of the population of the country for the benefit of others. If the guaranteed annual wage program could achieve benefits across the board for the whole of the Canadian population and guarantee them some stability of income, then I could quite understand how everyone with a heart and a social conscience could go for it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Did you not regard your national dividend as of benefit to everyone?

Oh, definitely, but what I am getting at is this. No one has yet put forward a proposal with respect to a guaranteed annual wage that takes the weight off the single industry in which the people are engaged who are to get the guarantee. That is the trouble. That is why it is so vastly different from the proposals we have made with regard to a national dividend.
Here is the next important point. A guaranteed annual wage program does not do anything but cause a redistribution of wealth which, if carried to its extreme, would reduce everybody to the same level of poverty. It does not increase by one red cent the purchasing power available to the people of the country. If we are to guarantee the workers of our country an annual income-something I am all in favour of-it seems to me that what we must have is a program that goes

Unemployment Insurance Act far deeper than merely a redistribution of the insufficient purchasing power that is at present in existence. That is why we are asking that this whole matter be clarified most carefully. We are not taking our stand against it for the moment, but we are giving it study.
I warn members of the committee that within the next few months they are going to be obliged to face up to this whole matter of a guaranteed annual wage as a solution for what my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre describes as the serious situation in which many workers find themselves today where they are asked to be on call for employment when the employers in the industries need them, but to be content to remain without income for the balance of the year. That is the problem and we shall have to face it. But whether the guaranteed annual wage is the answer I certainly am not prepared to say.
The unemployment insurance program, amendments to which we are considering today, is a technique which is based on redistribution of wealth as a means of stabilizing our economy. We in the Social Credit group supported the original unemployment insurance program because we realized that it would go to a certain extent, at any rate, in providing stability for an economy. It seems clear that the experience over the years would indicate that some redistribution of wealth is necessary if it is moderately applied. But as I have already pointed out, to carry it too far would not bolster up an ailing economy but would actually tend to destroy it by its own weight, and that is the kind of thing we must be careful about.
I think our experience over a period of 14 years shows that redistribution by itself does not go far toward stabilization. If it did we would not be having the trouble we are having today with unemployment. All the things that have been introduced into our economy since the end of the war in 1945 have not gone too far toward stabilizing the economy. Most of the measures have been based on the redistribution of wealth already in existence. Our experience with them should have proved by now that what we must find is some more fundamental solution that may take into consideration a certain amount of redistribution of wealth,, but based upon the important principle that when we go all out and produce the abundance that we can produce in this country, we must have a means of distributing that wealth so our people can use it.
We must develop the local market, because this Canadian market is by far the most important one we have for the goods we can 

produce. We must introduce measures that will make it possible for the consumers in this country to buy and use the goods we can produce. Otherwise we are going to get ourselves constantly into trade difficulties, unemployment difficulties and all manner of other difficulties.
We must get down to much more fundamental principles than merely the superficial redistribution of wealth. Redistribution of purchasing power is what it really becomes. When there is not enough of it, what good does it do in the long run merely to redistribute it? Let us see that there is enough in the first place so that our production can be bought and used by our people if they want it. Then if it becomes necessary to do some redistributing, let us do it on that modest scale that will not destroy our economy and press it down under the sheer weight of a thing that is superficial and impossible.
Since this legislation is to be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations it is not necessary for me to go into detail with respect to the proposals outlined by the minister in his admirable statement today. I merely say that we reserve our opinion on some of these specific matters-in fact, on all of them-until the bill is brought in and we have had a chance to study it in committee. Suffice it to say at the moment that we are glad to see these amendments being brought in. We compliment the minister on his forethought. I think he has gone a long way to improve this act. We shall give him support on every one of those provisions in the bill that we find to be good.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution proposing the amendment of the Unemployment Insurance Act supersedes a notice of motion that appears on the order paper today under my name but which I intend later to ask to have withdrawn. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to increase the regular and supplementary benefits to single and married unemployed workers.
In the Welland area there is a good deal of heavy industry, and over the last year and a half or more there has been considerable unemployment. Such highly responsible people as the heads of municipalities, heads of labour unions and others have made representations to me as to the inadequacy of the payments under the Unemployment Insurance Act. From going about among the unemployed in the practice of medicine, I would say that my observations bear out the fairness of these representations.

I should like to thank the Minister of Labour who, on behalf of the government, earlier this year introduced the amendment by which the supplementary benefits, now called seasonal benefits, were increased. This amendment has already become law and these increased payments are helping many unemployed employables get through the winter months when it is difficult to obtain employment. These further proposed revisions of the act will tend to simplify it. Many features of the act were difficult to understand, and I would think anybody who tried to figure them out would find that. Calculations were involved, and some who drew benefits were never convinced that they received their fair share of those benefits.
I am glad to know also that it will be easier to qualify under the act, and that some who have been in the labour force a shorter time than heretofore will qualify when they are not employed.
As under the present arrangement, workers are put into different categories in accordance with their weekly earnings. Contributions and benefits bear a much more direct relationship to the different ranges of earnings, and there is an increase of benefits mostly in the upper and lower income groups. I was glad to hear the minister say that no worker would lose any equity in the fund.
I notice that in the lower and upper income groups, for example, the benefits are increased by 25 per cent. It is proposed that these benefits should be paid for a maximum of 30 weeks. I saw figures some time ago which indicated that 90 per cent of all claimants drew benefits for 20 weeks or less. The 30 weeks' duration of payment of benefits would cover a very high percentage. I think the minister said today it would cover 95 per cent. A certain number of those falling within the small percentage of cases where 30 weeks was not a sufficient period of time would get supplementary benefits. It is pretty hard to figure how the supplementary benefits would work out, but I understand that in any 12-month period it is possible for workmen to draw up to 45 weeks' benefits.
I realize that the main principles are laid down in the legislation and that the commission will have power to make regulations to deal with procedures and details of administration. I hope these regulations will be sufficiently generous to include some of the borderline cases where it has been impossible to qualify under the act. I realize that most Canadians prefer gainful employment to idleness and drawing unemployment insurance. I also realize that unemployment as such does not come within the scope of discussion of these amendments.

Unemployment Insurance Act
The Unemployment Insurance Act has proven to be excellent legislation and is suitably adapted to the purpose for which it was intended, but like most legislation it needs to be amended from time to time to meet the needs of our people. It helps the workman to bridge the gap between periods of employment. This is of great benefit to the community in which he lives because he can continue to buy the necessities of life, thus helping the economy not only of his own community but of Canada as a whole.
I find many misconceptions in the minds of the people about the act. Many are of the opinion that only the workmen contribute to the fund and that the government contributes nothing, when in fact the government contributes 20 per cent and the employers and employees 40 per cent each. The government administers the fund through the Department of Labour, and when this cost is taken into consideration we find that the government actually contributes about one-third and the other two-thirds is shared equally between the employers and employees. I presume the same ratio will be closely approximated under these new amendments.
From observation I would say that the benefits have worked well in cases of short periods of unemployment, but when these periods have exceeded two months most of the unemployed have found it difficult to make ends meet. As I said before, the new schedule of unemployment benefits bears a more definite relationship to earnings, and for most ranges of pay the benefits are definitely and substantially increased. This will be of great assistance in helping the eligible unemployed to meet the ordinary costs of living.
When a worker has used up his benefit days it has often been difficult for him to qualify for the winter supplementary benefits under the act, either because he has been unable to obtain work or when he has obtained work it has been in non-insurable employment such as agriculture. As an example, such employment as temporary work on a farm, the picking of fruit in the early and late summer months, has aided the worker in keeping his family during these months but has failed to build up any benefit days which might help him to qualify for seasonal benefits during the winter months. I know it would be most difficult to include all lines of work and class them as insurable, but I cannot help think that a worker doing any such worth-while work is contributing as fully to the economy of Canada as if employed in insurable work.
The maximum benefit paid to a married man at the present time is $24 a week, and

Unemployment Insurance Act this is to be increased to $30 a week. A family had great difficulty in getting by on the $24 because of certain fixed charges they had to meet. First of all there is housing. Rents are high, and whether the worker pays rent or monthly payments toward mortgage retirement, taxes and insurance, it takes quite a sizeable amount from his $24 a week.
Then there are fixed and often increasing amounts to pay for services such as water and light. In Ontario, for example, the hydroelectric power commission has increased the cost of hydro power because of expansion and frequency change-over. Then we have the fixed costs for heating. I realize of course that in the case of families with children they are greatly assisted by family allowances made available by the government, but these amounts are often used entirely to meet the extra costs incidental to children attending school such as the buying of books, extra clothing, etc.
The point is that when the family budget is tight the amount available for the purchase of food is inevitably cut down. I am free to admit that some of the more inexpensive foods are more healthful and nutritious. On the other hand we must see that our people, and especially our children, have a well-balanced, nutritious diet for maximum health.
There are certain aspects of unemployment where the unemployment benefits do not meet all the needs of the family. In most provinces-and this is true in Ontario-medical and hospital insurance soon lapses and any sickness in the worker's family requiring hospitalization means that the municipality and the province must assume the cost. These costs have been going up markedly in the last year or two in certain areas of unemployment.
Then we have the problem of older workers, and by "older workers" I mean those beyond 40 or 45 years of age who find it difficult to get insurable employment. Because of the pension plans in various plants it is not economical to give employment to men over these ages. Many of these pension plans have been in operation a comparatively short time, with the result that those who have retired or are now retiring are receiving comparatively small pensions. I am convinced that it is wrong to retire anyone because he has reached a certain chronological age, whether in government or in industry. Those who are unfit retire of necessity, while the others who are fit and well able to carry on would be much happier and more contented if they were allowed to work beyond a certain arbitrary retiring age.
I have observed many of these people. Some of them whose main interest in life


was their work develop a moroseness, a sort of chronic mental illness which is soon followed by a physical breakdown. We should remember that some of the best contributions to the welfare of mankind have been made by those who have reached an age beyond our arbitrary retiring ages. Certainly I have seen many good workmen who were more than 60 or 65 years of age. In that regard, it should be noted that in some plants the retiring age is as low as 60. Our high standards of living and advancements in medical science are responsible for gradually increasing the proportion of the older age groups in our population; and unless we keep them productive we are creating a social problem. This means that we have an ever-increasing number of people living off our working class who, after all, create our wealth and pay the bulk of our taxes.
It should be within our ingenuity to devise ways and means of enabling these older workers to continue at work if they wish and can do so. In this way we would be helping the economy of our country and the mental outlook of these people. The real victims and sufferers in a state of unemployment are those able-bodied workers who, for one reason or another, are not eligible for any unemployment insurance. We have help for those who are unable to work but no organized public assistance for those we class as the employable unemployed.
This is the one serious gap in our social security services, and it has existed since 1940, since the enactment of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The provinces for the most part ceased to contribute to the cost of municipal relief, except for the unemployable persons.
In Canada, because of our climate, I think we are bound always to have some seasonal unemployment. I think, too, that in our free enterprise system-in fact in any system-it would be impossible always to eliminate the ups and downs in employment. Part of our economy, indeed part of the economy under any system, depends upon world commerce; and this will vary with the vagaries of nature, the scarcity and abundance of crops.
I am much in favour of the changes set out in this legislation-these increased payments -and I think they will be well received. I do think, if I had any criticism of the bill, that the payments in relation to the seasonal benefits are too rigid. April 15 is close at hand, and we are bound to have considerable unemployment when these benefits are terminated. I would like to see power given to the governor in council to extend the seasonal benefits for a limited time, when conditions warrant.

Tomorrow night the Minister of Finance will present his first budget and I am sure many hon. members, like myself, hope for certain changes. Whether we get our wishes or not I feel he will bring in a budget consistent with good government and our obligations in this uncertain world, and at the same time try to cut down the need for unemployment insurance. In this we wish him every success.

Mr. Chairman, I was greatly
worried when the minister spoke a little while ago, because I thought we were going to have an accident. I thought he was going to break his wrist patting the government on the back for its activities in connection with unemployment insurance.
One would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that this unemployment insurance was the gift of the government to those who are unemployed. There has been no recognition of the fact that the employee contributes 40 per cent and the employer 40 per cent, and that the government's contribution is only 20 per cent. Listening to the minister, one would have thought nothing had ever been done by way of unemployment insurance, outside of what this government has done.
I was very pleased indeed to hear the charming member for Hamilton West in her own inimitable fashion set the government right on this question as to who introduced unemployment insurance. It was the Conservative party. And who was it that killed it successfully for six years? It was the Liberal party. It was good to hear the truth come out at last because, as we know, truth will out; and I am glad it did.
Hearing the minister speak on behalf of the government and tell about the wonderful things he imagined they had done in this field, I was reminded of a story about a Texan who went out to Australia. You know, in Texas they claim everything is bigger and better, just as this government claim things are bigger and better under a government of the Liberal party, and just as the government claim that anything worth while that has been done has always been done bigger and better by them. Well, this fellow went out to Australia and was being shown around a sheep ranch. Things are really big out in Australia but no matter what he was shown he would say, "Oh, buddy, that ain't nothin'. It's bigger and better in Texas." Finally the chap who was showing the Texan around was getting a little fed up when, just at that moment, a kangaroo went whizzing by, nearly knocking the Texan down. He jumped back and said, "My Lord, what was that?" The fellow from Australia said, "Oh, don't you have grasshoppers in Texas?" 50433-170

That is exactly the kind of thing that happens here. We hear it said by those who support the government that nothing ever happens that the Liberal party did not introduce. Of course the Liberal government need not get mixed up about what a kangaroo looks like, because they have Jumping Jack with them every day. He is right there before their very eyes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: When do we laugh?

Everybody else has.
This act is certainly a great improvement for those who are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, but what I want to know is what is going to happen to those tens of thousands of people who on April 16 find themselves with no jobs and no unemployment insurance; with no entitlement and no benefits, either regular or supplementary.
When unemployment insurance was debated earlier in the session, the minister and the government assured us that by April 15 everything would be in good shape, and there would be no unemployment. When I asked the minister about it he said, "Oh, well, there will be very little unemployment at that time", and just passed it off in that way.
Well, Mr. Chairman, we all know that unemployment has not decreased, because the last figure was greater than the one before, and I should think the next one will be even greater still. As the hon. member for Welland has just said, April 16 is close at hand, and there will be a great number of people out of jobs and with no entitlement at that time. After that date, great numbers will be going to unemployment insurance offices; but they will simply be told, "Sorry, chum; there is nothing for you. After all, you have to remember that there really is no unemployment. The minister has said that it is only 'seasonal and regional'. Therefore we cannot give you any unemployment insurance."
So he will go home to his wife and say, "Sorry, dear; I can't give you any money to buy food and clothing. We can't get coal or pay the doctor's bill because, after all, the government says unemployment is only seasonal and regional, and there is nothing to worry about." And those people are going to get hungrier and colder and wetter and sicker; but so far as the government is concerned, it will not bother in the slightest degree because, after all, "This thing really is not unemployment", they say; "this is just something that is a passing phase."
The government think there are not enough people involved to embarrass them at election time. Therefore they are perfectly happy to cut these people off without even

Unemployment Insurance Act a thought, and leave them alone to figure out some way of paying their bills and buying food and clothing. I ask the minister and the government to view this matter from a humanitarian point of view, not just from that of dollars and cents; of columns of figures; or of lists of voters at election time. This is something which involves human life and human suffering. Today there are more than half a million people unemployed. We have 12 days to go to April 16. There are going to be just about as many unemployed at that time. Tens of thousands will have their unemployment benefits cut off at that time. Human suffering in this country is going to increase many times because of the action the government plans to take.
I urge the minister, solemnly and earnestly, to reconsider the decision to cut off unemployment supplementary benefits on April 15. As the hon. member for Hamilton West urged when this matter came up earlier in the session, these supplementary benefits should be extended to at least May 15. In view of the fact that unemployment has not decreased, that the figures are getting higher every month-we have had the second postwar peak in succession-it is obvious that there is going to be great human suffering if the government carries out its present plan. I urge the minister to reconsider. I hope before this resolution passes he will tell us that the government intends to do that, and in addition to extend the supplementary benefits to at least May 15.
I would ask the government seriously to consider starting these benefits again about November 1 if unemployment again appears to pose a serious threat, as it did last fall. If it appears next fall that unemployment will approach serious dimensions I ask the minister to look at this thing from the humanitarian point of view, and to realize that human suffering cannot be allowed to exist in the proportions in which it will exist after April 15 if something is not done.

In view of what my hon. friend has said may I ask him whether he believes that this fund should remain actuarially sound or whether it should be converted into a relief measure, which is inherent in what he said a moment ago?
It is very important.
It is extremely important.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: As a businessman, what would you say?
Right at this moment we have almost a billion dollar surplus in this fund.
Surplus or reserve?

One or the other; it is there. It is money that has been put in, 40 per cent by the employer and 40 per cent by the employee. It is there, ready to be used to meet this very great need. I say that at the present time the government should extend supplementary benefits to at least May 15, and if necessary longer than that. When this government calls together the conference on April 26 to discuss the agenda for a later dominion-provincial conference, it should discuss with the provinces the basis on which relief that is necessary in the future should be shared by the dominion, the provinces, and the municipalities.
I have suggested that we go back to the 40-40-20 basis that was used between 1939 and 1941, and work out a proposition with the provinces so that when people are unemployed through no fault of their own, and find that they have no entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits, they do not suffer actual hardship in the form of hunger, cold, .lack of clothing and lack of shelter. That is my suggestion to the minister and to the government.

I have no intention of drawing the fire of the hon. member for Hamilton West, because I certainly am not anxious to have the wrath of my charming and vivacious friend, as she has been termed, brought upon myself.
The government should be commended for the procedure taken in bringing in these amendments to a worthy act. It was most generous of the minister to refer in such a kindly way to my predecessor, the late Hon. Norman McLarty, who did a great deal to see that the original act was brought into effect. Hon. Norman McLarty represented the constituency of Essex West from 1935 to 1945 when, because of ill health, he had to withdraw.
The history of the Unemployment Insurance Act has been put on the record by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and that record, of course, will speak for itself. At this time I do not think that history is of too much importance except from the purely partisan point of view, particularly as to who did or did not do certain things at certain times. We are very grateful that we have this act, and we trust that it will continue in effect and that beneficial improvements will be made to it from time to time.
The constituency of Essex West, which I represent, is composed chiefly of the city of Windsor and one suburban township, and is very much interested in this bill. In that area we are a sort of mecca or focal point for labour. Labour is drawn to that area

by high wages. That high wage rate has been in effect for some time, and we have had ever-rising rates for many years. Then we are in close proximity to the city of Detroit, which is a large industrial United States city. In fact the city of Detroit, as I have so often said in this house, is on three sides of the constituency which I represent.
In the city of Windsor and within a radius of 50 miles, we have 2,500,000 people or more. There is a very high wage rate in that area and a very highly industrialized population. The climatic conditions of that area are easier and less rigorous than in other parts of Canada, with the result that a great many labour people throughout Canada are most anxious to live in my constituency or in close proximity to it, or generally in that part of the country. However, it does present problems to the municipalities. Apart from industrial strife and pointing the way to industrial improvements throughout the whole country, there are problems caused by the influx of labour. These are felt very much by the municipal authorities, and confront them day by day.
If I may quote a few figures, in 1954 the city of Windsor, in co-operation with the province of Ontario, appropriated $193,273 for relief purposes. Of course that was under provincial legislation; but it so happened that in that year moneys in the amount of $250,069.82 were spent, leaving a deficit of $56,796.82. The policy of the city of Windsor has been to assist heads of families, and heads of families alone, where there is dire need. Of course if a person is an unemployed employable and has exhausted his benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act the city does what it can to find him a job and assist his family. But they assist merely in the way of providing the bare necessities of food and fuel.
In 1954 there was paid out by the city of Windsor a total of $40,768.74 for which they had appropriated $10,000, leaving a deficit of some $30,768.74. Therefore we are most grateful for the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Act, when we stop to consider that at times there have been some 11,000 or 12,000 people registered as unemployed in our local office.
The community welfare council of Windsor has been studying this matter and has made recommendations to the minister. I noted that the minister stated that the benefits under the act are to be increased. The welfare council has recommended that they be increased to $35 a week for married men and $24 a week for single men. I think an increase of 25 per cent is most generous, and 50433-170i
Unemployment Insurance Act will go a long way in solving some of the problems and reducing the fear which besets a great many people.
We must realize at all times that the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act is to relieve the fear of unemployment. It is insurance against unemployment, just the same as the fire insurance we place on a house we may own. We pay our premiums and we know exactly what we are going to get if the property should be totally destroyed by fire. This is not a dole; this is not a subsidy for employment; we must keep constantly in mind that it is insurance which we have paid for and that the benefits are ours by right.
Generally speaking the labour unions and industry in my community are most anxious that there be an increase.	Times have
changed since 1940, when the act was first brought in. At that time the cost of living was not so high but wages also were not so high. The dollar of that time would probably be worth something like 60 cents today. So the unions and industry are united, I believe, in requesting that there be an increased contribution by both which would result in higher benefits to the unemployed. I think the recommendation made by the minister of $30 per week for married men is most desirable.
We should keep in mind also that while wages have gone up considerably, the cost of living has increased. I am not sure from what the minister said just what maximum will be allowed as income and what the average contribution will be, but I am sure all this will be taken into consideration so that larger allowances may be provided.
There is great objection to the present provisions of the act in my constituency, where the principal industry is the automobile industry. An employee may be working seven days a week for a time; and then when things become slack he may go on a three-day week or have to find other employment. I think the method of making contributions under this act should be overhauled. As I remember, the minister stated that there was some thought of changing that, and I am in accord with what he had to say.
Before I conclude I should like to say just one word in connection with the point brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that automation in industry is becoming more popular. I think that is a good thing. The Ford Motor Company of Canada has recently spent many millions of dollars in converting the plant at Windsor to one which is largely automatic. With the coming of automation and the bringing in of machines to do the work which man's hands have done:

Unemployment Insurance Act in the past, the worker will have to possess greater skill. That means that if the worker has not applied himself to acquiring the necessary skill his chances of being unemployed are much greater.
I urge upon all young people who are thinking of going into industry that they take advantage of the facilities provided not only by the provincial governments and the municipalities but by the federal government, which gives assistance under the vocational training plan carried on under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. In this machine age, :in this automatic age, in this atomic age which is coming we will need the most highly skilled technicians.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when I read the resolution that we are now debating I was somewhat at a loss to know just how we should regard this new amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. A remark the minister made just before we adjourned for supper left me still in some doubt when he challenged the hon. member for Broadview as to whether he considered that the Unemployment Insurance Act was to be regarded as a relief measure, or whether he wished it to be an actuarially sound fund.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether it really is or ever has been actually an actuarially sound fund-that is, a fund a professional actuary would tell us was sound-because we have had to dig into the public treasury periodically. More important still, we all know that if the necessity arises we are going to dig into it again. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the very fact this act is now being amended in this way is an indication that in the government's mind it is meant to do perhaps something more than the original Unemployment Insurance Act was intended to do because-mark this, Mr. Chairman-it has been brought in this year when, for the first time since 1940, the Canadian economy has taken a downward turn, the first time that unemployment has become a really serious, dangerous economic problem.
If the amendments to the act were merely designed to make it a more generous and effective measure for the relief of occasional unemployment, then one is forced to wonder just why the government did not do this last year or the year before, when the Canadian economy was in a much better position

than it is now to carry this load. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the government itself has really not quite made up its mind what the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act is to be.
It may be, of course, that the government is still hoping that before the provisions of this new amendment fail to cope with the situation, the unemployment situation will have improved to the extent that we can go back to the sort of position we occupied last year and the year before. However, I have the idea that in the back of their minds they know that the machinery of the Unemployment Insurance Act may have to be used in the fairly near future for a rather different purpose than its original intention; that is, to cope with a growing problem of, if not permanent at least very long lived, unemployment.
For that reason I think the suggestion made this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is one that should merit considerable inspection on the part of the government. If they are going to use the act as a measure to deal with more or less permanent unemployment, then eventually the government will have to establish some sort of machinery that will provide an annual guaranteed wage for Canadian workers. I think that is really the point we have come to in our thinking today, and that is a very long way from what our thinking was a few years ago. We appear to have reached the point now where most people are prepared to admit that any Canadian citizen who is able and willing to work is entitled to his livelihood, and that if he cannot get his livelihood by means of employment in industry then the community as a whole has to come to the rescue. I suggest that is one of the uses to which this unemployment insurance legislation will eventually be put.
It is perfectly true, as the hon. leader of the Social Credit group said this afternoon, that a guaranteed annual wage will constitute a redistribution of wealth. I was rather puzzled and wondered just why he considered that was a much more superficial thing to do than to inflate the currency and distribute the diluted mixture-
He did not advocate inflating the currency; get the record straight.

Well, it is over 30 years ago, Mr. Chairman, that a friend of mine put in my hands a book by the late Major Douglas, which I studied with a great deal of care. In spite of the fact that Major Douglas is English, it left something to be desired. Aside from the fact that his economic theories had some fundamental flaws

it was perfectly obvious from reading the A plus B theorem which I studied very carefully that in the final analysis the Social Credit theory is bluntly and plainly one of inflation-
Reflation, not inflation; there is a difference.

Well, "flation" anyway; "re" or "in", it is "flation" anyway. The difference amounts to this, Mr. Chairman, that rather than redistribute the wealth as suggested by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, our friends to the left here would rather increase the number of tickets for the available wealth, divide those up, and hope by some mysterious means to increase the real wealth coming to each member of society. I think the redistribution of wealth as proposed by the guaranteed annual wage is something we are going to have to face very soon.
As I said the other night on the air, I consider that the present unemployment situation is fundamentally much more ominous and serious than the problem we faced during the thirties, because at that time we were faced with a broken-down economic machine. Factories were closed down, goods were not being produced, services were not being provided and in that situation there was little cause for wonder at continual and rising unemployment. But today we have a very different situation and I submit, Mr. Chairman, it is much more dangerous and ominous. It is a situation in which our economic machine is running almost at full tilt, yet we have discarded some 600,000 of our working population, have pushed them right outside the fence.
As evidence that we have done this and that the government recognizes it, we have this resolution before us tonight. That can be the only explanation. I am not quarrelling with it but I am suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that it is an inadequate means of dealing with a serious and, as far as one can see, virtually permanent situation unless we introduce something in the nature of the guaranteed annual wage with its consequent redistribution of wealth. So while I am delighted to be able to support this measure, I think it is only right that the people of Canada should not be deluded into thinking it is a serious and effective means of coping with a problem that everybody except the government recognizes is the most serious we have faced since the end of the war.
We shall, of course, examine the details of the bill when it comes before us and endeavour to have it widened a little more

Unemployment Insurance Act than it is at present. Fundamentally, however, the government eventually is going to face the necessity of finding some means of providing a means of livelihood for those who have been discarded from our productive machine due to the methods by which we produce and distribute goods.
The suggestion of the minister that this is an actuarially sound insurance fund is, in my opinion, really whistling in the dark. While it is possible to present a facade of actuarial soundness by means of putting in a little bit more from the treasury, it is really rather a clumsy method of using this machinery to cope with a problem that this legislation was never intended to cope with.
I hope the government is not going to be satisfied to rest on its oars-and small oars they are; they are hardly more than little paddles-with what they produce in this resolution, but will start to cope with this problem that is going to cause the Minister of Labour continual and increasing headaches in the months to come.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to yield to the temptation tonight to get into a debate about Social Credit. I am saving my speech on Social Credit for a more suitable occasion. I am afraid that if anybody mentioned Social Credit too much we would have my good friend the hon. member for Lethbridge keeping us here all night and we would never get any Easter holidays.
Right you are.

I am a bit sorry that the hon. member for Hamilton West is not in her seat at the moment. If she were I think I might have some remarks to make about the historical background of unemployment insurance. The first time I aspired to parliamentary office was in the constituency of Hamilton West in the year 1931. Believe me, just to espouse unemployment insurance, as I then did, was to be considered extremely radical indeed or even red.
I am also a bit sorry that the hon. member for Broadview is not in his seat, because when I heard him speak today, weeping such copious tears with a smile from ear to ear, I could not help thinking of the song by that fellow who used to sing over the radio. You could not tell whether he was crying or laughing. The words of the song-I wept at your wedding-were to this effect: Your father was crying, your mother was crying and I was crying, too; and it ends up in a great burst of laughter.
Tonight for a few moments I want to deal with some of the serious points having to do

Unemployment Insurance Act with the unemployment insurance picture. Of all the social welfare measures that have been introduced in Canada in the past generation I think this is probably the most useful one to the most people. It has been a tremendous success. All the calculations on which it was based have been proved by experience to be too conservative. We had a longer period of sustained prosperity than even the most optimistic experts had predicted. The result is that today we have in the fund a reserve, a surplus or whatever you want to call it, which is much greater than any of the statisticians could have calculated in advance.
I am heartily in support of the minister's proposal to increase the benefits. I think certain other improvements in this act could be considered as time goes on. I for one have never been able to see the justice or the common sense of striking off the rolls at the time she becomes pregnant a married woman who is employed and needs employment. I think one of the changes we could consider in the act-if not now, certainly in future years-is to provide that where a woman is working and needs work, her benefits should be allowed during her period of pregnancy just as they would be allowed for any other type of involuntary unemployment.
Tonight for a minute or two I want to speak about what seems to me the greatest weakness in our whole unemployment compensation system in Canada. This name, of course, as we all realize, is a misnomer. As the hon. member for Peace River, the leader of the Social Credit group, pointed out today this is not really unemployment insurance; it is unemployment compensation. Of course we all know that this government would not survive and-if we want to take a long-range view- for that matter the whole western system of democracy as we now have it certainly would not survive unless this problem of chronic and large-scale unemployment were solved. I think we can all take that statement for granted, and no one has ever said it better or more to the point than did our Prime Minister who sits on our front benches today.
What is he going to do?

We will know partly what he is going to do tomorrow night, when the budget comes down, because that will be the first instalment.
Tonight I am going to talk about what seems to me to be really the greatest weakness in our unemployment compensation system in Canada today, and it is this. Those who need unemployment compensation most have no coverage whatsoever. I thought the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre 

made a most important and, I may say, surprising revelation today when he was quoting and trying to score a point against the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he read those quotations from the speeches and the letters of the late prime minister, William Lyon Mackenzie King.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that the prime minister of the day in 1940 had written to all of the provinces individually telling them that he was sure the Unemployment Insurance Act that was then being instituted would greatly reduce their burden of relief for the unemployed. I was just sorry that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had not brought that fact out a few weeks earlier, because for weeks and even months past we have heard ad nauseam the contention that the total responsibility rests with the federal government.
Does it not?
The constitutional position now is that the legal responsibility for the care of unemployed employables who are not entitled to any unemployment compensation definitely rests with the provinces.
You know better than that.

I for one wish to urge that at the dominion-provincial conference of this year we eliminate this greatest weak spot in our whole unemployment compensation system. Tonight I am not going to venture to suggest how these unemployed employables could be covered but I urge every government in Canada-not only the federal government but every provincial government -to bring this subject to a decision, to quit this business of passing the responsibility from one to another, to come to a firm decision so that never again at any time in the future could there be any doubt as to what happens; so that everybody in this great Dominion of Canada may be sure that he does not have either to starve or to steal.
The least we can do in times of temporary unemployment, even as serious as we have had this winter and last winter, is to see that everybody in Canada who is not covered by regular unemployment insurance, as set up in this act which is now being made more generous, gets adequate assistance on an agreed in advance formula that shares the burden fairly among the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities, so that never again shall any unemployed man or woman in this whole Dominion of Canada have to go around from pillar to post wondering where his or her livelihood is to come from the next day or week.

Mr. Chairman, I do not feel at all qualified to talk about

the technical aspects of the proposed changes in this act. As a matter of fact I feel that few are in that happy position. On the other hand, there are few who have not been affected in some way or other by this legislation in the last 14 or 15 years.
First of all, though I do not think hon. members to your right, Mr. Chairman, would wish it, I think we should dispel the growing feeling among the public that the changes suggested by the minister are going to be the answer to the very serious unemployment problem which faces us. I certainly get the feeling that the propaganda machine has been hard at work. I listened to the radio last night, and I am sure the newscast I heard would lead the unemployed to believe that parliament was embarking today on a program that would end unemployment forthwith.
Of course nothing could be further from the truth. First, it would seem that those whose need is greatest can expect little help. Those whose needs are less, and I admit there are few who need less and not more, those whose earnings might have allowed them to accumulate some savings, will gain more. I do think the major changes might have been directed toward helping those whose needs are greatest.
In addition, I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West that we should strenuously oppose restrictions on the rights of those who qualify for retirement under the age rulings in effect in certain industries, and who at present receive benefits for a period of 51 weeks. It is a wonderful help in the stress of transition for older workers. It enables them to adjust to a new setting, to get that cottage in the country, and personally I know of several who have done so. It enables them to settle down without drastic financial shock in moving from a good paying job to a nominal and sometimes inadequate pension.
I realize that unemployment benefits are in no way to be considered as a pension, nor should they be because as far as these people are concerned in nine cases out of ten the national employment service is unable to place older workers who retire at 65 and sometimes at 60. It should be remembered that these older workers cannot get the old age pension until they are 70 years of age. I definitely believe that there should be no cutting down of the 51-week benefit period for this class of recipients. We should be striving with all our power to make the declining years of our elders as pleasant and comfortable as possible.
Another point causes me some concern. It has to do with the requalification requirements. With conditions as they are this
Unemployment Insurance Act spring, I think it can be a very serious matter. I understand that a claimant will have to acquire credit for eight additional weeks in insurable employment since the commencement of his previous benefit year, must have at least 30 contribution weeks in the previous two years, and that contribution weeks more than a year old at the time of a subsequent claim cannot be used a second time to qualify either for rate or duration.
This requirement may have a very serious effect this year. It appears that we may carry a large group of unemployed right through the summer. If improvement is not noted soon, and it is a very big "if", there may be countless unemployed who will be unable to get eight weeks' credit before another autumn slack period closes down on them again. What then? They are out of luck, no matter how long they and their employers may have been contributing to this plan.
That brings me to my final point. It appears that anxiety to maintain individual equities in this scheme makes the whole program of restricted benefit. I think ordinary employers and employees have an entirely different conception of the function of the act than the technicians who draft the legislation. The ordinary layman, whether he be employer or employee, has provided the hard-earned dollars that have gone into the scheme, and it is mostly their money and not the government's. They have provided the money thinking that while they are working they are providing for those who are not, and securing their own future, feeling that if misfortune should strike them someone else will be working to provide for their help. That is, I believe, the basic thinking behind the ordinary insurance scheme, but not so here.
In order to provide effective relief I believe we will have to shake off the shackles of the individual equity requirements. The fund has plenty of money in it. I do not think it is necessary to provide additional help from the public purse, but the fund must be made an effective instrument in order that all those who need help may get it. If we do not make it so, then I think both employer and employee can allege that their money has been taken from them under false pretences.

Ordinarily on a resolution like this we would not try to go into the details of the legislation, but in this instance we have before us the statement of the minister. He opened up the act pretty wide and went into many of its ramifications.

I remember quite well the effort put forth by chambers of commerce, boards of trade, trust companies and others in this country. They put on a lobby in and around the house to prevent the passage of the Unemployment Insurance Act at that time. I remember many people coming to me and, mind you, these were the representatives of the captains of industry who have unemployment on their hands today. They did not want the act passed. They did not want the national employment agencies, and they do not want them now. I have no illusions about where these people stand so far as legislation of this kind is concerned.
Opposition at that time came from many directions. I remember some of those people saying to me that it was not the time to do it. It never is the time to pass social security legislation. They said that we were entering a war, that the financing of that war was going to be a terrific problem to the Canadian people, and this type of legislation would bankrupt the country.
I think the government, particularly the prime minister, showed a good deal of good judgment and courage when the act was introduced. The attitude taken was that if there was any time to embark upon legislation of this kind, that was the time to do it-[DOT] during the war-because there would be full employment. We know there never is unemployment during wartime. It was felt that the war would last for some time and everybody would be working and contributing to the fund, so that it could be built up to serve as a kind of shock absorber when the war was over. Well, that is what happened.
As the minister indicated this afternoon, there is in the fund at the present time over $900 million, and about $1 billion has been paid out in benefits. It seems to me this is a pretty good illustration of the soundness of the economic and social judgment of those who were responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Act. It worked, despite the prophecies of bankruptcy that were made at the time.
I listened to the minister's outline of what he proposes to do and, so far as it goes, I can see nothing wrong with it. He is going [Mr. GiUls.l

to lift the rates from $24 to $30 for recipients with dependents, and he will step up the rate of $17.10 to $23 for those without dependents. That is all very fine for those who have benefit rights. If one is unemployed and has the right to receive benefits, then he will profit by this change. But I would remind the minister that those who need help at this time are the thousands of people across Canada, some of whom have been unemployed for the last two years, who have exhausted their rights to regular and supplementary benefits. They find themselves outside, and they have nowhere to turn.
I suggest to the minister that in some sections of the country there is unemployment to the extent of 100 per cent, and that the industries that formerly employed these people are no longer operating. This is true in many of the textile centres, and it is also true in several coal sections of Nova Scotia. These are the people for whom I thought the minister would do something when amending the act.
While I agree with these increased payments, I say those persons who are not getting anything are the ones who should have received first consideration. The difference between $24 and $30 is not going to make anyone rich. If a man has a family it will not put much more food in his house. If benefits, even to the extent of $24, had been extended to persons in that position until they were gainfully employed again, at least it would have put something into their homes and would have assured a means of livelihood for the families of men in this position. I have in my hand a telegram sent to the leaders of the different parties in the House of Commons on behalf of the Pictou county industrial development committee. It is signed by Mr. A. M. Macintosh and comes from New Glasgow, Nova Scotia. I shall not read it but it says, in effect, that in the area of Pictou county the mine at Westville went out of production, and that 400 or 500 miners and their families at that point are totally unemployed and have no means of employment.
I realize the minister is doing something; I give him credit for that. He is trying to retrain some of the miners for other jobs in other areas, if they can find jobs when they are retrained. The minister knows, too, that the Allan shaft at Stellarton, within a few miles of Westville, went out of commission and about 1,400 employees have been thrown out of work. That whole area is completely and totally unemployed.

The telegram points out that in that area, affecting the towns of New Glasgow, Stellar-ton and Westville, over 1,500 people are receiving benefits, and that those benefits will run out by the 18th of this month. At that point there are 1,500 people who will not have anything after the date I have mentioned, and there is nowhere they can go to find employment.
A few days ago I sat in on the committee on railways and shipping and Trans-Canada Air Lines, and noticed in the capital budget of the Canadian National Railways that huge sums of money were spent and are going to be spent in the building of railway cars, sleepers and freight cars. In the Pictou area, about which I have been talking, there is a large and efficient plant that could build freight cars or sleeping cars or, for that matter, any other type of rolling stock used by the railways. I do not think orders to any extent are placed in that area, but I am wondering if in his spare time the minister might get in touch with his colleague the Minister of Transport to find out if something can be done which would benefit the 1,500 people in this Pictou area. I would ask him to get some orders for the company at Trenton to stimulate the area and create some employment. I leave this with the minister, but mention it only to show him that, while what he is doing is all right for those who have the right to benefits, it does not help those who are totally unemployed.
I do not think it is useful to quibble about responsibility in this matter. Whether we are in the municipalities, in the legislatures or in the House of Commons, as human beings and Canadian citizens it is our duty to do everything we can to see that other citizens in Canada are given at least food, clothing and shelter. In this matter we have hidden far too long behind the British North America Act, particularly in the matter of unemployment insurance, and we are trying to hide behind it again and place the responsibility for employable unemployed on the municipality. Under a constitutional interpretation that is where it is today.
After listening to conferences of mayors across this country for the last five or ten years everyone in the House of Commons knows that practically every municipality in the country is bankrupt. They have no means of taxation except against property. And in every part of the country, in every municipality, the property tax is as high as they dare put it; because if we keep on shoving up municipal taxation we will not find many people willing to buy houses and get their roots into the ground.
