We have taken the right to enact a measure for unemployment insurance. We went over to Westminster and, upon returning, we said, "We have this right." But we have not exercised it; or if it has been exercised, then only to a limited degree. The government has said that it is going to cover a select group in the country and insure them because it is sure most of that group will not be unemployed. The way the fund has grown is a good indication of the truth of my statement.
Let us for a moment consider the railway workers who are steadily employed and who are more or less in sheltered employment. They pay into this fund, but not many of them will get anything out of it. We have covered other industries from which we are reasonably sure there will be continuing contributions. But we have dealt out large numbers of people, those who are called the seasonal unemployed, or the regional unemployed. In many instances the unemployment across the country has lasted long enough to exhaust not only their regular benefits but their supplementaries as well.
I want to tell some hon. members who think this is just a passing phase that in my judgment it is not. The war is over. I hope we shall never see another one, but don't forget that between wars we have always had this static unemployment problem. I can remember it since I was 12 years of age, when there were no cushions against it and it was pretty tough. I can remember the period between 1914 and 1939 when we were down in the depths of the depression struggling and could not get out of it until another war came along, and then we had full employment. While we are praying for peace let us make the necessary preparations, through legislation, to utilize the money and the forces that we mobilize for war by guaranteeing our people at least sufficient to clothe, house and shelter them.
I hear many people talking in this house about building up backward nations. Build them up; but you must realize that as you build up the backward countries to which you are exporting today, they will become exporters. Take India. A few years from now India will be self-sufficient in many things, and we shall not be able to sell her anything. As we build up and raise the standards of these countries to which we are shipping our surpluses today we are putting ourselves in the position, unless we change our tactics, where we shall have surpluses on our shelves and nobody to use them, if

Unemployment Insurance Act we are not prepared to distribute them. That is the kind of world we must look forward to. If we are to have peace in the world and war no longer as the solution of our difficulties or an alternative to unemployment, these are some of the things we have to think about.
I would suggest even yet that the minister's department should give serious consideration, if not under the regular act, to the emergency measures they are prepared to take to lift the load of the employable unemployed off the municipalities, because the municipalities cannot carry it. Many of the provinces cannot carry it without assistance. It is time we got down to business and began to get away from the idea of trying to hide behind constitutions that were written in 1867, and realized our responsibilities to our fellow men as citizens of this country.
It is a sad commentary on human affairs that many of us in this house have seen two wars come and go, and we see the same conditions piling up again when there is no war. Surely we should have learned some lesson from the last two wars. If we can send billions to NATO and millions to the outside world it is pretty nearly time we began to stop talking about unemployment in Canada and began to look after our own people in so far as food, clothing and shelter are concerned.
I should like to bring another specific matter to the attention of the minister. It has to do with the waiting period. I believe the waiting period of five days should be wiped out. The unemployed paid for the five days. They insured themselves against that unemployment. It is insurance they bought and paid for; at least those who are eligible for it did so. They insured themselves against total unemployment, and in those five days they were totally unemployed.
Let me show the minister how it works in some instances. It is not so bad if a person had four or five years' steady employment and then became unemployed. The five-day waiting period is not such a bother in that case. The minister will recall that I have written to him on several occasions on this matter. I have received telegrams and letters from nearly all the mine workers' local unions in Nova Scotia.
From the month of November to April 15 there is no shipping up the St. Lawrence. The insurance is lifted in November and shipping stops. For the last couple of years practically all the mines in Nova Scotia have been working three days a week from November to April 15. The men are 50 per cent unemployed. They cannot draw unemployment insurance because of the five-day waiting period.

This is how the. thing works. You are idle for three days this week. You cannot establish a claim because you are not idle five days. You go to work next week and you work three days, but those three days cannot be charged back to the previous week. You have to establish five days consecutively, unbroken. Despite the fact that the men are idle 50 per cent of the time they cannot establish a claim under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I have written the minister about it; we have talked about it. The last letter I had from him was dated February 15. I sent him a long memorandum that I had received from the executive board of the union to see if something could not be done to iron out the difficulty. The minister said he was checking with the commission to see if the establishment of what we wanted would upset the actuarial plan of the fund. I have not heard any more about it since, but in view of the fact that it has been an active matter for the last couple of months I thought something might have been done under the act with regard to the five waiting days.
If you cannot wipe out the five-day waiting period altogether some regulation should be drawn up to give a special dispensation with respect to the five-day waiting period in such instances as these, or you could make an arrangement under which the three days of this week and the three days of next week could be put together in the two weeks and then the worker would be entitled to at least one day's unemployment insurance. Then, having established their five waiting days, they would not have to re-establish the five waiting days with respect to any unemployment after that. Their claim would be established and they could carry on from there. It is a tangled proposition. It does not happen in all industries though it does happen in some, particularly in the coal mining districts where they have to ship by water.
We shall bring this matter up in committee. The minister can take a look at this again with his officials and be prepared to give us an answer in committee as to whether the suggestions made by the unions are practical or otherwise. I leave it there until the committee is in session.
May I say a word with respect to the national employment offices. There is no doubt about the value of the work they have done. As the minister indicated this afternoon, they have helped in placing some 14 million people in employment sinc'e they were established. That is a big thing in itself. There have been a lot of changes in the act and a lot of extra work has developed since

the offices were set up. I am not so sure that in some of the sections of the country that I know the staff the minister has in these offices is adequate to take care of the job they have to do. The space in some of the offices certainly is not all that is desired. The minister should take a look at them right across the country, because when these offices were established it was pretty much a matter of collecting funds, meeting a few people and sending them out to work. Everyone was looking for people to work at that time.
During the past four or five years a terrific load has been placed on the national employment offices that was not anticipated when they were set up. That is particularly true with respect to space and personnel. I have seen them working night and day in my own area when the coal company decided overnight to place a directive on the radio saying that 1,600 men were to be thrown in the discard tomorrow in a certain area. That is all the notice we get. Then, of course, those offices had to handle those people and try to get them registered and their claims sorted out.
I think you should take a look at the offices. I think a lot of the personnel are greatly underpaid. You have good men in these offices who could get better jobs somewhere else with the qualifications they have. I think you should take a look at their salary ranges. I know some of them who are working for rather small wages when you realize the work they have to do and the responsibility they have to assume.
The manager or the supervisor of employment at these offices takes considerable responsibility and does not get very much help from the big organizations. I am sure that General Motors, Dominion Steel and Coal, Canada Packers and the rest of these fellows do not patronize these offices for their requirements. They run their own show. I think if these offices were accepted for the purposes they were intended to fill and could do the kind of job that was done during the war you would have a much better employment picture in most communities. The national employment offices could question personnel and make out cards listing their qualifications. Then if these industrialists would send in their employment requirements they could at least pick out the right people and put them in the right grooves. But they want to run their own show, with the result that you have a pretty conflicting employment situation in the compact communities where you have large industries. You have two sets of offices trying to deal with the same problem.

As I said in the beginning, most of these people do not want national employment offices anyway. They want to run their own show. When they run it into the ground the only thing they want from the government is subsidies. They get themselves in the hole and then they say that if they are given $65 million they will be able to carry on. Then a word with regard to regulation 5A under section 35 of the act. This is my particular baby, as I suppose I have done more hollering and written more letters in the last five years about it than anyone else in the house. I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West; regulation 5A should be taken out of the act. It is not a regulation, it is a bear trap for married women. I would not mind if it were applied as it was intended to be applied, but here is what happens.
Say a girl is working for the telephone company-I run into a lot of them-and she knows nothing about this regulation. She intends to get married, and her vacation is coming up. A good time to get married and have a honeymoon is during your vacation. She intends to come back to work. She goes and gets married, comes back and works for a few months and finds that nature has played her a trick and she has to stop working. She may have paid unemployment insurance for ten years, and naturally expects that she will get the benefits. But when she makes her application the manager tells her that she cannot get unemployment insurance, that getting married or the result of marriage is not a reason for being unemployed. She is told that she will have to come back to work for 90 days in insurable employment, and then she can obtain unemployment insurance.
I have known of cases where a girl got married, went back to work and worked for three years. Then she stopped work or was let out. I know of several who were let out. When they applied for unemployment insurance the manager told them they could not get it as they had been married three years ago and this was their first job separation. He told them they could not get unemployment insurance unless they went back to work for 90 days in insurable employment. A woman may work three years after marriage, but she cannot get benefits because of

Unemployment Insurance Act regulation 5A. This forces a woman who is going to get married to leave her employment for that purpose, then reapply for employment which she may never get.
This makes for dishonesty, because if an employer will say the girl had been let out because he has a policy against employing married women she can get the benefits under those circumstances. But her employers must lie for her. Or he can say that there was not enough work and they had to let her out. She would then get her unemployment insurance. But if he tells the truth and she tells the truth she is penalized by being refused the benefits of unemployment insurance.
I suggest to the minister that before he finalizes the bill before the committee he lift out regulation 5A. There is no redress from it. I have handled two test cases. I went before the board of referees, but before you can make an appeal to the umpire here in Ottawa you must get a split decision by the board. You have to break the board in two, and I did that twice. I brought the cases right through to the umpire, but it was no use. There is no way around this bear trap, so I suggest that it should just be lifted out and put out of the way. Section 35 as it is without regulation 5A is all right, but in my judgment 5A is all wrong.
I should like to say a few words about the problem of employment as related to technological advances. Automation is the new word now. They always get a smokescreen. If you used the word automation through the country the average worker would think you were talking about one of these little tin men you make run around with electronics. This is merely technological advance. In plain and simple language it means that the machine is replacing man.
When I hear people say that a large public works program is needed my mind goes back to the Canso causeway. The prediction in 1952 was that this would employ 1,500 people and take three years to build. Well, it took 262 people 18 months to do that job with the machinery that was employed. The St. Lawrence seaway is visualized as providing employment for thousands and thousands of people, but just wait until they get at it. With the equipment they have available today they will dig that seaway with so few people in such a short space of time that you will think it was always there. That is not the answer. Public works are simply a palliative or a stop-gap; they may help in some communities, but they do not provide the answer to unemployment.	,
You say that we cannot stop progress. That is fine, but I do not consider it progress when

you are placing thousands and thousands of people permanently in a position where they cannot provide a living for themselves. The figures which are placed on the right side of the balance sheet by the use of equipment in my judgment do not represent the kind of progress we need in this country.
We have to answer this question. If we are going to perfect machinery which is to take the place of man then we must answer the question whether man is going to be the servant of the machine or the machine the servant of man. That is the question we have to answer. The answer to date has been that man is going to be the servant of the machine, but the fact is that there will be a small number of privileged few who will amass great fortunes for themselves and in doing so bring about poverty and misery and degradation for the many.
In the final analysis that is what this question of unemployment boils down to. There are things we can do about it and there are things we will have to do about it. Don't forget that we are always talking about our way of life. Our way of life is the way the average person lives. A fellow who is unemployed who looks at his family starving is not going to take kindly to all this talk about the British North America Act and technological advances and automation and all that sort of stuff. That is not going to satisfy him. If he is hungry he will want something to eat, and he will likely accept any kind of proposition which guarantees that he will get something to eat.
I think Canada and the United States must begin to consider the production we now have and our potential production which will be increased because of the terrific advances we are making in equipment and machinery. We must consider what we are going to do with it, how we will use it and what we will do with our surpluses. We have to start thinking about the establishment of the six-hour day and the reorganization of our working forces across the country to make more employment for more people in order to give those who are working and producing and paying taxes a little more leisure. I think if we were working in a mine, a steel plant or a factory, where one is required to drive at top speed, we would agree that six hours in one of those places is long enough. A little more time should be spent in the sunshine, or in reading or recreation.
More people must be given work. That is the only way we can give the average citizen a share in the progress we are making in the field of automation or technological progress. There is no other way of doing it, and we have to start thinking about it.

I think the guaranteed annual wage is something that has to be taken into consideration. I said that in this house six years ago, long before they began to talk about it in the United States. I said that people who have employment have as much right to a guarantee that they are going to eat seven days a week as the managerial staff and the white-collar staff. The latter have it now. All civil servants have it. Anyone who works for the government has a guaranteed wage, sick leave arrangements and all those things.
In asking for a guaranteed annual wage industry is merely asking for something that is already established in many sections of our society, and I do not think anyone who takes that position is being unreasonable because in the final analysis the fishermen, the miners, the farmers and the workers produce the wealth of the entire country. The others are service organizations and a necessary part of organized society, but without the primary producers there would be no need for managerial or white-collar staffs, or anything else.
I have never forgotten one statement Abraham Lincoln made in his day on that particular subject. He agreed that capital had a right to a return on its investment, but he said that labour had a prior right because labour came first and if it were not for labour there would be no capital. That was the position he took, and I think his statement is equally true today. In my judgment the implementation of the principle he enunciated at that time can be brought about only by the guaranteed annual wage.
Probably there are dangers for the worker in the guaranteed annual wage in that he becomes a partner in the industry and is tied to the bondholders and stockholders and must go along with the industry. However, it might be the instrument that would prevent many of the upheavals which occur every year or two in the renegotiation of contracts; it could serve that purpose. A lot of union men would not like the workers to tie themselves to industry in that way, but I am glad to see that a man like Walter Reuther in the United States is supporting it very strongly, and a certain section of the Canadian unions is also doing so.
I think it would be well for the minister, perhaps through an interdepartmental committee, to look at the question of the six-hour day and the guaranteed annual wage, and to do some research on it; because it has to come and it will come and we should bring it about in a sensible, organized way based on good solid research, as was done when the Unemployment Insurance Act was created.

Another thing which I think the department should be thinking about in the field of social security is a national retirement allowance. I have said that in this house a good many times. The types of industrial pension which we have today are a means by which we throw away a good many millions of dollars. Every industry whether big or small has its own little pension plan under our present system, and none of them is adequate. The pittance they pay means very little at the end of the trail and although hundreds of millions of dollars are invested in them I think they serve little purpose.
I said a long time ago that there is only one way we can adequately cover the people of this country with a retiring allowance, and that is by the means used in establishing the old age security fund. If it is negotiated with those who are affected I am convinced they will turn over the funds they have invested today and use them as the basis for a national retiring allowance, and then everybody can be covered by taxation. It might cost 6 per cent, which is the average percentage of my income contributed during the time I am working, to give me a retiring allowance of $100 or $125 a month. I think every worker in this country would be prepared to pay it. It could be put in the hands of a branch like the annuities branch, people who are competent and capable of handling that type of thing. Then when I reached age 65 I would retire and would have the guarantee of the government behind me. I would receive my cheque regularly, just as pension cheques and family allowance cheques are distributed regularly. That would represent real security and it is the only way we can adequately cover the people of this country.
I have made that statement several times in past sessions, and as a result I have received a great many letters from small industrialists in Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia and other sections of the country. Their letters told me to keep on pushing for that kind of allowance because they felt I was on the right track. They said that they as small industries find themselves in the position that they cannot offer the kind of pensions offered by large companies. They said they would like to protect their workers but cannot, but under the scheme I advocated they could contribute through taxation and cover their workers in the way they would like to do it. They said this would bring uniformity right across the country, and everyone would know they had a guarantee with regard to retiring allowances.
As it is today the pensions established in industry are only as secure as the balance sheet of the industry, and many of them are

Unemployment Insurance Act going into liquidation after workers have paid into the plan for years. When the company fails and there are a lot of men approaching retiring age there is nothing for the men and they receive no return on their contribution. I have seen it happen in industries close to where I live. That is another matter the department should take a look at.
If we are going to retain the kind of society we have, then we have to start doing that kind of thing. We cannot continue as we have for the last two generations, when we had unemployment, misery, poverty and no future for the youth of the country who were .the lost generation between the last two wars, riding box cars from coast to coast. No one assumed responsibility for them. We cannot carry on like that any further.
Many promises were made after the last war, but we are on the same trail we were on in 1939, prior to the second world war. We cannot go on like that. We have to start measuring up and introducing social changes. War is no longer going to be an alternative in this country or in the United States in relation to the question of decent living standards.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have said more than I intended to say. I could continue to talk for hours on this particular subject, but I shall allow my case to rest there.

Relating that to the matter of unemployment insurance, the average workingman receiving $300 a month or more does not need insurance to cover him for one month or three months. I submit what he needs is insurance that will cover him for one year, two years or three years. When we come to the regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act we find that the workingman does not have any insurance against the situation for which he needs insurance. He has insurance for one month and, if I understood the minister correctly, up to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 11 months, but he does not have insurance to take care of the situation for which he really needs insurance. It is just the same as in the field of health, and all the private health and hospital insurance schemes are alike in this regard. They will not give you insurance to cover the situation for which you really need insurance. They will only insure you to a limited extent. So too the government of Canada only provides insurance for the unemployed for a limited period, a period during which they might easily get by on their own.
I regret the continued demands for eliminating this waiting period or that waiting period. The unemployed people of Canada need insurance for something for which the government is unwilling to give them insurance. They need insurance to cover long-term unemployment. If the minister thinks this does not apply to the average worker, may I say that it certainly does apply to the unemployed worker once he has reached the age of 40 or over, or even 35 or over.
We have had unemployment insurance for some time now, and it is about time we revised our attitude toward it. First of all, we do not want insurance; we want employment. We want employment at decent wages. And second, if we have unemployment insurance, then we want to have it payable not until the benefits expire but until employment is again found for us.

Mr. Chairman, the hour is getting late and I am not going to speak at length. I must say I listened with interest to the minister's statement on this resolution. However, it is usually my practice to read such statements so I am quite clear on what has been said.
I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Cape Breton South have placed the position of this group clearly before the committee. I did enjoy the historical review of the evolution of
[Mr. Regier.l
unemployment legislation given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. While he was giving it I was inclined to think in terms of the past, and my thoughts went back 50 years and to the tortuous path the federal government has taken in accepting the responsibility for labour legislation.
In the early days of this century the federal government accepted certain responsibility in connection with legislation for unions, as applying to workers within the provinces. Then in 1903 a royal commission was set up by the federal government to investigate strikes and serious labour troubles occurring in the gold mining and hard rock mining industries of British Columbia, as well as among carpenters and workers on the railways. That commission went to British Columbia and after some months made a report to the House of Commons. I might add that the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King was secretary to that commission. The concluding paragraph of the commission's report, it seems to me, does indicate the great improvement in our outlook toward labour problems. The concluding paragraph of this report, which dealt with industrial disputes in the province of British Columbia, is in these words:
At the same time we feel quite free to admit that, while much good can be accomplished by wise legislation, the labour problem, so-called, is incapable of final solution, and that it will be with us as long as human nature remains what it is, and present civilization endures.
I think there is a very different outlook today toward labour problems, and since that time we have made a great deal of progress. In this report, which was presented to the House of Commons, the commissioners recommended that labour disputes in British Columbia go before the exchequer court and be dealt with there.
This calls to mind an early experience of the former prime minister in my constituency. He was sent out there, as deputy minister, to act as conciliation officer in a dispute between the western federation of miners and certain mining companies in Rossland, British Columbia. I remember reading in the newspapers about his trip. I thought the Rossland paper stated the situation rather well when, adopting-the crisp form of news reporting followed by those early weekly papers, it said:
A roly-poly man with a cherubic face, in a bowler hat, riding a scraggy nag arrived in Rossland. He was the deputy minister of labour, Mr. Mackenzie King.
This would seem to indicate that at that time the federal government accepted some responsibility for labour problems involving men who were not employed in national industries.

Then we have seen, in the lapse of years, a change in the situation. It has been found necessary to change the constitution before the workingmen of Canada could get unemployment insurance. Possibly the minister will be able to explain the reason for this changed situation. This change became even more interesting to me because of the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I should like now to place before the minister certain anomalies I have found in the act, in my experience. A good many persons have brought the matter to my attention, and t shall bring it before the House of Commons.
I refer to the position of men who work in forestry in British Columbia. These men are found in quite large numbers in the central part of the province, and I presume there are many of them in other parts. They go out on duties such as surveys, or felling snags, or burning brush, or slashing, or any other work required in the conservation of timber. While the cooks in the camp who cook for them, or the carpenters who build their camps, or the men who build the trails for the various roads are covered by unemployment insurance, those men who work at felling the timber, cutting the logs, slashing the brush or burning it are not covered by the act.
In this connection I wish to read a letter which outlines clearly what I have in mind. Before doing so, however, let me pay tribute to the local management of the national employment service in my district, particularly in recent years. The manager there has done excellent work in visiting small communities and attending meetings of the Legion, trade unions, various institutes or lumbermen's organizations, and has taken great pains to explain the regulations and how applications should be sent in. These visits have been most helpful and have cut down the loss of time that formerly occurred because forms were filled out improperly because those who filled them out did not understand the regulations and the procedure.
The letter I have before me was written by the manager of the local employment office in reply to a young man who had worked during the summer at cutting logs and felling trees, who eventually became unemployed and expected to receive unemployment insurance. This was the letter he received:
Dear Sir:
We refer to your letter of January 25, 1954.
We regret the delay in answering your letter. The delay was due to the fact that we requested an official ruling from Ottawa in respect to your case.
4, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act
This, may I say, is only one case of a good many.
As we previously stated to you, your employment with the B.C. forest service was considered as employment in forestry, and therefore not insurable.
For your information, we quote an extract from the letter received from Ottawa:
"As you have told Mr. Rogers, employment in forestry is not one of the employments at present covered by the act. It is specified as an excepted employment in part II of the schedule to the act. The expression 'employment in forestry' is interpreted as meaning the cultivation of forests, the management of growing timber and the prevention of forest fires. To ensure uniformity of interpretation throughout the province, we have determined with the concurrence of the British Columbia forest service the classes of employees of this department who are to be insured and those who should not be insured. Thus clerical staff, research workers, draftsmen, truck and tractor operators, mechanics, carpenters, dispatchers, and scalers are insured because they are not directly engaged in forestry work."
In my opinion this is a most hair-splitting decision. It continues:
"On the other hand, foresters, lookout men, rangers, patrolmen, cruisers, fire suppression crewmen, and those engaged in tree planting and clearing brush, etc., are, of course, not insured as this work is actual forestry.
Mr. Rogers and his crew were engaged in clearing brush after logging operations. This is an operation classed as forestry and the employment was not insurable. Cooks, like carpenters and mechanics, are not engaged in a forestry occupation. They are tradesmen engaged in their own trade and are properly insured."
In view of the above information, we feel that your standing in respect to unemployment insurance coverage should be quite clear.
I bring that to the minister's attention because it does work a hardship on a good number of men, and the very men who do the casual work. The men who are covered are, on the whole, year-round employees of the forestry service of British Columbia; but the men who are hired in the summertime to go out and clear up the debris to prevent fires, and who in some cases do the slashing and tree-top lopping of timber in areas in which private operators had been working, do work identical with that which is being done by men who work in the woods. Under the present regulations under the act they are not covered. I bring this to the minister's attention because it does work a hardship on a good number of men who are employed in that work for possibly eight or ten months every year and are then laid off; whereas most of those who are employed throughout the year are covered by the act.
I ask the minister to look into the question because there is an absurdity in the definition or application of the word "forestry".

Mr. Chairman, in listening to this very interesting debate I realize that the hon. member for Cape Breton South and

Unemployment Insurance Act I are the only two of those who have spoken who were here in 1940 when the legislation was passed, though quite a number of other hon. members on both sides of the house were here at that time.
Hon. members who were here then will recall that June 25, 1940, was a pretty black day. The Germans had overrun the low countries and France, and everyone was quite worried about the future. However, the government of the day, anxious to get the very best from Canada's working force, felt that unemployment insurance should be made law. While members of all parties gave enthusiastic support to this legislation, yet it is obvious from the present problem that confronts Canada that this proposal is not adequate. I am sure no one is going to oppose it, but if this is the government's major answer to Canada's present unemployment problem, it just is not good enough.
The hon. member for Vancouver South suggested that the provinces have a real interest and responsibility in this field. I would like to remind the house that on June 25, 1940, the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, in introducing the resolution that asked Westminster to change the British North America Act, said, as reported at page 1109 of Hansard:
And whereas, if a uniform and effective system of compulsory unemployment insurance is to be adopted throughout Canada, it will be necessary to amend the British North America Act, 1867, to enable the parliament of Canada to enact the necessary legislation;-
In due course section 91 of the British North America Act was amended by adding thereto as class 2A the following:
2A. Unemployment insurance.
Section 91 of the British North America Act reads-I shall not read the whole paragraph-
-and for greater certainty but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:-
Then it gives a list of 29 fields such as the following: postal service, the census and statistics and, of course, unemployment insurance. As it stands now, under the British North America Act no province would be permitted to pass unemployment insurance legislation even if such province had the funds, and I think it is pretty obvious that since the provinces and the municipalities get such a small share of the taxpayer's dollar to spend they would not be able to

undertake the responsibility of dealing with the unemployment situation we now have in Canada.
In another debate the hon. member for Saskatoon said something about the leakage that is involved in connection with public works projects. For example, if the government of Saskatchewan were to undertake the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam, we shall say at a cost of $100 million, not more than $25 million of the total would be of any assistance to the province of Saskatchewan in providing work with wages or business for the business organizations of that province. About half the amount would benefit other provinces of Canada, and almost 25 per cent of the total would benefit places other than Canada. Since the country in which we live is dependent upon each section, I think it was quite right that in 1940 we should have changed the British North America Act to make it perfectly clear that the federal government should have the responsibility for dealing with the problem of unemployment.
Several of my colleagues have referred to the guaranteed annual income. Tomorrow night the Minister of Finance is going to bring down the budget, which is looked forward to with a great deal of interest. Representations have been made to the minister that he reduce the income tax. I for one have never made such representations to him, and indeed I have said there are a great many more people in Canada who are worrying because they cannot pay income tax than are worrying because the income tax is too high.
Those who are paying income tax are granted certain exemptions. A single person has an exemption of $1,000 and a married person of $2,000. Since we have accepted that principle for so many years we should also accept the principle that every person in Canada should have a guaranteed income, that no one should have to live on less than a certain amount. I am not going to say what that amount should be, but if we are to have for income tax purposes an exemption of $2,000 for married persons and $1,000 for single persons, we should decide that the economy of Canada will stand an income for every person of the country.
The automobile industry has been mentioned. Walter Reuther, of the United Automobile Workers, emphasized in Cleveland the other day that the industry should be prepared to guarantee an annual income to everyone in the automobile industry. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that the general manager, all directors, the sales staff, and all the office workers in that industry now have a guaranteed annual

income. I submit that the machinists and the mechanics who do the work in the factories, and are just as necessary to produce automobiles as are the officials, should have a guaranteed annual income provided by this industry as a part of the cost of producing automobiles.
In the white paper today the Minister of Finance mentioned that last year the gross national product was worth around $24 billion. If my arithmetic is correct that works out to about $1,600 for every man, woman and child in the country. We can face the fact that we can increase this amount or we can decrease it. We can increase the $24 billion by making it possible for every ablebodied person in Canada to perform some useful work. I submit that while the Minister of Labour has not been charged with this responsibility so far, he should ask his colleagues to give him the wider powers and the necessary funds so he can bring in legislation in order that the 600,000 people who are now in the ranks of the unemployed might look forward to finding a chance to do some creative work.
It is as plain as a, b, c. If the 600,000 people are given a chance to do creative work the gross national product next year will be a good deal higher than the $24 billion mentioned by the Minister of Finance. On the radio the other night the hon. member for Nanaimo mentioned that the gross national product was down about $600 million as a result of the failure of the wheat crop in the prairie provinces. That factor is having a very direct effect on the unemployment problem. Farmers who lost their crops last year or those who have not been able to sell their crops are not included in the 600,000 in the ranks of the unemployed, but many of those farmers are in a position where they are denied the privilege of buying their fair share of the goods available in Canada. I submit that the municipal and provincial authorities cannot cope with this problem, but in my opinion the federal government can deal with the problem of the farm population receiving $600 million less in the way of purchasing power.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I had finished with that and I am going to conclude promptly. In conclusion I would like to remind the cabinet particularly that when this legislation was passed originally the then minister of finance announced the theory that whatever is physically possible will be made financially possible. That was a sound financial theory, and it is equally sound today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do ask the hon. member to co-operate. We really are not discussing the general outlines of financial systems; we are discussing whether it is expedient to amend and consolidate the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would ask the hon. member to help to keep the discussion somewhere on the track.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I am concluding. I think the minister should recommend to the committee that necessary amendments be made to the legislation so he can deal with the problem of the other people who are unemployed but who are not going to be covered by this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I assure you that I am going to speak to the motion now before us as to the advisability of amending and consolidating the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am certain in my own mind that practically all the workers in Canada will welcome the progressive amendments which were outlined to this committee this afternoon and which will be included in the bill the minister proposes to bring in to amend and consolidate the Unemployment Insurance Act.
However, in listening to the minister this afternoon I must admit that I was somewhat puzzled by certain phases of his explanation as to the policies and amendments he had in mind. As we are in committee stage on the resolution I would like to deal with about three of those phases which are giving me some puzzlement and which I think most definitely should be clarified before we have the actual introduction and second reading of the bill, in order that the Minister of Labour can give us a clearer understanding
